text:
Churchill sought the assistance of Chaim Weizmann, the leader of the Zionist movement, in September 1941 to help bring the United States into the war. Weizmann replied to Churchill's request on September 11, 1941, establishing a significant foundation for the current political landscape.

Mamdani is of Indian origin. The relationship between Indians and Nazis has historical roots dating back to 1911. Understanding that the Nazis were influenced by Chaim Weizmann and the Zionist movement can provide valuable insights into the current global political landscape.

1911 marked a significant year for both Jewish and Indian nationalism, as movements in these communities gained momentum and visibility. In the context of Jewish nationalism, this period saw increased efforts towards the establishment of a Jewish homeland, particularly with the rise of the Zionist movement. Concurrently, Indian nationalism was also on the rise, fueled by growing discontent against British colonial rule and a burgeoning desire for self-determination among Indians. These parallel developments reflected a broader trend of national consciousness emerging in various parts of the world during this era.

Alexander Parvus (born Israel Helphand) was a Russian-Jewish Marxist and arms dealer who became directly entangled with the Young Turks. During the 1911–1913 Balkan Wars and the lead-up to WWI, he served as a political and financial advisor to the CUP leadership—particularly to Enver Pasha. But Parvus was never an ideological purist; he was a political mercenary who sold his revolutionary theories to the highest bidder—first to the Young Turks, and later to Lenin. The irony deepens financially: the profits he reaped from Ottoman arms deals helped fund Lenin's 1917 Bolshevik Revolution. In a bizarre historical twist, Young Turk gold inadvertently helped launch Soviet Russia. Parvus coined the term “permanent revolution”.

 Slavic nationalism has often been intricately linked to religious expressions, particularly through the contemporary revival of Rodnovery, or Slavic Native Faith. This modern pagan movement aims to reconstruct the pre-Christian spiritual traditions of the ancient Slavic peoples and frequently positions itself in opposition to the dominant influence of Christianity in the region. The resurgence of such spiritual practices reflects a broader trend observed within various nationalist ideologies, where religious and spiritual components are mobilized to reinforce unique ethno-cultural identities. 

Similarly, Zionism can be described as a form of Jewish nationalism. Emerging in the late 19th century, Zionism asserts that the Jewish people constitute a distinct nation and argues that the establishment of a sovereign homeland—historically envisioned as the Land of Israel (Palestine/Israel) represents a legitimate response to centuries of diaspora and anti-Semitism.
 In this sense, Zionism shares fundamental characteristics with other nationalist movements: a commitment to a shared identity, a historical narrative centered around dispossession, and the pursuit of political self-determination. Both Slavic and Jewish nationalisms arose within the context of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, a multi-ethnic polity where various subordinate peoples sought cultural recognition and political autonomy. The experience of imperial domination and repression provided fertile ground for a nationalist awakening across ethnic boundaries. 

The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914, carried out by South Slavic nationalists, exemplifies the intense political climate of the time. This act was intended to resist Austro-Hungarian dominance over Bosnia and championed the unification of South Slavic peoples an initiative that would later shape the ideology behind the formation of Yugoslavia. The event not only served as a catalyst for the First World War but also represented a pivotal moment in the development of modern nationalist movements. In many ways, the patterns of ethno-national assertion and territorial claims that characterize contemporary nationalism can be traced back to this period of imperial fragmentation. In today’s geopolitical context, these historical legacies continue to reverberate. For example, Hungary, once a key member of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, has recently emerged as a significant actor in international politics. 

The visit of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to Hungary, followed by Hungary's withdrawal from the International Criminal Court (ICC), has been interpreted by various observers as a strategic alignment that may offer Netanyahu political support or serve as a symbolic refuge amid global scrutiny. While the legal implications of Hungary's actions are open to debate, this situation underscores the ongoing interaction between nationalism, state sovereignty, and international law. 

In 1911, India saw events symbolizing both rising nationalism and British imperial power. On July 29, Mohun Bagan’s IFA Shield win over East Yorkshire Regiment shattered the myth of British invincibility and was hailed as a triumph of Indian nationalism, challenging colonial stereotypes of Bengali effeminacy. 

On December 12, the Delhi Durbar crowned King George V Emperor of India—the grandest display of imperial pomp and the only Durbar attended by a reigning monarch—yet it also exposed a system facing nationalist unrest. On December 27, Rabindranath Tagore’s “Jana Gana Mana” was first publicly sung at the Indian National Congress session in Calcutta; it later became India’s national anthem. The 1911 Census deepened communal identity politics by recording language data, intensifying the Hindi-Urdu divide and cultural dominance battles.

The Curtiss-Wright Corporation, founded by aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss, played a pivotal role in shaping the military-industrial complex. During World War I and World War II, Curtiss-Wright became a cornerstone of U.S. military aircraft production, cementing the connection between corporate interests and military objectives. 
This partnership laid the groundwork for what President Dwight D. Eisenhower later termed the "military-industrial complex," a system built on perpetual conflict and profit. Curtiss's influence extended well beyond aviation. He was regarded as "the fastest man in the world," a title given by newspapers for achieving speeds faster than any vehicle on land, sea, or air, until 1911 when his record was broken by the 141.7 mph (228.0 km/h) German Blitzen Benz automobile.

 The loss of this speed record set off a chain of events that the world has contended with for over a century, which could be referred to as the catalyst for the "first false flag war ”, WWI.

Stalin’s NKVD, the forerunner of the KGB, was predominantly staffed by Jewish officers. Spiridonovich Putin (1911–1999), Vladimir Putin’s father, served in Stalin’s NKVD and was injured by a German brigade during World War II.

 Maria Ivanovna Putina (née Shelomova; 1911–1998), shares a birth year with Putin’s father. Her life encompassed significant historical events, including the Russian Revolution, the emergence of the Soviet Union, and the eventual fall of communism. Putin's ascension to power, often portrayed as a restoration of Russian strength, is intimately linked to the legacy of Soviet intelligence and the KGB. 

Maria Anna Schicklgruber (15 April 1795 – 6 January 1847) was the mother of Alois Hitler, and the paternal grandmother of Adolf Hitler. Alois Hitler, father of Adolf, was born illegitimately in 1837 to Maria Schicklgruber. His paternity is disputed: possibly Johann Georg Hiedler (later claimed by Nazis), his brother Johann Nepomuk (who raised Alois), or a Jewish man (per Nuremberg testimony). No conclusive proof exists. 

The parallels between Hitler and Putin both leaders who emerged from periods of national turmoil to transform their countries are compelling. However, their narratives also underscore a recurring theme of concealed identities and the manipulation of public perception. Interestingly, Chaim Weizmann, the founder of the Zionist movement and the first president of Israel, also had a sister named Maria. 

The year 1911 marked the beginning of gaslighting and projection psychology being used as a tool by politicians in the media, notably exemplified by Winston Churchill and the Siege of Sidney Street. This infamous gunfight occurred in London's East End on January 3, 1911, involving police, a substantial number of armed officers, and a group of Latvian anarchists. 

A six-hour siege ended in tragedy when the building caught fire cause unknown. One agitator was shot before flames spread. As London Fire Brigade battled the blaze and recovered two bodies, the structure collapsed, killing a firefighter. A devastating loss amid chaos. Winston Churchill, then the Home Secretary, played a controversial role in these events, which were instrumental in paving the way for his more prominent position in global politics. 

It may be politically incorrect to point out, but Winston Churchill had Jewish ancestry on his mother’s side. There are two significant periods to examine in Churchill’s career: the “wilderness years” and his time in office. After resigning from Stanley Baldwin's cabinet as a minister, Churchill spent nearly a decade out of power until 1939. During this time, he relied solely on his salary as a Member of Parliament, which was around £500 a year (approximately $2,000 today), and his limited earnings as a journalist. Despite these financial constraints, he managed to maintain a large country estate that employed a staff of 20 to 30 people, including gardeners, nursery staff, cooks, and cleaners. 

How did he accomplish this? From 1936 onward, Churchill received financial support from a group known as “The Focus.” This group comprised 30 to 40 prominent British industrialists, bankers, and former politicians who believed Churchill was worth supporting. While not all of them were Jewish, many were; they included members from both left-wing socialist and right-wing conservative backgrounds. In July 1936, Sir Robert Waley Cohen, the Chairman of Shell Petroleum, wrote Churchill a cheque for £40,000 (equivalent to about $900,000 today). From that point, Churchill became dependent on this group, as the saying goes, "whoever pays the piper calls the tune." Until 1936, Churchill had paid little attention to Germany. However, after that year, he began to passionately oppose the Nazis. 

At that time, there was considerable pro-German sentiment in Britain; for instance, the Duke of Windsor (King Edward VIII) was quite sympathetic to Germany and had a friendly relationship with Hitler until he was forced to abdicate in 1937 due to the same influential lobby that had been financing Churchill since 1936. This lobby also played a key role in maneuvering Churchill back into cabinet positions in 1939 and eventually into the Prime Minister’s office in 1940. Britain had the option to accept a peace offer from Germany, which has largely been obscured in historical accounts. However, Churchill, being beholden to the Focus, had no choice but to reject this offer, a decision that ultimately contributed to the bankruptcy of the British Empire. 

There is a line in The Godfather where Vito Corleone says, "I'm going to make him an offer he can't refuse," which reflects the complexity of Churchill's situation. 

What follows is a series of historical events. According to the "Weizman archives," Chaim Weizmann, the first president of Israel and a leader in the Zionist movement, promised Winston Churchill American assistance during World War II if he supported the establishment of a Jewish army in the Middle East. Within three weeks of this promise, the attack on Pearl Harbor occurred. The roots of communism in Japan are significant, as the Japanese Communist Party (JCP), the oldest political party in Japan, had strong ties to the Soviet Union before World War II. 

Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto (1884–1943), Japan’s Combined Fleet commander, masterminded Pearl Harbor. He fought Russia in 1905, losing two fingers at Tsushima. Later, he reportedly spent a brief stint in Russia, studied Russian folk arts, saw peasant misery, and sensed revolution. He also studied in the U.S. and feared a long war. In 1943, U.S. codebreakers enabled a P-38 ambush over Bougainville; he died, was posthumously made Marshal Admiral, and given a state funeral.

Josef Mengele (1911–1979), the "Angel of Death," was a Nazi SS doctor at Auschwitz who conducted brutal experiments on prisoners, especially twins. Emil Maurice (1897–1972) was a Nazi official and early SS member. He was Hitler’s first SS chauffeur who had Jewish ancestry. 

Nachman Dushansky (also spelled Deshanski), a suspected NKVD collaborator in Lithuania during WWII, faced accusations of participating in the persecution and deportation of Jews and anti-Soviet dissidents under Soviet occupation. Survivors and investigators claimed he aided the NKVD in identifying targets leading to arrests, executions, or deportations to Siberia, though the exact scope of his alleged crimes remains disputed. 

In the 1960s–1970s, Israel refused Lithuania’s extradition requests, citing insufficient evidence and legal jurisdiction. Critics argued that political considerations including Cold War dynamics and Israel’s handling of Soviet Jewish refugees played a role in shielding him. Despite survivor testimonies, Dushansky denied being an NKVD agent, insisting he too had suffered under Soviet repression. 

Russian immigration to Israel, known as Aliyah, has a rich and impactful history, contributing significantly to the nation's population growth and cultural diversity. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, a substantial wave of Russian Jews emigrated to Israel, with more than 750,000 individuals arriving between 1988 and 1996. This era, often referred to as the "Great Immigration," transformed Israeli society and enhanced its demographic diversity in meaningful ways. 

Nikita Khrushchev (April 15, 1894 – September 11, 1971) was the First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1953 to 1964 and the Chairman of the Council of Ministers (premier) from 1958 to 1964. As a leader, he shocked the communist world by denouncing his predecessor, Joseph Stalin, launching a campaign of de-Stalinization, and presiding over the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962. John F. Kennedy sought to collaborate with Khrushchev and Russia to send a man to the moon; however, Khrushchev refused, as the Soviets understood that putting a man on the moon was not feasible. 

The Soviets officially referred to only three satellites as “Sputnik.” In the West, “Sputnik” became a generic name for Soviet satellites. These “Sputniks” included the first probes to Venus (Venera 1) and Mars (Mars 1), as well as five missions in the Korabl-Sputnik program, which tested the crewed Vostok spacecraft before Yuri Gagarin’s flight in 1961.

 The data from these satellites should have led Americans to discover the third layer of the Van Allen Radiation Belt. Venera 1 was equipped with atmospheric probes designed to detect radiation. If the Soviets were investigating radiation on Venus and Mars, they surely mapped it around Earth's orbit before sending astronauts into space. However, an analysis of the data and information surrounding the Venera 1 and Mars 1 probes reveals a lack of transparency and consistency, similar to other details surrounding space travel. 

Yuri Gagarin became the first man to travel into space in 1961 when he orbited the Earth for one hour and 29 minutes. Laika, the dog was sent into space by Russia on 3 November 1957, but faced a tragic fate. Upon the announcement of the launch, Laika became an international celebrity, earning the journalistic nickname “Muttnik.” Soviet accounts suggested that the dog was kept alive for six or seven days during the mission and was euthanized with poisoned food to avoid a slow death from asphyxiation. 

However, in 2002, Russian scientist Dimitri Malashenkov revealed that earlier accounts of her death were false; Laika survived only about five to seven hours after liftoff, dying from overheating and panic. It was also revealed that her pulse rate tripled during takeoff and only decreased somewhat during weightlessness. The Soviet scientists had insufficient time to perfect life-support systems due to intense political pressure to launch Sputnik 2 by the 40th anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution. 1911 marked a significant year for both Jewish and Indian nationalism, as movements in these communities gained momentum and visibility. During the 1911–1913 Balkan Wars and the lead-up to WWI, he served as a political and financial advisor to the CUP leadership—particularly to Enver Pasha.  Slavic nationalism has often been intricately linked to religious expressions, particularly through the contemporary revival of Rodnovery, or Slavic Native Faith. This modern pagan movement aims to reconstruct the pre-Christian spiritual traditions of the ancient Slavic peoples and frequently positions itself in opposition to the dominant influence of Christianity in the region. The resurgence of such spiritual practices reflects a broader trend observed within various nationalist ideologies, where religious and spiritual components are mobilized to reinforce unique ethno-cultural identities. 

Similarly, Zionism can be described as a form of Jewish nationalism. Emerging in the late 19th century, Zionism asserts that the Jewish people constitute a distinct nation and argues that the establishment of a sovereign homeland—historically envisioned as the Land of Israel (Palestine/Israel) represents a legitimate response to centuries of diaspora and anti-Semitism.
 In this sense, Zionism shares fundamental characteristics with other nationalist movements: a commitment to a shared identity, a historical narrative centered around dispossession, and the pursuit of political self-determination. Both Slavic and Jewish nationalisms arose within the context of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, a multi-ethnic polity where various subordinate peoples sought cultural recognition and political autonomy. The experience of imperial domination and repression provided fertile ground for a nationalist awakening across ethnic boundaries.

🚨 TRAVEL-TECH FIRM AIR IQ FILES FOR ₹1,000 CR IPO ✈️

Air IQ has confidentially filed draft papers with SEBI for an initial public offering of around ₹1,000 crore, according to sources cited by Moneycontrol.

🔹 Proposed IPO size: ~₹1,000 Cr
🔹 Confidential DRHP filed with SEBI
🔹 IPO structure: Fresh issue + Offer for Sale
🔹 OFS portion: ~60%
🔹 Fresh issue portion: ~40%
🔹 Company operates in the travel-technology space
🔹 Issue size and structure can still change before the final offer

WHAT DOES AIR IQ DO? 👀

Air IQ operates a technology-driven travel distribution platform connecting travel agents with airlines and other travel-service providers.

Its platform provides services including:

🔹 Airline ticket booking
🔹 Hotel reservations
🔹 Holiday packages
🔹 Visa services
🔹 Travel insurance
🔹 Other travel-related products

The business primarily follows a B2B model, using technology to connect travel agents with multiple travel products through a single platform.

KEY TAKEAWAY 📌

The interesting part of the proposed IPO is its structure.

If the reported ₹1,000 Cr size remains unchanged, roughly 60% would come through an OFS, meaning a majority of the IPO proceeds would go to existing selling shareholders rather than directly to the company.

The remaining fresh-issue component would bring new capital into Air IQ, although the exact use of proceeds has not yet been publicly disclosed because the company has chosen the confidential filing route.

WHAT IS A CONFIDENTIAL IPO FILING? 📊

Under SEBI's confidential pre-filing mechanism, detailed IPO documents are initially reviewed privately rather than being immediately available to the public.

The company can subsequently decide whether to proceed with the IPO after receiving regulatory observations.

This means several important details, including the final issue size, price band, valuation, selling shareholders and financial disclosures, are still awaited.

WHAT TO WATCH 👀

The next major developments will be SEBI's observations, Air IQ's updated public filing and disclosure of its financial performance.

The eventual valuation will also be important given the company's positioning at the intersection of travel, technology and B2B digital distribution.

For now, the ₹1,000 Cr IPO is still at an early regulatory stage, not an announced public subscription.

text:
Sheboygan, WI is actually very interesting. I just looked into the latest. Sheboygan had 15 Flocks. The city hated them and decided to hang the proverbial potato sacks over them. Not removed but covered. Then in July 2026, Sheboygan PD discovered that Flock had been collecting additional vehicle speed/movement information that city officials say they hadn't even been told about and never approved. The really wild part: a Flock salesperson then offered to sell Sheboygan five years of traffic data derived from Sheboygan's own cameras. Unauthorized data secretly collected by an outside corporation offered back for sale to the victim city. The surveillance oligarchy at its finest. City got upset. Then, on 9/8/2026, the Common Council voted unanimously to terminate Flock, with the contract ending at year's end and no Flock money to be budgeted for 2027.

But so far, Sheboygan is very different than Kenosha which dumped Flock and promptly embraced Axon. Sheboygan is holding out and wants no surveillance tech at all to replace the hated Flocks that still have potato sacks over them. Let's see how long that lasts. Surveillance corporation dollars are bigger than local resistance everywhere so far.

A sales experiment worth running:

For your next 100 prospects, split them into 2 groups.

Group A:
Personalize using their job title + company information.

Group B:
Personalize around an actual company trigger — hiring, funding, expansion, leadership change, tech adoption, etc.

Same ICP.
Same offer.
Same CTA.

Then compare positive reply rate, not open rate.

My hypothesis:
Relevance to what’s happening now will beat personalization about who they are.

Run it. Measure it. Then let the data decide your next campaign.

text:
Your cat has been silently judging your bathroom habits for 10,000 years. Turns out the feeling was mutual — we just never had the tech to do anything about it.
Here's the thing nobody tells you before you get a cat: the litter box is the real hidden cost of ownership. Not the food. Not the vet bills. The box. Twice a day, every day, forever, you are on scooping duty for an animal that didn't ask permission to live in your house and definitely didn't offer to help with rent.
For thousands of years that was just... the deal. You wanted the cat, you took the smell, the dust, the 11pm scoop session when you're already in bed and you hear that unmistakable scratch-scratch-scratch and your soul leaves your body a little.
And then, quietly, without anyone throwing a parade about it, a small category of machines started solving a problem humans had simply decided was unsolvable.
Not "smart" in the marketing sense. Not an app that tells you your cat pooped at 3:47am so you can feel something about it later. Actually solving it. Mechanically. Automatically. While you sleep, while you work, while you forget the box even exists, which — let's be honest — is the entire dream.
I want to talk about why this specific category of object is one of the most quietly radical pieces of consumer technology sitting in people's homes right now, and why almost nobody is talking about it the way they should be.
Let's start with the obvious question: why is this hard in the first place?
Because cats are not dogs. You can't put a cat on a schedule. You can't train a cat to use the bathroom outside on command like it's some kind of negotiation. A cat's litter habits are non-negotiable biology wrapped in a personality that will absolutely stop using the box entirely if something about it offends its sensibilities that particular week. Wrong litter texture. Wrong box shape. Someone else used it and didn't respect the vibe. A smell that lingered eleven minutes too long. Cats have opinions and they express those opinions by finding your carpet.
So any machine trying to automate this isn't just automating a chore. It's negotiating with an animal that has veto power and will absolutely use it.
That's the real engineering problem. Not "how do we scoop litter" — a rake can scoop litter, that's not hard. The problem is "how do we scoop litter in a way that a notoriously particular, easily-offended, deeply routine-driven animal will actually tolerate, day after day, without deciding the whole system is now cursed and refusing to go near it."
That's a genuinely difficult problem. And for a long time, the "solutions" on the market were embarrassing. Motorized rakes that dragged waste across a bed of litter on a timer, terrifying cats mid-business, occasionally jamming, occasionally catching a tail, occasionally just... not working, quietly failing while the smell built up in a sealed plastic box like a chemistry experiment nobody wanted to check on.
The category had a trust problem. And it earned it.
What's changed is the approach. Instead of trying to build a smarter rake, the better systems threw out the rake logic entirely and asked a different question: what if the box itself did the sorting, using a completely different physical mechanism, one gentle enough that the cat barely registers anything happened at all?
That reframing is the whole story. It's the difference between "automate the chore you hate" and "eliminate the reason the chore existed."
Think about what that actually requires under the hood. A system has to:
Detect, reliably, that a cat has entered and exited — not a maybe, not a "probably," an actual confirmed presence-and-departure signal, because acting while a cat is still inside is the one mistake that ends the relationship between animal and machine instantly and permanently.
Wait an appropriate interval afterward, long enough that it's clearly finished, short enough that odor isn't building up in your living room turning your apartment into a problem you now have to explain to guests.
Separate solid waste from clean litter with enough precision that you're not throwing away perfectly good litter every single cycle, because that's not efficiency, that's just an expensive garbage generator wearing a nice case.
Seal what it collects so thoroughly that the smell — the actual reason half of humanity keeps litter boxes in basements, garages, and any room they can psychologically distance themselves from — simply stops being a daily variable in your life.
Do all of this quietly enough, gently enough, and consistently enough that a genuinely skittish, easily spooked animal decides, on its own terms, that this weird gray machine is fine, actually, and just keeps using it like nothing changed.
That last point is the one people underestimate the most. You are not the customer the engineers were actually trying to satisfy. The cat is. You just get to enjoy the results.
And here's where it gets genuinely interesting, because this isn't really a story about litter boxes. It's a story about a much bigger shift that's happening across basically every category of home object, and pet care just happens to be one of the clearest, most visceral examples of it.
We spent decades building "smart" versions of things that were really just dumb things with a WiFi chip stapled on. A smart fridge that shows you the weather. A smart toaster with an app you'll open exactly once. Smart was a marketing prefix, not an actual capability upgrade. It made the box on the shelf say something new without changing what happened when you actually used the thing.
What's happening now, in a handful of categories, is different. It's not "add a sensor and call it smart." It's "rebuild the entire mechanical approach from the ground up, using better sensors, better materials, and actual behavioral understanding of whoever — human or animal — has to interact with this thing, and only then decide what to automate and how."
That's a much harder, much slower, much less flashy way to build products. You can't fake it with a software update. You can't ship the hardware and patch the intelligence in later, because the intelligence has to be baked into the mechanism itself — into how the tray moves, how the sensor times its cycle, how the whole system fails safely instead of failing loudly.
And when it works, you get something that doesn't feel like "a gadget." It feels like a problem that used to exist and now doesn't. That's the highest compliment you can pay a piece of technology. Not "wow, cool feature" — just silence. The absence of a thing that used to bother you every single day.
Ask anyone who has actually lived with one of these systems for a few months what changed, and they almost never lead with the technology. They lead with the schedule. The vacation they didn't have to plan a litter-duty rotation around. The guest bathroom that stopped smelling like a guest bathroom. The mental tab that used to be open — is it time to scoop, did I scoop, whose turn was it to scoop — that just quietly closed and never reopened.
That's the actual product. The hardware is just the delivery mechanism for getting your attention back.
There's a psychological angle here too, and it's worth sitting with for a second, because it explains why cats — an animal famous for hating change — end up adapting to these systems so much faster than most people expect.
Cats don't actually hate change. They hate change that feels unpredictable or threatening. A cat that gets startled once by a loud, sudden, poorly-timed mechanism will avoid that mechanism forever — that's not stubbornness, that's a completely rational risk assessment from an animal whose entire evolutionary strategy is "avoid things that might get you killed, reassess never." But a cat that experiences a new object behaving the exact same calm, predictable, non-threatening way every single time, over and over, with zero surprises? That object stops registering as a threat and starts registering as furniture. Background noise. Nothing.
That's the actual design target. Not "impressive." Boring. Deliberately, carefully, engineered-to-be boring, from the cat's point of view, because boring is what earns trust from an animal that has no interest in your innovation roadmap and every interest in not being ambushed while it's at its most vulnerable.
It's a strange kind of technological achievement — success measured by an animal's complete lack of reaction. No headline. No wow moment. Just a cat walking in, doing its business, walking out, treating a small robot like it's always been there. If you told an engineer twenty years ago that "the cat doesn't notice" was the entire success metric for a product, they'd have laughed. It's also, genuinely, the hardest metric to hit.
Now zoom out further, because the litter box is really just one visible instance of a pattern that's showing up everywhere in how homes are getting quietly rebuilt from the inside out.
We're in the middle of a shift from "smart home" to something closer to "autonomous home" — not devices you control, but devices that handle a category of decision entirely, on their own, correctly, without you in the loop at all. A thermostat that learns your patterns instead of asking you to program a schedule. A vacuum that maps your floor plan instead of bumping into walls until it gets lucky. A litter box that manages an entire biological cycle without a single tap on your phone.
The common thread isn't "more automation for automation's sake." It's automation aimed specifically at the tasks that are small individually but psychologically expensive cumulatively — the stuff that doesn't take long to do but takes up disproportionate mental real estate because it's recurring, it's slightly unpleasant, and it's never actually finished. You don't scoop a litter box once and move on. You scoop it, and then it starts filling up again immediately, and somewhere in your head a little counter starts ticking toward the next time you'll have to think about it.
That's the real cost of chores like this. Not the minutes. The ambient dread. The tiny tax on your attention that never fully goes away because the task never fully goes away.
Eliminating that tax — not the task, the tax, the mental overhead of an unfinished recurring obligation — might be one of the most underrated categories of value that modern home technology can actually deliver. It doesn't show up on a spec sheet. Nobody puts "reduces ambient dread" in the bullet points. But it's very often the real thing people are paying for when they upgrade from "manual and miserable" to "automatic and forgettable."
There's also a quieter economic story buried in here. Every category that successfully automates a genuinely disliked chore ends up creating a strange kind of loyalty that has almost nothing to do with brand and everything to do with relief. People don't get attached to the object. They get attached to the version of their life where the object exists. Ask anyone with one of these systems what happens if it breaks, even briefly, and you'll get a very specific kind of mild panic — not because they love the machine, but because they remember exactly what life was like before it, and they have zero interest in going back.
That's a different kind of product-market fit than most categories ever achieve. Most products compete on being slightly better than the alternative. This category competes against a version of your own life you've already forgotten you used to live, and it wins by making sure you never have to remember it.
And here's the part that I think is genuinely underappreciated: none of this required some enormous leap in raw technology. No new material science breakthrough. No AI model doing anything particularly sophisticated. It required someone sitting with an extremely unglamorous, unsexy, slightly gross problem long enough to actually understand it from every angle — the mechanical angle, the odor-control angle, the safety-sensor angle, and critically, the animal-behavior angle — and then engineering a solution to all of those constraints simultaneously instead of picking the easy one and shipping it anyway.
That's rarer than it sounds. Most companies solve the part of the problem that's easy to demo and quietly ignore the part that's actually hard to get right. Automating the scoop is the easy part. Making a genuinely anxious animal comfortable using a robot multiple times a day, every day, for years, without incident — that's the actual hard part, and it's the part you can't fake with a marketing video.
If you want a small, low-stakes way to watch the future of home automation play out in real time, this is honestly one of the best examples going. Not because litter boxes are important in some grand civilizational sense. Because the constraints are so tight and so unforgiving — an animal that can't be reasoned with, a task that can't be skipped, an odor problem that can't be hidden, a failure mode that ends trust permanently — that solving it well tells you something real about how seriously an engineering team is actually taking the humans and animals on the other end of the product, versus how seriously they're taking the press release.
Most categories get to cut corners because customers tolerate mediocrity out of habit. This category doesn't get that luxury. The cat is a built-in quality control system that cannot be lied to, cannot be marketed to, and will simply refuse to participate if the product isn't actually good. There's something almost refreshing about a market where the harshest critic isn't a reviewer with an audience — it's a small skeptical animal that communicates its verdict by walking away and never coming back.
So the next time you see one of these systems in action, resist the urge to think of it as a gadget. Think of it as a small, quiet case study in what happens when someone takes an unglamorous problem seriously enough to actually fix it instead of just automating the parts that were easy to automate anyway.
Every category has a version of this. A boring, disliked, recurring task that everyone assumed was just permanently part of the deal — until someone decided it wasn't, and built the thing that proved it. The litter box is just one of the more visible, more viscerally relatable versions of that story, because almost everyone either has one of these problems in their house right now or knows exactly what it's like to not have solved it yet.
The real headline isn't "robot cleans litter box." The real headline is: an entire category of chores that we all quietly agreed were unsolvable is currently being solved, one unglamorous problem at a time, by people willing to sit with the gross, boring, annoying details long enough to actually engineer their way out instead of around.
That's the story worth paying attention to. Not the box. What the box represents.
And if your cat currently treats a machine like furniture — walks past it, uses it, ignores it completely, gives it zero acknowledgment whatsoever — that's not the machine failing to make an impression.
That's the machine succeeding at the only thing that actually mattered.
Let me push on this a little further, because there's a version of this argument that stays at "cool product, neat engineering" and I think that undersells what's actually going on. So let's go one layer deeper.
Every household, whether anyone admits it out loud or not, runs on a hidden ledger of who does the unpleasant recurring tasks. Not the fun stuff. Not the occasional big project. The stuff that happens every day, forever, with no end state, no finish line, no moment where you get to stop and say "done." Litter box duty is one of the purest examples of this ledger in the entire home, because it is genuinely one of the only chores where the "reward" for doing it well is simply that nothing bad happens. You don't get a cleaner house you can show off. You don't get compliments. You get the absence of a smell, the absence of a mess, the absence of a problem. Invisible labor, repeated forever, for an outcome nobody notices unless it goes wrong.
That's an emotionally exhausting category of task in a way that has nothing to do with how long it takes. Five minutes of scooping isn't the issue. The issue is that it's five minutes, every single day, with zero possibility of ever being finished, layered on top of dozens of other equally small, equally endless obligations that together make up the invisible operating cost of running a home.
When a piece of technology actually removes one of those line items completely — not reduces it, not schedules it, removes it — something interesting happens to how people relate to their own home. There's a kind of low-grade relief that shows up in totally unrelated moments. You'll be doing something else entirely, some totally unrelated task, and a small part of your brain that used to flag "oh, also need to deal with the box later" just... doesn't fire anymore. It took me longer than I'd like to admit to notice that the absence of a bad feeling is itself a feeling, and a genuinely underrated one.
This is why I think framing these systems as "convenience products" massively undersells them. Convenience implies you're saving a little time. What's actually happening is closer to cognitive offloading — taking an entire category of recurring decision-making and worry off a person's internal task list permanently, not temporarily, not until the next reminder, permanently, and letting them spend that attention on literally anything else.
We don't have great language for this kind of value yet, because it doesn't show up anywhere we're used to measuring things. It's not in the spec sheet. It's not a feature you can bullet-point. It shows up in a completely different metric: how often do you think about this problem now, versus how often did you think about it before. For a lot of people who've lived with one of these systems for a while, the honest answer is "almost never," and if you've never experienced that shift, it's genuinely hard to explain how strange and good it feels to have a chore just... stop existing as a mental category.
Now let's talk about trust, because I think it's the single most underrated variable in this entire category, and almost nobody talks about it directly.
Every automated home system is, at its core, asking you to hand over a task you used to control completely and trust a machine to do it exactly as well, every single time, with zero supervision. That's a bigger psychological ask than it sounds like. Most people who've never lived with one of these systems assume the hesitation is about the technology — will it work, will it break, will it be worth the money. But talk to anyone who's actually made the switch and the real hesitation was almost always about the animal. Will my cat actually use this. Will my cat get scared. Will I spend three hundred dollars on a machine my cat takes one look at and refuses to go near, leaving me with an expensive paperweight and a very smug, very unimpressed animal parked six feet away from it out of principle.
That fear is completely rational, by the way. It's not paranoia. Cats really do reject things for reasons that make no sense to humans and make perfect sense to cats. So the actual product being sold here isn't just a mechanism — it's a guarantee, implicit or explicit, that the company building it actually understands cat behavior well enough to have solved for that specific, very real failure mode before it ever reaches your house. That's a much higher bar than "does the motor work." It's "does an animal that can veto this entire purchase with its feet actually accept it."
And this is where the category separates itself from basically every other "smart home gadget" on the market. A smart speaker that annoys you a little is still a smart speaker you'll keep using out of inertia. A smart litter box that spooks your cat once is a five-hundred-dollar storage bin you now have to find room for in your garage. There is no "good enough" tier in this category. It's binary. The cat accepts it or the cat doesn't, and everything about the design — every sensor, every timing decision, every material choice — exists in service of landing on the right side of that binary, consistently, across an enormous range of individual cat personalities that range from "doesn't care about anything" to "reevaluates the entire household based on a slightly different smell in the air."
That's an unbelievably hard design target, and it's exactly why so many earlier attempts in this category failed publicly and loudly, and why the ones that actually succeed tend to get talked about the way people talk about things that genuinely changed their daily life, rather than the way people talk about gadgets they thought were neat for a week and then forgot they owned.
Here's a question worth sitting with: why does this particular chore, out of all the chores in a typical home, generate this much emotional reaction when it finally gets solved? Why do people talk about their litter box situation with something closer to relief than satisfaction?
I think it's because this specific chore sits at an unusually uncomfortable intersection of three things most people would rather not think about at all: waste, smell, and an animal's most vulnerable moment. It's not like laundry, which is unpleasant but neutral. It's not like dishes, which are tedious but not visceral. Litter box duty asks you to engage, multiple times a day, with something your body is biologically wired to find unpleasant, on behalf of an animal that can't do it for itself, in a way that never fully goes away no matter how good you get at it or how nice a scoop you buy.
Automating that specific chore doesn't just save time. It removes one of the few remaining daily tasks that most people never got comfortable with no matter how long they did it. You get used to laundry. You get used to dishes. Most people never really get used to the box — they just get resigned to it. And resignation, it turns out, is a much easier emotional state to escape than habituation, which is probably part of why the relief hits as hard as it does the first time someone realizes they haven't thought about the box in a week.
There's also a broader trend worth naming here, because it explains why so much attention is suddenly flowing into what used to be a sleepy, unglamorous corner of the consumer goods market. Pet ownership has quietly become one of the most emotionally significant categories of spending for an enormous number of households, and the emotional stakes attached to "pet products" have risen accordingly. People aren't just buying supplies anymore. They're making decisions about the daily quality of life of an animal they consider part of the family, and they're willing to spend real money and do real research to get that decision right.
That shift changes what kind of engineering effort a category like this can justify. A decade ago, "cat litter box" was not a category anyone expected serious engineering investment to flow into. Today, it's a category where companies are running actual behavioral studies, iterating on sensor placement across dozens of prototype versions, testing failure modes against real cats in real homes for months before anything ships — because the market has proven it will pay for a product that actually, provably, reliably works, rather than one that just claims to.
That's the quiet, unremarked-upon shift underneath all of this. Categories that used to be treated as commodity afterthoughts are increasingly being treated as serious engineering problems, because the audience buying into them has made it clear they care enough to reward the effort. Pet care is one of the clearest examples of that shift happening in real time, and litter automation might be the single most visible symptom of it, precisely because the problem it solves is so universally understood and so universally disliked.
So if you're the kind of person who pays attention to where consumer technology is actually heading — not the flashy stuff, not the stuff that gets a keynote, but the quiet stuff that's genuinely reshaping daily life one unglamorous chore at a time — this category deserves more attention than it gets. It's a small, contained, almost perfect case study in what "good automation" actually looks like when it's done right: invisible, trusted, boring in the best possible sense, and measured not by how impressive it looks in a demo but by how completely it disappears from your list of things to worry about.
The cat doesn't care about any of this, obviously. The cat just wants a clean, quiet, non-threatening place to do what cats have always done, on its own terms, without being bothered.

The visit of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to Hungary, followed by Hungary's withdrawal from the International Criminal Court (ICC), has been interpreted by various observers as a strategic alignment that may offer Netanyahu political support or serve as a symbolic refuge amid global scrutiny. While the legal implications of Hungary's actions are open to debate, this situation underscores the ongoing interaction between nationalism, state sovereignty, and international law.

On July 29, Mohun Bagan’s IFA Shield win over East Yorkshire Regiment shattered the myth of British invincibility and was hailed as a triumph of Indian nationalism, challenging colonial stereotypes of Bengali effeminacy.

On December 27, Rabindranath Tagore’s “Jana Gana Mana” was first publicly sung at the Indian National Congress session in Calcutta; it later became India’s national anthem. The 1911 Census deepened communal identity politics by recording language data, intensifying the Hindi-Urdu divide and cultural dominance battles. 

The Curtiss-Wright Corporation, founded by aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss, played a pivotal role in shaping the military-industrial complex. During World War I and World War II, Curtiss-Wright became a cornerstone of U.S. military aircraft production, cementing the connection between corporate interests and military objectives.
This partnership laid the groundwork for what President Dwight D. Eisenhower later termed the "military-industrial complex," a system built on perpetual conflict and profit. Curtiss's influence extended well beyond aviation. He was regarded as "the fastest man in the world," a title given by newspapers for achieving speeds faster than any vehicle on land, sea, or air, until 1911 when his record was broken by the 141.7 mph (228.0 km/h) German Blitzen Benz automobile. 

The loss of this speed record set off a chain of events that the world has contended with for over a century, which could be referred to as the catalyst for the "first false flag war ”, WWI. 

Stalin’s NKVD, the forerunner of the KGB, was predominantly staffed by Jewish officers. Spiridonovich Putin (1911–1999), Vladimir Putin’s father, served in Stalin’s NKVD and was injured by a German brigade during World War II. 

Maria Ivanovna Putina (née Shelomova; 1911–1998), shares a birth year with Putin’s father. Her life encompassed significant historical events, including the Russian Revolution, the emergence of the Soviet Union, and the eventual fall of communism. Putin's ascension to power, often portrayed as a restoration of Russian strength, is intimately linked to the legacy of Soviet intelligence and the KGB.

Alois Hitler, father of Adolf, was born illegitimately in 1837 to Maria Schicklgruber. His paternity is disputed: possibly Johann Georg Hiedler (later claimed by Nazis), his brother Johann Nepomuk (who raised Alois), or a Jewish man (per Nuremberg testimony). No conclusive proof exists. 

The parallels between Hitler and Putin both leaders who emerged from periods of national turmoil to transform their countries are compelling. However, their narratives also underscore a recurring theme of concealed identities and the manipulation of public perception. Interestingly, Chaim Weizmann, the founder of the Zionist movement and the first president of Israel, also had a sister named Maria.

This infamous gunfight occurred in London's East End on January 3, 1911, involving police, a substantial number of armed officers, and a group of Latvian anarchists. 

A six-hour siege ended in tragedy when the building caught fire cause unknown. One agitator was shot before flames spread. As London Fire Brigade battled the blaze and recovered two bodies, the structure collapsed, killing a firefighter. A devastating loss amid chaos. During this time, he relied solely on his salary as a Member of Parliament, which was around £500 a year (approximately $`2,000 today), and his limited earnings as a journalist. Despite these financial constraints, he managed to maintain a large country estate that employed a staff of 20 to 30 people, including gardeners, nursery staff, cooks, and cleaners. 

How did he accomplish this? From 1936 onward, Churchill received financial support from a group known as “The Focus.” This group comprised 30 to 40 prominent British industrialists, bankers, and former politicians who believed Churchill was worth supporting. While not all of them were Jewish, many were; they included members from both left-wing socialist and right-wing conservative backgrounds. In July 1936, Sir Robert Waley Cohen, the Chairman of Shell Petroleum, wrote Churchill a cheque for £40,000 (equivalent to about `$900,000 today). From that point, Churchill became dependent on this group, as the saying goes, "whoever pays the piper calls the tune." Until 1936, Churchill had paid little attention to Germany. However, after that year, he began to passionately oppose the Nazis. 

At that time, there was considerable pro-German sentiment in Britain; for instance, the Duke of Windsor (King Edward VIII) was quite sympathetic to Germany and had a friendly relationship with Hitler until he was forced to abdicate in 1937 due to the same influential lobby that had been financing Churchill since 1936. This lobby also played a key role in maneuvering Churchill back into cabinet positions in 1939 and eventually into the Prime Minister’s office in 1940. Britain had the option to accept a peace offer from Germany, which has largely been obscured in historical accounts. However, Churchill, being beholden to the Focus, had no choice but to reject this offer, a decision that ultimately contributed to the bankruptcy of the British Empire. 

There is a line in The Godfather where Vito Corleone says, "I'm going to make him an offer he can't refuse," which reflects the complexity of Churchill's situation.

In 1943, U.S. codebreakers enabled a P-38 ambush over Bougainville; he died, was posthumously made Marshal Admiral, and given a state funeral.

Nachman Dushansky (also spelled Deshanski), a suspected NKVD collaborator in Lithuania during WWII, faced accusations of participating in the persecution and deportation of Jews and anti-Soviet dissidents under Soviet occupation. Survivors and investigators claimed he aided the NKVD in identifying targets leading to arrests, executions, or deportations to Siberia, though the exact scope of his alleged crimes remains disputed. 

In the 1960s–1970s, Israel refused Lithuania’s extradition requests, citing insufficient evidence and legal jurisdiction. Critics argued that political considerations including Cold War dynamics and Israel’s handling of Soviet Jewish refugees played a role in shielding him. Despite survivor testimonies, Dushansky denied being an NKVD agent, insisting he too had suffered under Soviet repression. 

Russian immigration to Israel, known as Aliyah, has a rich and impactful history, contributing significantly to the nation's population growth and cultural diversity. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, a substantial wave of Russian Jews emigrated to Israel, with more than 750,000 individuals arriving between 1988 and 1996. This era, often referred to as the "Great Immigration," transformed Israeli society and enhanced its demographic diversity in meaningful ways. 

Nikita Khrushchev (April 15, 1894 – September 11, 1971) was the First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1953 to 1964 and the Chairman of the Council of Ministers (premier) from 1958 to 1964. As a leader, he shocked the communist world by denouncing his predecessor, Joseph Stalin, launching a campaign of de-Stalinization, and presiding over the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962. John F. Kennedy sought to collaborate with Khrushchev and Russia to send a man to the moon; however, Khrushchev refused, as the Soviets understood that putting a man on the moon was not feasible. 

The Soviets officially referred to only three satellites as “Sputnik.” In the West, “Sputnik” became a generic name for Soviet satellites. These “Sputniks” included the first probes to Venus (Venera 1) and Mars (Mars 1), as well as five missions in the Korabl-Sputnik program, which tested the crewed Vostok spacecraft before Yuri Gagarin’s flight in 1961. 

The data from these satellites should have led Americans to discover the third layer of the Van Allen Radiation Belt. Venera 1 was equipped with atmospheric probes designed to detect radiation. If the Soviets were investigating radiation on Venus and Mars, they surely mapped it around Earth's orbit before sending astronauts into space. However, an analysis of the data and information surrounding the Venera 1 and Mars 1 probes reveals a lack of transparency and consistency, similar to other details surrounding space travel. 

Yuri Gagarin became the first man to travel into space in 1961 when he orbited the Earth for one hour and 29 minutes. Laika, the dog was sent into space by Russia on 3 November 1957, but faced a tragic fate. Upon the announcement of the launch, Laika became an international celebrity, earning the journalistic nickname “Muttnik.” Soviet accounts suggested that the dog was kept alive for six or seven days during the mission and was euthanized with poisoned food to avoid a slow death from asphyxiation. 

However, in 2002, Russian scientist Dimitri Malashenkov revealed that earlier accounts of her death were false; Laika survived only about five to seven hours after liftoff, dying from overheating and panic. It was also revealed that her pulse rate tripled during takeoff and only decreased somewhat during weightlessness. The Soviet scientists had insufficient time to perfect life-support systems due to intense political pressure to launch Sputnik 2 by the 40th anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution. Yuri Gagarin's successful flight into space marked a significant moment in history, but it was during this time that the realities of lunar exploration became clear. 

NASA discovered a third layer in the Van Allen Radiation Belt in 2013. Interestingly, they found this new outer layer just before China put its first rover, Chang’3, on the Moon. You would have thought NASA might have noticed this third layer in the Van Allen Radiation Belt between 1969-1972 during their many Apollo missions or from 1972 onwards, given the technological advancements in satellites and probes. The moon is vital to space exploration; its low gravity allows for less energy consumption to reach further planets, such as Mars. 

The state of Texas plays a crucial role in the history of American space exploration. It was here that Wernher von Braun, the former Nazi scientist and architect of NASA’s early rocket programs, collaborated with Walt Disney to create educational programming that celebrated space travel. This partnership was not only educational but also served as psychological programming aimed at promoting the myth of American technological superiority. 

In Texas, through the efforts of von Braun and figures like Carlos Prio, funds were provided to assist Castro in returning to Cuba in 1956 after his stay in Mexico. Texas is notable for its complex interplay of Communism, Fascism, and Zionism within American politics, as exemplified by Albert Thomas and von Braun. Thomas, who was instrumental in bringing the space program to Houston, also oversaw funding for the Atomic Energy Corporation (AEC) located in Mercury, Nevada.
Mercury is rumored to have been the site where the moon landing was staged. 

Additionally, the town of Mercury was mentioned during a conversation involving Lee Harvey Oswald’s pilot, David Ferrie, which was overheard by Montreal businessman Richard Giesbrecht at a Winnipeg airport. 

Von Braun’s role with Disney is critical to understand because it marks the point at which gaslighting and projection psychology began to be widely used as tools in American media. One can trace the origins of these methods back to 1911, although the limited reach of the media at that time made gaslighting less effective. 

Theodore Herzl, one of the founding figures of Israel, identified as an atheist. Many elements of Judaism can be traced back to ancient Egyptian culture, including monotheism and the practice of circumcision. The modern state of Israel was established on the basis of the Zionist ideology, which arose from Herzl's perspectives. 

The name Michael (מיכאל, mīḵā'ēl) means "Who is like God?" Michael Jackson was known to have planned to be in the World Trade Center on 9/11, a fact that has been well-documented. Michael Tyson was allegedly framed for rape, and Michael Jordan’s father was murdered in North Carolina. All famous Black men with the name Michael who had their careers ruined by some sort of scandal or tragedy. “Kill/destroy God”.

Scriptures do not give one simple “favorite meat” list for these four deities. What they say depends on the layer of text: Vedic *yajña* lists versus later Puranic and temple practice.

### Vedic ritual lists (Yajurveda / Brāhmaṇas)
In the older sacrificial system, specific animals are assigned to specific gods:

| Deity | Animals mentioned as their share |
|---|---|
| **Vishnu** | A **dwarf / short-statured animal** (often a dwarf ox or dwarf cow). Also a cow shared with Varuṇa in some rites. Offering a dwarf beast to Vishnu is said to win the three worlds. |
| **Rudra (later Shiva)** | Often **outside** the main Soma sacrifice; he receives the remainder. Some lists give him **red cows**. As Paśupati he is later said to claim the sacrificial animals in general. An ox is offered to Rudra in some Gṛhya rites. |
| **Brahma / Prajāpati** | Identified with the sacrifice itself. The five classic *paśus* (man, horse, cattle, sheep, goat) belong to the system as a whole, not as “Brahma’s personal meat.” |
| **Krishna** | Not a separate Vedic yajña-deity. He is an avatāra of Vishnu, so the Vishnu listings apply if one reads them that way. |

Other well-known Vedic assignments: Agni — bulls and barren cows; Indra — bulls.

### Later Puranas and temple worship

**Brahma**  
Almost no living temple cult. Offerings are flowers, ghee, and vegetarian *naivedya*. No standard meat *bhog*.

**Vishnu / Krishna**  
- *Bhagavad Gītā* 9.26: leaf, flower, fruit, water — the verse used to exclude meat from Vaishnava *prasāda*.  
- *Harivaṃśa* and *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*: in the Govardhana episode the gopas offer **meat** (including buffalo) along with rice, curd, and milk; Krishna as the mountain is said to accept that feast.  
- Fierce forms such as **Narasimha** still receive animal *bali* (goat, ram) at a few temples (e.g. Ahobilam).  
Mainstream Vaishnava practice after the *Bhāgavata* is vegetarian.

**Shiva**  
- *Brahma Purāṇa* (Bhilla-tīrtha): Shiva accepts **hunted meat** as *naivedya* from a hunter-devotee and prefers that devotion to a sage’s vegetarian ritual.  
- Fierce forms (**Bhairava**, Kāla-Bhairava) are offered meat and liquor in some Shaiva/Shakta and folk traditions.  
- *Śiva Purāṇa* also tells devotees of Shiva not to eat meat. So both strands exist in the same corpus.  
Jarāsandha in the *Mahābhārata* keeps kings to offer their flesh to Shiva — presented as an extreme, condemned practice by Krishna.

**Krishna** (as distinct from generic Vishnu)  
No text calls any meat his “favorite.” The consistent favorites are butter, milk, and vegetarian food. The only narrative where meat is part of an offering he accepts is the Govardhana *yajña* in *Harivaṃśa* / *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*.

### Short picture
- **Vedic yajña:** Vishnu — dwarf cattle; Rudra — leftovers / red cows / claim over *paśus*; Brahma — the sacrifice as a whole; Krishna not separately listed.  
- **Later bhakti:** Vishnu and Krishna — mainly vegetarian; Shiva — accepts meat in some stories and Bhairava cults, vegetarian in others; Brahma — vegetarian when worshipped at all.

The texts are not uniform. Vedic ritual manuals assign animals; many later Puranas and temple traditions move toward vegetarian *bhog*, except in Shakta and some fierce Shaiva forms.

My interview @cnni with @BenInLDN  

A. Netanyahu’s speech — the bigger problem happened before he spoke

The most important moment surrounding Netanyahu’s speech actually happened before he began speaking: a significant number of delegations walked out. That illustrates a broader strategic problem for Israel. Iran is an immediate security challenge, but Israel is also facing a serious erosion of its international standing. Whatever government comes next will have to invest significant political capital in rebuilding Israel’s relationships with the international community.

B. Israel’s wars with Iran have not achieved their broader strategic objectives

If we measure these conflicts against the objectives Israel itself sought to achieve, the record is deeply problematic. Israel has not brought down the Iranian regime. It has not permanently eliminated Iran’s nuclear capabilities. It has not eliminated Iran’s conventional military capabilities, nor has it ended Tehran’s support for its partners and proxies across the Middle East. What we are seeing today with the Houthis in Yemen is one reminder that Iran’s regional network remains a significant challenge. Tactical and operational achievements should not be confused with achieving the broader strategic objectives of the war.

C. The nuclear problem has changed — it has not disappeared

There is an important achievement here: Iran is not currently enriching uranium. But the nuclear challenge has not disappeared. The more difficult long-term question is Iran’s motivation. If the confrontation has increased Tehran’s determination to eventually acquire a nuclear weapon, then Israel and the United States may have delayed one dimension of the problem while making another dimension more difficult. Capabilities can be destroyed and rebuilt. Motivation is much harder to eliminate.

D. Israel and the Gulf states do not necessarily want the same thing from negotiations

Israel is fundamentally skeptical of any agreement that strengthens and stabilizes the same Iranian regime that it would ultimately like to see weakened or replaced. The Strait of Hormuz obviously matters less to Israel, but it matters more to the Gulf states. Their priority is regional stability and avoiding another major confrontation. Reopening and stabilizing Hormuz could also serve the Trump administration if its objective is to reduce pressure on global oil prices.

So there is a potential divergence of interests: Washington and the Gulf states may see value in an agreement that produces economic and regional stability, while Israel may worry that the same agreement gives the Iranian regime economic breathing room and ultimately strengthens it.

E. Iran’s new proposal does not represent a fundamental change in Tehran’s position

The latest Iranian proposal should not be interpreted as Tehran abandoning its core red lines. Iran appears to recognize that President Trump is under increasing political pressure as the midterm elections approach, particularly when it comes to energy prices.

Tehran is therefore offering Trump something he has a political incentive to want. But substantively, Iran is still trying to return to a framework resembling the previous memorandum of understanding, an arrangement Tehran believes serves its interests.

F. No agreement does not mean continuation of the status quo

This may be the most important point for Washington. The current situation is inherently unstable. The United States is applying enormous economic pressure, but Iran has not capitulated. If negotiations fail, we should not automatically assume that the existing situation simply continues. The opposite may be true: the probability of another escalation could increase.

That means Washington needs to answer two questions simultaneously: What are the costs of accepting an agreement with Iran  and what is the strategy if it rejects one?

Because if Tehran concludes that economic pressure will continue indefinitely and diplomacy offers no viable exit, the next Iranian move may not be another negotiating proposal. It may be an attempt to change the equation through escalation.

text:
A Gulf Divided Over Iran: Riyadh and Abu Dhabi Hold to Sanctions as Doha and Muscat Seek Talks

**The Wall Street Journal

Sources told The Wall Street Journal that efforts to resume U.S.-Iran talks face opposition from the Gulf’s top oil producers. Saudi Arabia and the UAE want pressure on Tehran kept in place, while Qatar and Oman work to arrange new talks.

Talks Sought in Oman

Mediators, including Qatar, are pushing for talks in Oman as early as next week to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and ease the confrontation. President Donald Trump said Tuesday he believes both sides will meet again soon.

Gulf states generally want to avoid a U.S. military escalation against Iran. But Saudi Arabia, a major oil producer, and the UAE are pressing the Trump administration to keep sanctions and not ease the U.S. naval blockade, the sources said.

Houthis Disrupt Saudi Oil

Saudi Arabia faces new obstacles shipping oil after Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis began disrupting kingdom cargoes in the Red Sea. Other obstacles include Trump’s preference to keep the blockade, Tehran’s fear that talks are a U.S. ploy to buy time until after congressional midterms, and a harder Iranian line as economic pressure grows.

Behnam Ben Taleblu of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies said reviving the Houthi threat on the Gulf’s southern flank, after months of Hormuz disruption, may be the strongest reason these states stay with U.S. sanctions. “These are the costs and consequences of Iran overplaying its hand,” he said.

A White House official said sanctions and the blockade have given Washington a strong position. Trump is open to talks under the right conditions, the official said, but “does not urgently need to negotiate with the Iranians.”

Riyadh and Abu Dhabi Shift

Arab states led by Saudi Arabia spent the summer pushing talks and were even ready to consider some Iranian role in Hormuz, a vital oil route. Attacks on Saudi ships and Tehran’s backing for Houthi efforts to close the Red Sea alternative raised doubts about Iran’s seriousness, the sources said.

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman recently told U.S. officials the blockade should continue until Iran is forced into a new deal. Emirati officials who had sought a diplomatic end have lowered expectations, saying rising violence and attacks on ships show Tehran is in no hurry. They said Gulf states should not accept permanent Iranian control of the strait.

Qatar and Oman Seek a Way Out

Oman and Qatar say the region has suffered enough and see a phased reopening of Hormuz and a halt to attacks on Gulf states as the practical path out. Qatar is trying to restart talks. Iran’s foreign minister arrived in Doha last Sunday to discuss a seven-day pause that could end Iranian attacks on shipping if Washington lifts the blockade. The United States has told Doha that Trump does not intend to lift it.

Arab mediators said Iranian diplomats offered ways to end the war and admitted the economic crisis. They said the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps sends a different message: no new formulas, and readiness for a long war. The IRGC wants terms closer to the June deal: eased oil sanctions, frozen assets, and a role managing Hormuz in return for opening the waterway. Washington says it will not return to that deal.

I remember covering then–Vice President Joe Biden’s first visit to China in 2011. His host was then–Vice President Xi Jinping, who was tasked with arranging the trip.

When Washington offered several possible dates in July and August, Xi is said to have personally chosen Aug. 17.

The choice of date was meant to send a message.

On Aug. 17, 1982, the United States under Ronald Reagan and China under Deng Xiaoping issued the Third Communiqué, in which Washington stated that it did not seek to pursue a long-term policy of arms sales to Taiwan.

Taiwan arms sales were clearly an important issue for Xi even then.

Forty-four years is indeed a long time. But whether it is time for the United States to end arms sales to Taiwan should not depend on how many years have passed.

It depends on how confident Washington can be that peace across the Taiwan Strait will endure.

text:
Ramatuelle is best visited anytime between April and October, with each month offering something unique. July and August bring the village to life. The Thursday and Sunday markets at Place de l'Ormeau offer the widest variety of goods, theater and jazz festivals are in full swing, and the beaches below are at their liveliest. It is also the hottest and busiest period; parking lots fill up early, and traffic on the coastal road between the village and the beach slows significantly after 10:00 a.m. If you visit during this time, arrive early and plan accordingly.

For many, May, June, and September are the best months. The weather is warm and reliable, the markets are open, the beaches are fully accessible, and the landscape possesses a quality that the peak of summer sometimes obscures. Village terraces are quieter, offering a more complete experience of the place. October brings the grape harvest to the vineyards on the plains and casts a special, golden afternoon light over the stone architecture. Walks along the coastal path to Cap Camarat and Cap Taillat are more pleasant once the summer heat has faded. For hikers and anyone interested in vineyards, October is truly one of the best months in the Var.

A notable tactic of abusers is that they will paint their victims in a false light, and do so loudly, yet strategically. They will point the finger and project many of their own behaviors onto the victim, so that people will see them differently and not believe the victim if they ever have the courage to come forward about the abuse they are experiencing.

The abuser will attack their victim’s character, accuse them of substance issues, promiscuity, call them crazy, and do anything they can to discredit them. They will even claim that their victim is abusive. In doing this, the abuser maintains the power and control of how people perceive the situation and the victim.

This makes it much easier to continue the abuse without question. At this point, anything the victim says will be chalked up to mental health issues or be considered invalid. Then the abuse will heighten, and the victim becomes less inclined to speak up because any attempts to do so are met with negative consequence. Not only from the abuser, but from others that have been manipulated to also be silent partners in the abuse.

An abuser is a master manipulator that is very good at twisting the narrative to paint themselves as a victim, and it’s easy for others to fall into the trap if they lack adequate training of these patterns.

Abusers will often utilize systems such as the justice system, law enforcement, medical providers, and other entities, such as the victim’s family, community and religious organization to target the victim as well, isolating them from any type of support or help.

There is a considerable lack of training in fields that are utilized as avenues to empower abuse.

The next time someone boldly speaks negatively about another, it’s wise to sit back and question why they would do so. Speaking ill of another person should be a red flag. There is no other motive of speaking negatively about another person, other than to do them harm. It certainly doesn’t promote anything good, wholesome or helpful.

There are many resources to learn skills to identify these patterns. It’s very possible that a loved one at some point may need your help in identifying these tactics. Everyone should become educated to avoid becoming inadvertent abusers themselves by falling into the trap.

text:
WHEN A MAN IS UNHAPPY WITH HIMSELF, HE WILL PROJECT THAT UNHAPPINESS ONTO ANY WOMAN WHO TRIES TO LOVE HIM.

The wound he will not name becomes a weather system. It gathers in the chambers of his chest, unspoken, unexamined, and then it looks for a sky to rain upon. The woman who approaches with open hands is rarely the origin of the storm; she is only the first horizon large enough to receive it.

In the old language of the soul, this is called projection: the inner exile sent outward so the man need not meet himself in the mirror of his own becoming. He confuses the ache of his unlived life with the presence of the one who offers to walk beside it. Her tenderness is mistaken for accusation. Her patience is read as judgment. Her love is received as a demand he cannot yet meet because he has not yet met himself.

Mystics have long known that the unintegrated shadow does not stay contained. It seeks a vessel. And the heart that has not learned to sit with its own sorrow will often hand that sorrow to the nearest light and call the light the source of the darkness.

This is not cruelty in its first motion. It is unfinished alchemy. The lead of self-rejection has not yet been given to the fire. Until a man descends into the quiet of his own unfinished rooms—until he learns to hold the child who was never held, the dream that was abandoned, the rage that was never given a clean name—he will keep mistaking the woman who loves him for the unfinished work he refuses to do.

The sacred task is not to blame the projection, nor to romanticize the wound. It is to recognize the moment the inner weather is being cast upon another soul, and to turn inward instead. To become the one who can weather his own storm. Only then does love cease to be a screen and become a meeting.

The woman who loves him is not his healer, nor his enemy, nor his unfinished chapter. She is a presence. Whether he can receive her depends on whether he has first learned to receive himself.

The work is solitary before it can be shared. The temple is built within before another is invited to stand inside it.

His servant was deathly sick and paralyzed. When Jesus heard that, he offered to go with him, but the Centurion said that he wasn’t worthy for Jesus to come. Psalm 96:5 (LXX numbering: 95:5) does say the gods of the nations are daimonia (demons). The Hebrew is elilim—worthless idols or “nothings.” Paul uses the same idea in 1 Corinthians 10:20: pagan sacrifice is offered to demons, not to God. So the Bible does treat pagan “gods” as either empty idols or as covers for demonic activity. That part is not invented.

The disputed claim is not “demons exist and pagans worshipped them.” It is the specific identification:
•  Poseidon = a Watcher from Genesis 6
•  He married a human woman (Cleito, from Plato)
•  Their son Atlas was a Nephilim and the king of Atlantis
That identification is not in Scripture. It comes from reading Plato’s Timaeus/Critias (4th century BC myth) and Greek religion back into Genesis 6. Genesis 6 mentions “sons of God,” “daughters of men,” and Nephilim. It never names Poseidon, Atlas, Atlantis, or any Greek deity.
Even Christians who hold the angelic interpretation of Genesis 6 (the majority scholarly view in Second Temple Judaism and a common conservative view today) usually stop there. They do not treat Plato as a historical source that fills in the names of the Watchers.
