text:
Dr. Margaret "Mom" Chung, the first known American-born Chinese female physician, a trailblazing medical pioneer, and an influential patriot who supported Allied troops during World War II.... 

In medical school, Margaret Chung (1889-1958) wore masculine clothes, answered to “Mike,” and entered a profession where almost nobody expected to see a Chinese American woman.

Born in California in 1889 to Chinese immigrant parents, Chung grew up poor as the eldest of eleven children. She worked her way through school and entered the University of Southern California College of Physicians and Surgeons. In 1916, she became the first known American-born Chinese woman to earn a medical degree.

Even that achievement could not overcome prejudice.

Chung hoped to become a medical missionary in China, but a missionary organization rejected her. American hospitals offered few opportunities to a Chinese woman, so she went to Chicago for further training before eventually returning to California.

By the 1920s, she was performing surgery, treating Hollywood patients and establishing a medical practice in San Francisco's Chinatown. She also helped develop services for Chinese women and children.

Her personal life defied convention just as thoroughly.

Chung never married. She cultivated a masculine persona in her younger years, preferred tailored suits and was known as “Mike.” She also had intimate relationships with women, including poet Elsa Gidlow. Historians have examined Chung as part of queer history, although she lived before today's language of sexual identity became commonplace and did not publicly define herself using modern labels.

Then “Mike” became “Mom.”

During World War II, Chung opened her home to American servicemen, eventually acquiring hundreds of unofficial “sons.” Pilots, sailors and soldiers called her Mom Chung. She cooked for them, wrote letters, offered medical advice and used her growing political influence to advocate for women serving in the military.

Margaret Chung spent her life crossing boundaries of race, gender, sexuality and profession.

America had very specific ideas about what a Chinese American woman could become.

She spent decades proving those ideas wrong.

text:
CAN THE DOW AVOID A FOURTH STRAIGHT LOSING WEEK? EUROPE IS ABOUT TO END ITS OWN STREAK AT THREE:

Europe is three hours into Friday's session and higher across the board: FTSE 100 at 10,717, +37.01 pts / +0.35%; DAX at 25,459, +192 pts / +0.76%; CAC 40 at 8,098.15, +16.72 pts / +0.21%, each so far in Friday's session, trading now. The Stoxx Europe 600, about 600 companies across 17 countries, is at 640.37, +3.94 / +0.62%. Hold that into the 11:30am ET close and Europe books its first weekly gain after three straight weekly losses.

The verdict for the US open: Friday's relief is worldwide, and it is thinnest in the one market Wall Street takes its cue from. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed Thursday at 51,349.98, -161.61 / -0.31%, down 0.64% on the week. To dodge a fourth straight losing week, it has to finish today above last Friday's 51,682.64, a gain of about 0.65%. Dow futures at 51,842.00, +125 pts / +0.24% since Thursday's close, cover just over a third of that. The holdout is the 10-year Treasury yield: 5.173%, still a hair above Thursday's 5.162% close, while Europe's borrowing costs fall.

Asia's night was split. The Nikkei 225 closed at 66,364, +850 pts / +1.30% in Friday's session, up 2.1% in a two-day week shortened by holidays. The Hang Seng closed at 24,510, -251 pts / -1.01%, down about 1% on the week, with mainland buyers locked out by the Mid-Autumn Festival. The Shanghai Composite sits at 3,888.37, -48.15 pts / -1.22% in Thursday's session, its latest; it has not traded since.

Europe's lift has a plain source: cheaper oil. Brent crude, the global benchmark, is at $105.49 a barrel, -$1.11 / -1.04% since Thursday's settlement - the official end-of-day price - on reports that US and Iranian negotiators are exploring a step-by-step path to reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Europe imports most of its fuel, and the morning's winners and losers show it: travel and leisure shares +1.2% by mid-morning, airlines among the leaders, energy producers the weakest group at -0.7%.

Friday is a give-back day almost everywhere, each market clawing back part of what the week took:
- The dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six major currencies: 101.07, -0.21 / -0.21% today, but still headed for its first back-to-back weekly gains since June.
- The yen: 157.91 per dollar, from 158.83 Thursday, after Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said President Trump raised the weak yen with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. Still on course for a second weekly loss.
- Gold: December futures at $4,327.00 an ounce, +$29.00 / +0.67% since Thursday's settlement, yet 2.2% below last Friday's $4,424.90.
- The VIX, which measures what investors pay for protection against a stock slide: 15.38, -0.29 / -1.85%.

Gold rising alongside stocks is not a run for safety; a run for safety sells stocks, and the VIX is falling. It is mostly a softer dollar. Gold is priced in dollars, so a weaker dollar makes it cheaper to buy with euros or yen.

The exception is the one New York watches. Each 10-year government yield against Thursday's close, in basis points - hundredths of a percentage point:
- Germany: 3.60%, -0.8
- Britain: 5.36%, -2.1
- France: 4.68%, -3.0
- US: 5.173%, +1.1, after touching 5.20% overnight

The US 10-year closed last Friday at 4.998%, so it has climbed about 0.16 point this week. New York Fed President John Williams said Thursday in London that another rate hike by year-end would be "reasonable," though he would not commit to October. Futures traders put the odds of another quarter-point hike at the Fed's October 27-28 meeting above 70%. The Fed raised its key rate to 3.75%-4.00% on September 16.

That yield is a big part of why Wall Street split in two this week. Smaller companies lean harder on borrowed money, much of it at rates that float, so a 10-year above 5% reaches their profits first. Since last Friday's close:
- Nasdaq Composite at 26,939.37, +3.34 / +0.01% on Thursday: +1.6% on the week, all of it and more on Monday
- S&P 500 at 7,704.13, -1.90 / -0.02% on Thursday: +0.7%, on course to end a two-week losing run
- The Dow: -0.6%
- Russell 2000 at 2,835.57, -3.09 / -0.11% on Thursday: -0.9%, heading for a third straight weekly loss

This morning's futures repeat the pattern: Nasdaq 100 futures at 30,918.75, +152 pts / +0.49%; S&P 500 futures at 7,787.50, +20.50 pts / +0.26%; Russell 2000 futures at 2,862.70, +5.90 pts / +0.21%, each since Thursday's close. The biggest companies lead, the smallest lag, the Dow sits in between.

The strongest case against reading too much into that gap: about 333 points is an ordinary day for the Dow lately. It has moved more than 300 points in a session at least six times since September 10, in both directions. A soft report at 8:30am that pulls yields down could supply the rest. And overnight moves often fade by the 9:30am ET open.

What would change the read: a 10-year back under Thursday's 5.162% before the open says Europe's relief crossed the Atlantic, and the Dow's 0.65% comes within reach. A push back through the overnight 5.20% makes a fourth losing week the likely finish. The number that decides it: 51,682.64 at the 4pm close.

Next, Eastern time:
- 8:30am: the Census Bureau's advance report on August orders for durable goods - goods built to last three years or more. July's first read: +1.1%, to $339.3B; forecasters expect about -0.3%.
- 9:20am: Kansas City Fed President Jeffrey Schmid speaks.
- 10:00am: the University of Michigan's final September consumer survey. Early read: sentiment 47.8 vs 51.7 in August; households expecting 4.6% inflation over the next year, up from 4.0%.
- 2:00pm: Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack speaks.

Europe's losing streak is ending on cheaper oil. The Dow's is waiting on a lower 10-year yield, and at 5.173% the bond market has yet to offer one.

A productive start to our World Scout Committee meeting at Gilwell Park, with an important focus on how we can work together to serve more young people. ⚜️

Hearing from World Scouting’s five Regions — Africa, Arab, Asia-Pacific, Europe, and Interamerica- — was a reminder of both the different realities our members face and the shared purpose that connects us. There is so much we can learn from one another when we take the time to listen.

We also welcomed representatives of the World Association of Girl Guides and Girl Scouts (WAGGGS) to explore opportunities for stronger collaboration. Building meaningful partnerships starts with trust, respect for each organization’s identity, and a clear understanding of what we can achieve together.

Alongside discussions on board diversity and future World Scout events, I’ve valued the conversations between sessions: reconnecting with colleagues, hearing different perspectives, and working through challenges together.

For me, the question running through all of this is simple: how will our decisions help more young people experience the adventure, belonging, and opportunities that Scouting offers?

That’s the responsibility, and the privilege, of this work. Grateful. Hopeful!

text:
The photo in that post shows the first hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) consignment from India landing at Newark Liberty International Airport on April 11, 2020.

It was shipped by Teva (from its Watson Pharma plant in Goa) on an El Al cargo flight and contained 2.4 million tablets plus 9 metric tons of active pharmaceutical ingredient (API). This was the initial part of the 3.58 million tablets + 9 MT of API that India authorized for the U.S. after Trump spoke with Modi.

What happened after it landed
The shipment entered the U.S. pharmaceutical supply chain and the Strategic National Stockpile. The Trump administration acquired tens of millions of HCQ doses (donated or purchased from companies including Teva, Novartis, and Mylan) for potential COVID-19 use under an FDA Emergency Use Authorization issued in late March 2020.

By June 2020, after the FDA revoked the EUA (citing lack of benefit in hospitalized patients and cardiac risks), the stockpile still held about 63 million unused HCQ doses. About 31 million doses had already been distributed to hospitals and some pharmacies. Some unused product was later offered back to manufacturers or slated for destruction; other portions were donated abroad (e.g., 2 million doses to Brazil that largely sat unused).

There is no public tracking of these exact pallets beyond arrival in the U.S. They were not a unique “Trump personal shipment”—they were a commercial/government procurement that went into the national stockpile and commercial distribution like other HCQ imports that year. Later Indian exports to the U.S. totaled around 50 million tablets.

The drug remains available today by prescription for its approved uses (lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, malaria), but it is no longer authorized or recommended for COVID-19.per @grok

text:
This is why Pandarus uses an iron arrowhead in the Illiad to shoot Menaleus.

People don't understand how much historical information is encoded into the Illiad.

1) Apollo was an Eastern god and an Archer. Apollo is on the side of the Trojans.

2) Characters in myths had names which described them. Mene (memory; but also a root which in PIE more generally meant holding onto something) + leos (loss; from PIE *lewHs) = Focused on what he lost / clawing back what was stolen from him / consumed by trying to get back what was taken from him.

3) The one on one fight between Menaleus and Paris was an allegory for the war up until that point. The Greeks were winning fairly easily. Then the Trojans started using archers (new tactical strategy) and they used iron arrow heads (new tech). 

That's what Pandarus represents. And his name means something like "piercing everything" or "plaguing everyone" or "hurting everyone".

4) It describes the changing strategy for the Trojans. They started out fighting head on with the Greeks, and they lost. Then they switched to mostly hiding in the city, protecting themselves by shooting off the walls. 

The Illiad says the Greeks tried numerous times to siege Troy, but they were unsuccessful. The only thing that worked later was the Trojan Horse. Which most likely wasn't a horse even 😂

And because of the mentioning of the unsuccessful siege of Troy, I actually like the idea of the Trojan Horse being a boat.

Or, it could just be a pun because Epeius is similar to the ancient Greek word for horse (ippos; most likely an ancestor from what turned into Pontic Greek, which is why we see an I instead of an e, and a pp instead of a p for replacing the qu/kw). So if you're part of an audience and you hear the words Epeius and Ippos, they don't sound completely different. They have the same basic word structure/consonants, and the vowels are similar in form. 

So Epeius could be the horse, himself.

In the funeral games for Patroclus, Achilles says the winner of the boxing match will get a mule. Horses/mules were draft animals. So using that as a symbol for slave in poetry is definitely possible. And it would explain why a character who is described as a very large man, isn't allowed to fight in the War. He isn't listed as a King until years later in a new writing.

Then, Epeius offers to be one of the boxers. If the theory holds, then he does this to be able to fight for his freedom because if he wins, then he gets himself as a prize. And he does. However, the Greeks probably don't trust him completely yet in order to fight in battle with them. 

Which is also why he's the perfect person to try and convince the Trojans to let him into the city of Troy. But he has to be able to tell a convincing story. What's another name for a story in ancient Greek? Oh yeah, that's an Epos.

So you see, it's probably just puns upon puns upon puns since it was an oral art form and the words sound similar enough, it gives the audience things to laugh at along the way.

But I also like the Phoenician boat theory. If the Phoenecians were neutral, or on the side of the Trojans, then using one of their boats to smuggle in soldiers is an awesome idea. 

Pair that with a former slave claiming he got away from the Greeks, or was himself left as a sacrifice, and it's more plausible that the Trojans believed his story, or that they speared him in the gut (Homer doesn't say "wooden" explicitly, he uses a word that could mean "spear", so he could be calling Epeius a "spear(ed) horse").

If the Trojans thought that spearing Epeius in the gut would prevent him from being able to betray them, it makes sense why they'd bring him into the city.

Anyway, this post got further away from new military technology than I expected, but I hope you still found all the information interesting.

text:
I had not realised before that the Bronze Age Collapse was literally *caused* by iron.

Bronze age powers like the Egyptians, Hittites and Babylonians used bronze weapons, made by combining copper and tin. Tin was so scarce that only the richest and most powerful groups could access it and the bronze weapons it allowed. (Tin was so rare that it was being transported from Cornwall to the Middle East more than 1000 years BC.) The scarcity of tin gave these empires a near-monopoly on violence.

Iron weapons are not actually any better than bronze ones – they're not stronger or easier to work with, as I'd assumed. They're just much, much easier to mass produce once you have bloomeries, which are the first furnaces that were hot enough to melt iron in a way that made them useable for weapons. 

Bloomeries meant that iron ore, which was widespread, could be used to make weapons anywhere. That led to warlords, bandits and city-states rising in a massive decentralization of military power, which the Bronze Age empires were unable to resist.

After the invention of the bloomery, skeletons show a measurable increase in weapon-inflicted injuries. 'Destruction layers' with bones and signs of burning have been found from this time at archaeological sites including Troy. Ancient writers – including Herodotus, Ovid, and the writers of the Old Testament – believed the invention of iron had unleashed a new age of violence.

New at Works in Progress, WEAPONS OF MASS DECENTRALIZATION: how iron itself brought about the Bronze Age Collapse. And what technologies could do the same today?

text:
Again with the same tired, selective script. Britain didn’t “ship every bit of food out other than potatoes” as some evil masterplan. Grain, butter and livestock were cash crops grown on better land specifically to pay rent to landlords. Potatoes were the subsistence crop on the tiny, marginal plots that fed the families. When the blight hit, the food the poor actually ate disappeared. The rent crops kept leaving because the economic system demanded it. Brutal? Yes. A deliberate “starve the Irish” order? No.
Penal Laws were being dismantled decades earlier: major Catholic Relief Acts passed in 1778, 1782 and 1793, full emancipation in 1829. By the famine, that’s 50+ years, not “about 40.” The land issue was real, but the explosion of tiny plots came from Ireland’s own population doubling between 1800 and 1841, combined with partible inheritance (dividing land among sons) and short-term conacre leases. That system pushed millions onto the one crop that could sustain a family on a few acres of bad soil. Those patterns were locked in long before the blight arrived in 1845.
The killer was Phytophthora infestans — a biological disaster that wiped out the potato across Europe. Ireland’s catastrophe was made far worse by pre-existing poverty, monoculture and density, plus slow and ideologically rigid British relief. Irish economic historians like Cormac Ó Gráda have documented this for decades: the famine was a natural shock hitting a fragile system, not a genocide engineered in London.
You keep repeating “NONE of it would’ve happened without your greed” because it lets you ignore Irish agency entirely: in land practices, population growth, empire service, and political choices. It’s the same hypocrisy you show across this entire thread. Real suffering doesn’t need cartoon villains and selective history to be valid. But that’s all you offer.

Though a difficult stretch on Pebble Beach’s infamous “Cliffs of Doom” and a final-round 81 ultimately took him out of first place, his aggressive play and precision fundamentally changed how the @USGA approached tournament course setups—When Morgan turned 50 in 1996, his career experienced an extraordinary transformation. He transitioned from a “very good” regular tour player into one of the most dominant senior golfers in history, ultimately securing 25 @ChampionsTour victories—He registered 161 top-10 finishes in just 431 starts, meaning he finished in the top ten in nearly 40% of the tournaments he entered—Morgan’s legacy is also deeply rooted in his home state of Oklahoma. Born in Wewoka, he did not begin playing golf until age 15 and didn’t receive any college scholarship offers,  making his ascent to the highest tiers of professional golf an inspiration for late-bloomers. And speaking of things that are supposed to defend us…
FIGHTER JETS. 📷
We spent YEARS figuring out what should replace the CF-18.
Competitions.
Evaluations.
Requirements.
Experts.
Military capability.
And finally:
F-35.
88 OF THEM.
DECISION MADE.
Excellent.
HAHAHAHAHAHA.
YOU MUST BE NEW TO CANADA.
⸻
Because then Trump happened.
Canada-U.S. relations went completely sideways.
And suddenly we’re reviewing whether we really want all those American F-35s after all.
Maybe we want the Swedish Gripen.
So now we’re apparently trying to decide between:
THE PLANE WE ALREADY SPENT YEARS CHOOSING…
and the plane that ISN’T AMERICAN.
Because…..
TDS.
Apparently our fighter procurement now has a relationship status:
IT’S COMPLICATED.
⸻
Meanwhile we’re still paying into the F-35 program.
The first aircraft are coming.
And the review is STILL GOING.
⸻
This isn’t fighter procurement anymore.
THIS IS BUYING A CAR AFTER A DIVORCE.
“I really want the Corvette.”
“Then buy the Corvette.”
“BUT MY EX LIKES CORVETTES.”
FOR FUCK’S SAKE.
BUY THE AIRPLANE THAT BEST DOES THE FUCKING JOB.
⸻
And here’s the part that makes this entire post even more ridiculous:
We’re reconsidering buying American fighter jets…
because we’re worried about our relationship with America…
while apparently preparing for…
AMERICA TO INVADE US.
⸻
So theoretically we could end up defending ourselves FROM the Americans…
because we didn’t want to buy the American aircraft…
that we’d originally decided was the aircraft we wanted to defend ourselves WITH.
And…..
Just for Funzies…
WHY TF would America sell us the most sophisticated fighter jets on the planet before they decide to invade?
That seems like a fairly significant oversight in Operation Take Canada.
Got it?
GOOD.
NEITHER DO I.

⸻
And while we’re discussing potential enemies…
remember that time members of China’s People’s Liberation Army came to CFB Petawawa in 2018 to observe Canadian winter-survival training? 
CANADA:
“Welcome! Here’s how we survive winter.”
Timbits and almost always fresh coffee.
ALSO CANADA:
“Holy shit, the Americans might come!”
Guys…
I feel like our threat-assessment flowchart needs work.
Apparently the friends are enemies, the enemies are on a field trip, and Brenda still needs your WHMIS certificate.
⸻
AND BEFORE WE GET TO THE AMERICAN ADMIRAL…
We need to meet:
GENERAL JENNIE CARIGNAN.
Canada’s actual:
CHIEF OF THE DEFENCE STAFF.
As in…
THE PERSON IN CHARGE OF THE CANADIAN ARMED FORCES.
⸻
In October 2025, General Carignan stood in Ottawa and delivered a formal apology on behalf of the Canadian Armed Forces for its history of systemic racism, racial discrimination and harassment.
And she became emotional.
She teared up.
⸻
Now - before somebody deliberately misunderstands me:
Racism and discrimination inside the military are legitimate issues.
People were harmed.
Leadership absolutely should deal with that.
That’s not the joke.
⸻
THE TIMING OF THIS ENTIRE FUCKING STORY IS THE JOKE.
Because remember where we are in our little Canadian defence adventure.
The Army has literally described itself as:
“UNPREPARED FOR CONFLICT.”
We can’t recruit people efficiently.
I applied to be a diver and THREE FUCKING YEARS LATER they offered me HR.
⸻
We’re short personnel.
We’re trying to rebuild readiness.
Our submarines have spent enough time being repaired that they should qualify for Aeroplan points.
We’ve moved the Coast Guard into Defence.
We’re contemplating hundreds of thousands of supplementary reservists.
And the person sitting at the very top of the Canadian Armed Forces is on national television…
TEARING UP DURING AN APOLOGY ABOUT THE CULTURE INSIDE THE MILITARY.
Again:
Important issue.
But if you’re watching this entire story unfold from outside Canada…
you’ve got to be wondering:
WHO EXACTLY IS PREPARING FOR THE INVASION?
⸻
Because we’re apparently still trying to get the fucking workplace sorted out.
And THAT brings us to…
THE AMERICANS.
Because surely the other side of the border is equally concerned about this imminent military confrontation.
Right?
RIGHT?
⸻
NOW WE ARRIVE AT MY ABSOLUTE FAVOURITE RECEIPT.
Because earlier this month a Canadian reporter actually asked U.S. Admiral Samuel Paparo whether he would obey an order to attack Canada.
The Admiral LAUGHED.
Not metaphorically.
THE FUCKING MAN LAUGHED. 
He called the idea:
“ABSOLUTELY AND UTTERLY PREPOSTEROUS.”
Reporter keeps going.
Because apparently nobody taught him the first rule of holes.
STOP FUCKING DIGGING. 
⸻
So eventually the Admiral basically says:
Would you also like my attack plans for…
THE MARTIANS? 
FUCK ME.
That’s it.
POST OVER.
You cannot improve upon that.
An actual American Admiral basically told Canada:
WE ARE NOT INVADING YOU.
PLEASE ASK ME SOMETHING LESS STUPID.
LIKE OUR WAR PLAN FOR MARS.
⸻
BUT CANADA SAID:
HOLD MY DOUBLE-DOUBLE.
Because three weeks later Mark Carney talks to The New York Times.
And the possibility of U.S. military action comes up.
Carney calls it an:
“EXTREME TAIL RISK.”
He ALSO says:
“THAT’S NOT A BASE CASE.”
Now…
I speak a little banker. 
Allow me to translate.
EXTREME TAIL RISK + NOT THE BASE CASE =
THIS IS REALLY FUCKING UNLIKELY. 
And frankly?
Government SHOULD plan for extremely unlikely shit.
That’s their job.
Pandemics.
Blackouts.
Cyberattacks.
Wars.
Natural disasters.
Aliens.
Apparently Martians.
Put it in the binder.
Dust it once a year.
MOVE ON.
⸻
BUT THEN CTV ENTERS THE CHAT.
And suddenly the story becomes:
PM CARNEY PREPARES FOR RISK THAT TRUMP MIGHT ORDER U.S. MILITARY TO INVADE CANADA.
OH FOR FUCK’S SAKE.
CUE THE ELBOWS AGAIN.
CUE FLIGHT OF THE VALKYRIES. 
SOUND THE AIR RAID SIRENS. 
GET STEVE FROM FISHERIES HIS HELMET.
BRENDA!
CANCEL THE RESPECTFUL WORKPLACE TRAINING!
WE’RE GOING HOT!
⸻
Meanwhile Admiral Paparo is somewhere in the United States staring at the television:
MARTIANS.
I SAID FUCKING MARTIANS. 
⸻
So let’s connect the dots.
Our Army said it was unprepared for conflict.
Our recruiting system managed to turn joining the military into The Amazing Race.
I applied to be a DIVER and three years later they offered me HR.
We opened recruitment to permanent residents.
Then contemplated a giant supplementary reserve with public servants.
The same public service where the Auditor General called the CRA and got accurate answers to general individual-tax questions 17% of the time.
Our submarines have spent so much time undergoing repairs and refits they should have Aeroplan status.
We moved the Coast Guard into Defence.
We’re STILL reviewing the fighter jets we already spent years deciding to buy…
WHILE THE FIRST F-35s ARE COMING.
China’s military once came over to watch how we survive winter.
Our Chief of the Defence Staff publicly apologized for serious cultural problems INSIDE the military.
An American Admiral LAUGHED at the idea of invading Canada.
Then compared it to fighting Martians.
Our Prime Minister called invasion an EXTREME TAIL RISK and specifically said it WASN’T the base case.
And somehow the national conversation became:
 THE AMERICANS MIGHT BE COMING. 
⸻
Guys.
I was gone for ONE FUCKING DAY. 📷
I’M NOT DIGGING A BUNKER.
I’m firing up the BBQ.
Americans bring the beer.
Canadians bring the burgers.
Coast Guard can bring the ice.
Steve from Fisheries is on potato salad.
Brenda from HR will conduct the mandatory BBQ orientation.
The submarines will arrive when available.
And if the Martians show up?
THEN WE ACTIVATE THE PUBLIC SERVICE.
⸻
Clarity is Courage:
Sometimes you don’t need another political opinion.
You just need to put the receipts in chronological order…
and appreciate what a magnificently fucking weird country we live in.
 Share my Cookies:
If we’re going to survive the invasion, we’re going to need snacks.
And apparently…
a really good HR department.

Hey everybody, it's your boy Person back with another Legacy Project interview! Today, we're sitting down with Staff Sergeant Steven Connelly to learn about his journey from Brooklyn to building a successful career in the United States Army.

Steven shares how he graduated high school unsure of his direction, worked a variety of jobs, and ultimately found purpose, opportunity, and stability through military service. From serving as a Ground Radio Technician to becoming an Army Paralegal, his story is a powerful example of how one decision can completely change the trajectory of your life.

In this interview, we discuss:

🇺🇸 Why Steven joined the Army
⚖️ His role as a Paralegal Specialist (27D)

💰 The GI Bill and tuition assistance programs
🌎 Traveling and living in places like South Korea, Germany, Poland, and Lithuania
🏠 Building financial stability and independence
📚 How the Army can help students pursue careers in law and other professions
🔧 Future goals beyond military service
💡 Advice for young people searching for direction after high school

One of the biggest takeaways from Steven's story is that it's okay not to have everything figured out immediately after graduation. Sometimes the right opportunity can provide the structure, training, and experience needed to build the future you want.

Whether you're considering college, the military, a trade, or are simply trying to find your path, this conversation offers valuable insight into the opportunities available through military service.

text:
Good morning ☕️🦀🇺🇸 Friday, September 25, 2026 — pre-market
 Futures are modestly higher into the open as oil and Treasury yields ease off Thursday’s spike. AI/chip names are carrying the bid; the Dow is still on track for a fourth weekly loss.

Week so far: Nasdaq ~+1.6%, S&P ~+0.7%, Dow ~−0.6%. Tech and communication services led; energy and rate-sensitive industrials lagged.

What is driving the tape

Oil is the overnight relief valve. WTI is back under $93 (~$92.90, −1.7% to −1.8%). Brent is near $105.60 (−0.9%). That pullback follows reports that U.S. and Iranian negotiators are still exploring a phased path: Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for Washington lifting its port blockade. Hostilities have not stopped — Houthi pressure on Saudi infrastructure remains in the mix — so the crude bid is softer, not gone. Brent is still above $100.
Yields cooled, but they are still historically high. The 10-year is around 5.16–5.18%, down a few basis points from Thursday’s ~5.20–5.22% print (highest since 2007). The 30-year tagged ~5.50% Thursday, a 2004-area high. CME FedWatch has roughly a 71% chance of at least a 25 bp hike in October, up from ~50% earlier this week. Hot activity data plus $100+ oil is the story.
AI is offsetting the macro grind. Chip names are the pre-market leaders: AMD, Marvell, Intel, and Cerebras each ~+2%. Nvidia and Tesla are marginally higher. The standout single-stock move is Akamai (AKAM) +21–23% after Anthropic committed to at least $11.6B over seven years for cloud infrastructure/software, with a possible $9B expansion. Meta is roughly flat after a strong Thursday and is sitting just shy of a $2T market cap, on pace for a fifth straight up week.

Trump–Xi optics. Xi’s U.S. state visit wraps today (tea session plus National Archives). Thursday’s White House dinner included Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Tesla’s Elon Musk. Public comments were warm (“great meeting” / “great visit”); few operational details have filtered into the tape.

Cross-asset snapshot
•Gold futures ~$4,310 (+0.7%); silver ~$65 (+1.6%). Spot gold is still headed for a weekly loss after the dollar/yields squeeze.
•Dollar off the very highs; USD/JPY ~157.8 (−0.7%). DXY has been near a two-month high.
•Asia: Nikkei +1.3%; Hang Seng −0.3%.
•Europe: DAX +0.6%, Euro Stoxx 50 +0.6%, FTSE −0.4%.

Calendar — Friday
•8:30 AM ET — August Durable Goods. Consensus: headline −0.4% (prior +1.1%); ex-transport +0.5% to +0.6% (prior +0.4%). Core capex (nondef ex-air) is the line that matters for the “growth still hot” narrative.
•10:00 AM ET — UMich Consumer Sentiment final (Sep). Prelims clustered around 47.5–47.8. Watch 1-year and 5-year inflation expectations.
•Fed speak: NY Fed’s Williams, KC Fed’s Schmid, Cleveland Fed’s Hammack. The market is already pricing more restriction; hawkish confirmation would keep the long end sticky.

Next week’s heavier tape: Case-Shiller / consumer confidence / JOLTS (Tue), then ADP, GDP third print, and August PCE (Wed).

Premarket names
Gainers: $AKAM on the Anthropic contract; chips as a group; some thin names ($INLF, $APUS, $SUGP) with the usual pre-market noise. Soft: $COST Costco slightly lower after earnings; MGM-complex names still digesting yesterday’s take-private withdrawal (People Inc. was bid on a separate MGM-bid rumor).

Setup into the open

This is a relief bounce inside a tight, rate-and-oil tape — not a clean risk-on reset. Nasdaq/S&P can finish the week green if durables don’t surprise hot and oil stays offered. The Dow still needs help from energy/industrials that have been paying the yield/oil tax.

Watch 8:30 durables first, then whether WTI holds under $93. If Hormuz headlines flip back to “no deal,” crude and the 10-year will reassert themselves quickly. Have a good Friday.

text:
A bent piece of steel. One lever. No electricity. No motor. No manual. And it quietly solves a problem that machines costing tens of thousands of dollars still can't solve without wasting a third of the crop.

Watch it work and your brain does something strange. It stops thinking about sugar. It starts thinking about survival.

Not in the abstract, headline sense of the word. In the specific, unglamorous, kitchen-table sense — the kind that gets calculated in fractions of a stalk, not in quarterly earnings.

Here's the part nobody mentions when they talk about sugarcane. The plant itself is almost free. It grows in ditches. It grows on the side of the road. It grows faster than most people can use it. What isn't free — what has quietly drained small farmers for generations — is turning this season's cane into next season's crop.

Sugarcane doesn't grow from seeds the way you'd assume. It grows from itself. You cut a stalk into short pieces, each one carrying a small bud — an "eye" — and you bury that piece in the soil. That bud becomes the next stalk. Multiply that by a few thousand cuttings and you have a field. Multiply the field by a season and you have an industry that touches sugar, rum, ethanol, ink, plastics, and a hundred products most people never connect back to a stalk of cane.

Now here's the catch nobody puts in the brochure. Cutting those pieces by hand, with a machete, hour after hour, day after day, is brutal, slow, and wasteful. Cut too much stalk around the bud and you throw away cane you could have sold. Cut too little and the bud gets crushed and never sprouts at all. Every miscut isn't just a mistake. It's money walking off the field and never coming back.

For decades, the "solution" offered to farmers was the same solution offered to every problem in industrial agriculture: buy bigger. Buy an imported, diesel-powered, steel-framed seed-cutting machine priced like a used car. Built for plantations running thousands of hectares — not for the family working two hectares by hand, the ones who actually make up most of the world's rural population.

So somewhere — not in a lab, not in a pitch deck, not on a demo-day stage — someone with a welding torch and a stubborn refusal to accept that price tag built something else instead.

A hand-lever. A curved blade. A frame you could put together from scrap in an afternoon if you knew what you were doing. No motor, because a motor breaks — and when it breaks three hours from the nearest repair shop, the whole operation stops dead. This thing doesn't stop. It runs on the same fuel that's been powering farms since long before diesel existed: a human arm, and a reason to keep going.

This is exactly why a clip like this stops your thumb mid-scroll. It isn't really about sugarcane. It's about watching a problem get solved cleanly, in real time, with almost zero waste — a rhythm your brain recognizes as "correct" before you've even worked out why. Every clean cut is a tiny resolution. Every discarded scrap falling away in one precise motion is a small hit of order imposed on raw, chaotic material. Your nervous system rewards you for watching that. It's the exact mechanism behind every genuinely "satisfying" video that has ever gone viral — and this one earns that reaction honestly, without a single edit or trick required.

Now scale the tension up, because this is where it stops being content and starts being consequence.

In many sugarcane-growing regions, seed material alone can account for a meaningful chunk of a smallholder's entire input cost for the season — before fertilizer, before irrigation, before the labor to plant, weed, and eventually harvest. Just the raw material required to start growing again. A tool that cuts that waste down, even modestly, isn't a gadget. For a family running the numbers on a kitchen table, it can be the difference between breaking even and borrowing from a moneylender to survive until the next harvest.

Multiply that by the number of smallholder cane farmers on the planet, and you're not talking about a handful of hobbyists. You're talking about tens of millions of households whose entire yearly income depends on a few brutal weeks of cutting, planting, and praying for rain at the right time. A machine like this stops being "oddly satisfying content" the second you understand the math behind it. It becomes quiet, unglamorous infrastructure for feeding a continent, one household at a time.

Meanwhile, venture capital keeps pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into "the future of agriculture" — sensor-laden drones, AI-driven yield prediction, autonomous harvesters that need a service contract and a firmware update just to keep functioning. Some of it is real. Some of it is genuinely useful. Almost none of it is built for the farmer watching this video right now, quietly doing math in his head about whether he can even afford seed cane for next season.

Nobody puts a hand-lever seed cutter on a keynote stage. It doesn't have an app. It doesn't have a subscription tier. It doesn't have a Series A round or a valuation. It has a welded joint, a blade angle someone adjusted through dozens of failed attempts, and a farmer three villages over who heard it actually works and wants one built for him too.

This is the oldest kind of innovation there is, and it's the kind history keeps forgetting to credit. Economists even have a name for it — "appropriate technology" — tools scaled not to what looks impressive in a demo, but to what the people who need them can actually build, repair, afford, and keep running with the skills and materials they already have on hand. It's the same instinct behind the spinning wheel that let a colonized nation weave its own cloth instead of buying it back at a markup from the very people who'd shipped the raw cotton out in the first place. It's the same instinct behind a thousand tools you've never heard of, built by people whose names never made it onto a patent filing — because they were too busy solving the actual problem in front of them to stop and file paperwork for one.

There is no press release for this kind of engineering. No investor update. No headline reading "startup raises twelve million dollars to disrupt sugarcane propagation." Just a welder, a farmer's complaint, and a few stubborn afternoons of trial and error until the blade finally stopped crushing buds and started slicing them clean, every single time, without fail.

We love to talk about innovation like it only happens behind glass walls, in offices with a skyline view and a foosball table in the corner. It doesn't. Just as often, it happens on packed dirt next to a pile of freshly cut cane, measured not in funding rounds or press coverage but in one brutally honest metric: how many buds survive the cut and actually sprout. The people building tools like this will never appear on a "founders to watch" list. They should. They're solving harder problems with far less room for error, and far less credit, than most of the people who do make those lists.

Ask yourself, honestly: how many products costing thousands or millions of dollars have you personally used this year that solve a problem this precisely, this cheaply, with this little margin for failure? A blade. A hinge. A lever. And a bud that goes from "discarded scrap" to "next season's entire livelihood" in under two seconds, over and over, thousands of times a day, without ever needing to be plugged in.

Zoom out for a second and look at where this crop actually lives on a map. Sugarcane is grown across more than a hundred countries, from Brazil to India to Thailand to Pakistan to swaths of Africa and Southeast Asia — regions that, between them, hold a staggering share of the world's rural population. This isn't a niche crop grown by a handful of specialists. It's one of the most widely cultivated plants on the planet, and an enormous number of the hands that grow it belong to small family operations, not corporations. Which means an enormous number of the people affected by how efficiently seed cane gets cut are exactly the people least likely to ever see the "premium" version of the machine that does it.

Now think about who's actually swinging that machete for ten hours a day in the first place. In a lot of these regions, a huge share of the physical cutting and planting labor falls on women, and often on children helping after school or during breaks, simply because the household needs every available hand during planting season. Repetitive strain injuries. Cuts. Blistered palms. Hours bent at the waist under direct sun. None of that shows up in a satisfying video, and none of it should be romanticized — but it's exactly why a tool that turns "hundreds of individual, risky machete strokes" into "one controlled lever pull" isn't just an efficiency upgrade. It's a small but real reduction in how much a family's body gets used up just to stay fed for another year.

There's a version of "right to repair" happening here too, and it puts most of the modern tech industry to shame. You know the drill with consumer electronics: a part fails, the manufacturer doesn't sell replacements, the warranty is void if you open the case, and the "solution" is to buy a new one. Now look at a tool like this. Every joint is visible. Every wear point is something a local blacksmith can rebuild with a hammer, a file, and an afternoon. Nothing about it is designed to expire on a schedule. Nothing about it requires calling a hotline in a country you'll never visit. If it breaks, it gets fixed, by someone who lives close enough to hear about it breaking in the first place. That's not a limitation of low-tech design — that's the entire point of it.

And here's the part that looks a lot like open-source software, except nobody ever called it that. A tool like this doesn't spread through a marketing budget or a distribution deal. It spreads because one farmer's neighbor saw it work, asked who built it, and either bought one or had their own local welder copy the idea and improve on it slightly. No license. No royalty. No "patent pending" stamped on the frame. Just a good idea traveling at the speed of trust between people who already trust each other, mutating slightly with every copy the way all real folk technology does — a slightly different blade angle here, a reinforced joint there — until, a few years later, half a district is using some version of the same tool and nobody remembers exactly whose workshop it started in. That's not a failure to protect intellectual property. That's intellectual property working exactly the way it should when the goal is feeding people instead of billing them.

It's worth remembering that this pattern isn't new — it's just unfashionable to talk about. Long before factories, most real gains in productivity came from exactly this kind of small-scale mechanical cleverness: a better spinning wheel, a foot-powered loom, a hand-cranked mill. Tools scaled to a household, not a corporation, that let one family produce meaningfully more without needing outside capital, outside electricity, or outside permission. Somewhere along the way, "innovation" got redefined to mean something that needs a data center behind it. It didn't have to. It still doesn't.

There's also something worth sitting with about the phone that's almost certainly filming this. For the person holding it, that device may be the same phone used to check crop prices, send money to a relative in another town, and post the exact video you're watching right now. Two economies are colliding in that single shot without either one noticing: a subsistence economy running on hand tools and hard-earned skill, and an attention economy running on algorithms designed half a world away, both meeting for a few seconds in someone's back field. The fact that this clip can travel from a patch of cut cane to a screen in your hand in the time it takes to read this sentence is its own kind of quiet miracle — one that gets zero credit compared to the AI headlines dominating everyone's feed this week.

So what do you actually do with all of this once the scroll moves on, as it inevitably will? Probably not much, and that's fine — most of us aren't going to end up building agricultural tools. But you can stop assuming "low-tech" means "unsophisticated." You can stop assuming the most impressive engineering happens exclusively behind a keynote podium. You can start asking, every time you see something dressed up as revolutionary, who it was actually built for — and who got left out of that room entirely. That single habit, multiplied across enough people paying attention, is worth more than any hashtag.

And this isn't only a sugarcane story. It's a pattern that shows up anywhere resources are tight and the stakes are real, unglamorous, and immediate. Cassava peelers rebuilt from bicycle parts. Grain threshers welded together from old oil drums. Irrigation pumps powered by nothing but a see-saw a group of kids is happy to keep pumping for the fun of it. Seed drills bent from rebar. Corn shellers driven by a hand crank a grandmother can still operate at seventy. None of these make headlines. All of them quietly keep more people fed, employed, and out of debt this year than most of what gets applauded on a pitch competition stage.

Let's actually run the math, roughly, because vague appreciation is cheap and specifics are where the real weight of this sits. Picture a family cutting seed cane by hand across a single small plot. A slightly better blade angle, a slightly more consistent cut, a slightly lower rate of crushed buds — say the tool saves them the equivalent of a modest fraction of their seed material every single season. On its own, in year one, that barely registers. It might buy a little extra fertilizer, or cover part of a school fee, or simply mean one less trip to a lender charging interest rates that would be illegal in most of the world that isn't desperate. Now run that same modest saving forward, season after season, for a decade. Compounded against fertilizer costs that never go down, against a market price for sugar that swings without warning, against unpredictable rain — that small, unglamorous edge is frequently the entire difference between a household that slowly builds a cushion against a bad year, and one that never gets the chance to. Nobody puts that chart in a pitch deck. It's not the kind of story that trends. It's just the quiet, compounding math of survival, running in the background of a fifteen-second video most people will watch once and never think about again.

Someone in the replies is always going to say some version of "sure, but a real machine would still do it faster." And they're right — for a plantation running a thousand hectares with the capital, the electricity, the spare parts supply chain, and the trained technician to keep an industrial cutter running, the bigger machine wins on raw throughput every time. Nobody's arguing otherwise. But that comparison quietly assumes a version of the world that doesn't exist for most of the people actually growing this crop. It assumes reliable electricity. It assumes access to credit at a rate that isn't predatory. It assumes a repair technician who can reach a remote plot within days, not weeks. Take away any one of those assumptions — and for a huge share of the world's cane farmers, at least one of them is always missing — and the "better" machine stops being better. It just becomes expensive and idle. The real comparison was never big machine versus small machine. It was always: a tool that works with what you actually have, versus a tool that only works in the world you wish you had.

Here's the part that should actually bother you a little. The "expensive version" of almost every one of these tools already exists. It's sitting in a catalog somewhere, glossy, imported, and priced completely out of reach for the exact people who need it most. The gap between "a solution exists" and "a solution is usable" is where most of the world's real poverty actually lives — not in the absence of technology, but in technology that was never built with the right person's constraints in mind. Every hand-built machine like this one is a quiet rebuttal to that gap. It says: fine, if the right tool doesn't come to us at a price we can pay, we'll build our own version, out of what we've already got, and we'll make it good enough to trust with our entire season.

Think about what "good enough to trust" actually means here. This isn't a hobby project. If that blade slips, or that hinge fails, or that lever snaps under pressure in the middle of a harvest window, a family doesn't get an inconvenience — they get a lost season. So every design choice you're looking at has already survived a far harsher review process than most venture-funded hardware ever goes through: repeated real-world use, by people with zero tolerance for failure, with nothing to fall back on if it breaks. That's not a low-budget alternative to good engineering. In a lot of ways, that's what good engineering actually looks like once you strip away the marketing.

There's also a quieter economic story hiding underneath all of this, one that rarely gets told because it isn't dramatic enough for a headline. Small efficiency gains, repeated across a large enough population, over a long enough time, don't stay small. A few extra usable buds per stalk. A few less minutes per basket. A slightly lower rate of crushed cuttings that fail to sprout. On a single afternoon, on a single farm, that looks like nothing worth mentioning. Stretched across a growing season, across a village, across a region, across every sugarcane-growing community running the same math independently and arriving at the same simple tool, that's the kind of compounding advantage that shows up years later as one region simply staying afloat while a neighboring one, using the same land and the same rainfall, quietly falls behind.

And sugar itself is a bigger deal in your life than you probably give it credit for. It isn't just what's stirred into coffee. Sugarcane byproducts show up in ethanol that fuels vehicles, in molasses that flavors and preserves food far beyond dessert, in bioplastics companies are racing to scale up, in the raw material behind products that never advertise where their base ingredient actually came from. Somewhere near the very start of that entire chain — long before a factory, a brand, or a shelf — is a farmer standing over a pile of cane, deciding how many usable buds they can get out of what they've got, using whatever tool they can actually afford.

That's the honest reason a video like this hits differently than the average "cool machine" clip. It's not nostalgia for a simpler time that, frankly, wasn't simpler for the people living through it. It's not just "oddly satisfying" in the shallow, algorithm-bait sense of the phrase. It's something closer to relief — a small, very specific kind of relief that comes from watching solid proof that you don't need a fortune to solve a real problem well. You need to understand that problem more precisely than anyone trying to sell you the expensive version ever bothered to.

Strip away everything else and the contrast comes down to a short list, and short lists are usually where the truth hides:

The industrial machine needs diesel. This needs an arm. The industrial machine needs a loan. This needs an afternoon with a welding torch. The industrial machine needs a technician on call. This needs a neighbor who's watched it get fixed once. The industrial machine depreciates the second it leaves the dealership. This gets more valuable with every season it survives, because survival is the only spec that ever mattered. The industrial machine was designed for a spreadsheet. This was designed for a bud that either lives or doesn't.

None of that is romantic. It's not a rejection of bigger machines, or electricity, or capital, or scale — plenty of farmers would take an upgrade in a heartbeat if the terms actually made sense for their land and their bank balance. It's simply a reminder that "advanced" and "appropriate" are two different questions, and the world keeps mixing them up in exactly one direction: assuming more expensive automatically means more advanced, when for a huge share of the planet, the genuinely advanced tool is the one engineered to work inside constraints most designers never have to think about.

There's a mid-century economist, E. F. Schumacher, who spent an entire career arguing for exactly this — technology sized to the person using it, not to the ego of the person selling it. He wasn't arguing against machines. He was arguing against the assumption that bigger is automatically wiser. Decades later, most of the tools that actually reach the poorest, most remote, most overlooked farmers on the planet still look a lot more like this hand-lever cutter than like anything you'd see demoed at a robotics conference. That's not a coincidence. That's the market quietly voting, season after season, for what actually works when nobody's there to bail you out if it doesn't.

So here's the actual question worth sitting with, longer than the three seconds this video usually gets before someone scrolls past it: how much of what we call "progress" is really just complexity dressed up as improvement — sold to people who never had a say in the design, at a price that assumes they don't need it that badly? And how much real progress is happening right now, unfilmed, unfunded, and uncredited, on a dirt floor somewhere, by someone who simply refused to accept the price tag they were handed?

Next time someone insists the future of agriculture only looks like a six-figure machine wrapped in a software subscription, show them this instead. Then ask them, honestly, who they think is actually feeding the world while that future gets built.

Save this before it disappears into the feed. Send it to the person in your life who thinks real innovation only wears a hoodie and just closed a funding round. The engineers who matter most to the largest number of people on this planet are already out there right now — cutting buds one clean stroke at a time, with a blade they built themselves, solving a problem they simply refused to accept as permanent.

If tools like this deserve more attention than yet another app pitching itself as "AI for farmers," drop a 🔥 below. And tell me the most brilliant piece of low-tech genius you've personally seen that nobody online is talking about — the tool, the fix, the workaround someone built out of pure necessity because the "official" version was never built for them in the first place. I want to see it. I'll read every single reply, and I'll repost the best ones so the people who built these things get a fraction of the attention they actually deserve.

Because here's the uncomfortable truth underneath all of it: the world is not short on brilliant engineers. It never has been. What it's short on is a system that notices them when they don't come with a pitch deck, a headquarters, or a press team. Every single day, somewhere on this planet, someone with no formal training and no funding solves a problem that's been quietly bankrupting their community for generations — using scrap metal, a few tools, and a stubbornness that no accelerator program could ever teach. Most of the time, nobody's filming it. Most of the time, nobody claps. It just gets used, season after season, by people who don't have the luxury of caring whether it's impressive. Only whether it works.

This time, someone happened to be filming. That's the only difference between this tool and the thousand others just like it that will never cross your feed. So don't just scroll past it like it's another fifteen seconds of algorithm bait. Look at it for what it actually is: proof, recorded almost by accident, of exactly how much real problem-solving is happening in places the headlines never think to look.

text:
Hadessa Clyde Wanted to Preg-Check Cattle. Wyoming Voted No.

Step 3 + Step 5 — Learn or Use a Skill / Strengthen Your Local Roots

Ground beef averaged $7.16 a pound in August. The U.S. herd behind it is the smallest in 75 years, and every fall a lot of those cows get pregnancy-checked at about $5.25 a head. In Wyoming, only a veterinarian can be paid to do that. A Fremont County producer named Hadessa Clyde asked lawmakers to change it.

"Nobody wants to work anymore," she told the Legislature's Joint Agriculture Committee in Sheridan on Tuesday. "Well, I want to do this work." She planned to charge about what the vets charge. The committee voted 8-5 to kill the bill. Doing the job for pay without a license stays a crime, with up to six months in jail and a $750 fine.

Katalina Pfeil's family has ranched in northeast Wyoming since before it was a state. She took ultrasound classes and now checks her own herd at 30 days of gestation, early enough to cull an open cow before feeding her all winter. The law already lets her do that. It doesn't let her do it for the neighbor. "As we say around here," she told the committee, "the less you call a vet, the more they like you."

A skill that's legal to use on your own cows, and a crime to use on the ones across the fence.

Most people don't notice that the other side had a real argument. Both sides agreed Wyoming is short on large-animal vets. Dr. Doug Honken warned that if lay checkers take the fall work, "you will never get another large animal veterinarian to come to the state of Wyoming." Sen. Barry Crago put it more simply: for some clinics, preg-checking is the business. The logic underneath it is that routine fall work is what keeps someone around for the 2 a.m. calving call.

So the fight wasn't really between good guys and bad guys. It was between two ways of dealing with the same scarcity. One protects the professionals who are still there. The other trusts the people who are willing to learn. It's interesting that the law only offers two settings, the licensed professional and the family working its own animals. There's no category for the capable neighbor in between.

There's a certain kind of rancher who has watched this pattern for a long time. When the vet can't come until next week, they learn to do it themselves. The same thing happened with fencing, then welding, then processing, and now ultrasound. Every skill picked up that way means one less call to make and one less appointment to wait for.

Some of them will read this vote as a door closing. Others will notice the door that stayed open. The skill itself is still legal to learn and legal to use at home. What can't happen yet is the next step, one family's skill becoming something the whole road can rely on. The part of self-reliance that runs into a license is usually the part where it stops being just about yourself.

Wyoming didn't settle the question on Tuesday. It kept the old answer in place for now. Meanwhile the shortage everyone agreed on is still there, and so are the ranchers who took the classes anyway.

text:
Gen Z Isn't as Reckless as You Think. In Malaysia, Where You Invest Matters as Much as What You Buy

When people picture young investors, they often imagine high-leverage futures, meme coins and Telegram groups shouting trade calls. The latest data tells a different story.

【The global data: Gen Z is surprisingly old-school】

A Binance Research report released in August, reported by WikiBit, looked at how different generations on the exchange trade stocks, tokenised stocks and stock perpetual futures. The findings were unexpected.

By early August, ETFs made up about 25% of Gen Z's stock trading volume, more than double the share for millennials. Gen Z accounts averaged 13 stock perpetual trades a month, fewer than baby boomers at 19. Leveraged and inverse ETFs made up just 2.65% of Gen Z's net stock inflows. In other words, leverage was kept for short-term positions, while their principal went elsewhere.

One caveat matters: this is global Binance user data, drawn mostly from emerging markets over a short period. It is not Malaysian data.

【What does Malaysia's data say?】

Local numbers point in a similar direction.

The Securities Commission Malaysia (SC) says investors under 35 now make up 43% of active retail trading accounts, and young investors have opened more than half of all new retail accounts each year over the past five years. The SC also notes that ETFs appeal to young investors because they are low-cost, simple and accessible, although many still look overseas for ETF exposure.

On Malaysia's licensed digital asset exchanges (DAXs), the Malaysia Digital Asset Platform Association (MDAPA) estimates that Gen Z makes up about 20% of customers, growing by roughly 10% a year. The association also observes that young investors on local platforms tend to be conservative, while many others trade on overseas platforms that offer more products.

Total trading value on regulated DAXs reached RM17.14 billion in 2025, up 23% from 2024.

There is one gap, though: young Malaysians are the least engaged in long-term retirement planning. Only 6% of Private Retirement Scheme (PRS) members are under 30.

【The real risk: not what you buy, but where you buy it】

The products in the Binance report, from US stocks to tokenised shares and stock perpetuals, come with a basic problem in Malaysia: Binance is not registered here.

In 2021, the SC publicly reprimanded Binance for illegally operating a digital asset exchange and ordered it to disable its website and apps in Malaysia. As of 20 July 2026, the SC lists only five registered DAXs: HATA Digital, Luno Malaysia, MX Global, SINEGY DAX and Kinetic DAX.

That means even if you buy only the "safest" ETF on an unregistered platform, you are outside local regulatory protection if the platform collapses, your account is frozen or your withdrawal gets stuck. The SC has announced that registered DAXs will join the Financial Markets Ombudsman Service (FMOS) in 2026, giving investors a formal avenue for complaints. Users of unregistered platforms have no such route.

The SC has also stepped up enforcement this year. It has taken administrative action against four unregistered DAXs and, since 14 April, has worked with technology companies including Google to restrict unregistered platforms from advertising to Malaysians on social media.

【Bring the same caution to choosing a platform】

The data suggests young investors already know not to stake their principal on leverage. The next step is to apply the same caution to where they put their money:

1. Check the register first. Before depositing, look up the SC's list of registered DAXs or use its Investment Checker.
2. Check the alert list. See whether the platform appears on the SC's Investor Alert List.
3. Look into the platform's background. Search the platform on WikiBit to see its regulatory information, risk warnings and user exposure reports before you decide to fund an account.
4. Know your local options. If you want ETF exposure, look at ETFs listed on Bursa Malaysia. The SC has also updated its ETF guidelines to allow digital currency ETFs.

Gen Z has brought back "buy and hold." In Malaysia, it is time to make "verify before you deposit" a habit too.

This article is for general education only. It does not take into account anyone's financial situation and is not a recommendation of any platform or product.

Sources: Binance Research (as reported by WikiBit), Securities Commission Malaysia, Asia Asset Management, The Edge Malaysia.

text:
TRUMP CANNOT CONCEDE BECAUSE HE CANNOT ADMIT HE IS STUCK: THE STORY WASHINGTON TELLS ITSELF WHILE THE WAR DRAGS  

Jim Hanson, Military analyst connected to the White House went on Piers Morgan Uncensored and recited the official story. Iran is broke. The regime is hanging by its fingernails. Time will finish the job. Trump is in charge. The plan is working. That is not analysis. It is the administration talking to itself so it never has to look like the weaker side.

THE STORY THEY NEED TO BELIEVE
➡️ Hanson says Tehran has no oil revenue, cannot feed its proxies, and will break.
➡️ He says nobody thinks the Islamic Republic survives as Iran’s government.
➡️ He treats months of unresolved war as early innings against a decades-old system.
➡️ The claim does the political work Trump needs: if collapse is inevitable, no concession is required.

“WE OPENED IT”
➡️ On Fox, Hanson said: “They can’t open the strait. It’s open. We opened it.”
➡️ “President Trump showed the world who’s in charge… of the world’s energy supply… of the world’s most powerful military.”
➡️ “I think the world is recognizing that his plan is working.”
➡️ Seven months on, that sentence is the tell. If the plan were working, he would not have to announce it.

WHY TRUMP CANNOT MAKE A REAL DEAL
➡️ Any concession to Iran would be read, by Trump himself, as losing.
➡️ Hanson still describes the endgame as pressure until the regime changes or is worn down.
➡️ Gulf capitals are told to “step up.” Two straits become energy leverage. The other side is supposed to fold.
➡️ Even a show deal would not be kept if it made Washington look weaker. That is not a path to settlement. It is a path to more of the same.

THE FINGERNAILS FANTASY
➡️ “Their days are numbered.”
➡️ IRGC “hanging on by their fingernails,” Hormuz “about all they’ve got left,” proxies fading.
➡️ “President Trump’s got the pressure on, and they will break.”
➡️ This is the same clock that was supposed to run out in two to three weeks, then five to six. The clock keeps getting reset. The posture never does.

WHAT THE TOUGH TALK HIDES
➡️ Hanson insists there will be no nuclear strike and no ground invasion.
➡️ The “choice” he offers Tehran is convert or be ground down.
➡️ Hyperbolic annihilate-language is waved away as pressure. The refusal underneath it is the policy: do not be the weaker party, even if that means there is no off-ramp he can accept.

THE BOTTOM LINE
Hanson’s interview is useful because it is honest about the psychology. The administration has decided Iran is already losing, so admitting a stalemate would make Trump the loser. That belief is why a durable deal is not on the table. Strength that cannot concede is not strategy. It is a trap with better lighting.
The plan is working only if you never have to define what winning looks like.

text:
Iran offers Trump deal before US election
Tehran says it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days if Washington lifts its blockade and returns to a ceasefire framework
Published 25 Sep, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/9LoOIBLO7m
Iran has offered the US a new deal aimed at ending the months-long conflict before the midterm election in November, directly challenging President Donald Trump’s claim that Tehran is deliberately waiting until after the election to reach an agreement.
Trump claimed in a speech at the UN on Tuesday that Iran is deliberately stalling the talks to see how Republicans perform in the November 3 midterm election, and predicted that Tehran would make a deal “right after” the vote. He also threatened to “annihilate” the Islamic Republic if negotiations fail.
“We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told reporters on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York on Thursday. “We wish Americans to return to the MOU before the midterms,” he said, referring to the memorandum of understanding reached by the US and Iran in June.
“We did reach an agreement with your president… The problem is that America, instead of conducting dialogue, descended into the arena by bombing us first, by blocking every pathway,” Pezeshkian said in an interview with Fox News. “We will stand resolutely to defend ourselves. We never sought war… It’s America that must choose whether it wants to end this or not.”
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran has submitted a proposal in which the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened within around a week and negotiations on Iran’s nuclear program rapidly resumed. The proposal was sent through mediators during talks in New York this week.
Under the plan, Tehran would restore navigation through the crucial oil shipping route in exchange for Washington lifting its economic blockade, easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports, and releasing some frozen Iranian assets. Iran is also seeking an end to hostilities on other fronts, including Israel’s combat operations in Lebanon.
US and Iranian negotiators are discussing a phased arrangement in which the blockade and restrictions on Hormuz would be addressed first, Reuters reported, citing Iranian, regional, and Western diplomatic sources.
Tehran has not abandoned its claim to regulate Hormuz, with Iranian officials continuing to insist that the waterway should be managed by Iran and Oman and that fees should be charged for services provided to passing vessels.
Araghchi said the proposal largely follows the terms of the June memorandum rather than introducing new demands, adding that Iran is waiting for a response.
Araghchi has also held a series of meetings with foreign counterparts in New York, including Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Moscow has said there is “no alternative” to a diplomatic settlement of the crisis provoked by the “illegal actions” of the US and Israel.
The renewed diplomatic push comes amid mounting pressure on both sides. The US blockade has sharply restricted Iran’s oil exports, while Tehran’s controls over Hormuz have disrupted one of the world’s most important energy corridors and helped push oil prices above $100 a barrel and US diesel prices to historic highs.
Pezeshkian, who is the first foreign head of state to speak at the UN while his country is at war with the US, told the chamber on Wednesday that Tehran is prepared for “dialogue and diplomacy” but will not negotiate under threats of force and “will never bow our head or bend at the knee.”

The Gateway Pundit reported on Wednesday that Judge Kelly appeared skeptical during a hearing on Trump's media ban.

A lawyer for the outlets accused the Trump Administration of banning the news organizations "completely out of the blue" and urged the judge to restore their access immediately.

"I think it is fair to say that process … wasn't followed here, talking about predeprivation process," Judge Kelly said, according to CNBC.

Judge Kelly concluded the hearing without issuing a ruling but said he will rule 'soon.'

President Trump said he expects to lose the case even though it is assigned to one of his appointees.

"… We'll go for appeal because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown" "sources" shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office…" Trump said.

And he is right.

Early Thursday, Kelly's ruling rests on the outlets' Fifth Amendment due process claim. He found they were likely to show that their passes were revoked without prior notice or an opportunity to respond, and that the White House had not established clear standards beforehand for conduct that could lead to revocation.

The administration argued that national security concerns justified the ban. But Kelly said the record offered little factual support for that claim, including no explanation of how the cited reporting damaged national security or how restoring the passes would endanger it.

The ruling is temporary. The restraining order lasts 14 days while the case continues, and the court plans expedited briefing on whether to issue a preliminary injunction. The order requires the plaintiffs to post a $1 bond by October 1. It does not resolve the full lawsuit or finally decide every claim.

China gets a tariff pause. India faces a Russian oil tariff threat.

On September 23, 2026, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that Washington and Beijing had extended their Busan Agreement until January 10, 2027.

During President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington, the two sides agreed to avoid new tariffs and trade restrictions on each other.

The timing matters. Just five days earlier, on September 18, President Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.

It allows tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy.
China is among the largest buyers, yet the US–China understanding gives Beijing protection while India remains exposed.

We saw this pattern in July 2025, when Washington spared China but imposed an additional 25% tariff on India for buying Russian crude.

If Russian oil purchases are the issue, why does India face the tariff while China gets an exemption?

The tariff threat appears aimed at forcing India to cut Russian oil purchases and sign a deeply unequal bilateral trade agreement.
Washington could offer a lower rate in return for concessions, but that would give India no lasting certainty.
India should not trade its energy security for temporary tariff relief or let US tariff threats dictate its national energy policy.
