text:
REGIONAL SPORTS ROUNDUP
September 25, 2026

HIGH SCHOOL

THURSDAY RECAP
In volleyball, Marshall County stayed perfect in the 4th District with a straight-set win over Murray High last night Taylor Gymnasium. The Lady Tigers jumped out 6-1 leadhe opener before the Lady Marshals rallied for the win. The scores were 25-16, 25-13, 25-19. Jazmyne Jones led the Lady Tigers with 6 kills and 3 blocks as Murray fell to 12-11 overall and 0-4 in the district while Marshall improved to 14-4.

In boys high school soccer, Calloway County fell at Christian County 2-0

FRIDAY NIGHT PREVIEW
Murray High continues its four game homestand tonight when McCracken County visits Ty Holland Stadium. The 5-0 Tigers are ranked 2nd in 3A have won all three meetings with the Mustangs since 2023, including a 59-56 shootout last season. Murray High comes into the game averaging almost 269 yards per game on the ground. McCracken County's success has been through the air behind quarterback Cole Presswood, who has thrown for 15 touchdowns and almost 1400 yards. Kickoff time is set for 7 with pregame coverage beginning at 6 on WNBS and the Froggy 103 App. 

Calloway County returns home tonight looking to rebound from last week's road loss against Warren East in its district opener. The 3-2 Lakers face a powerful 4-1 Logan County team averaging 48 points per game. Lakers running back Brayden Tupper has become a force averaging nearly 122 yards per game on the ground, while teammate Matthew Briedwell has passed for 18 touchdowns. Logan County is led by quarterback Christian Helle, who has thrown for nine touchdowns while the Cougars Lane Bush averages over 105 yards rushing per game. Kickoff is set for 7 pm at Jack Rose Stadium with pregame coverage at 6:30 on 104.5 WBZB and the Zeno Radio App. 

COLLEGE

WTEN AT AP INVITE
Murray State tennis continues its fall schedule today at the Austin Peay Invitational in Clarksville. The three-day event features Murray State, Austin Peay, Western Kentucky, Chattanooga and Alabama A&M, with the Racers opening against Chattanooga and Alabama A&M before facing additional competition Saturday. Murray State finished 10-11 last season and returns Valeria Chaikovskaia, who went 12-7 at No. 1 singles.

CROSS COUNTRY TO MIZZOU
Murray State’s men’s and women’s cross-country teams compete Saturday at the 2026 Gans Creek Classic, hosted by Missouri in Columbia. The women run a 6K at 9:45 a.m., followed by the men’s 8K at 10:30 a.m. The field includes 19 schools, including nationally ranked No. 26 Missouri, Arkansas, Kentucky, Tennessee and Texas. The Racers are coming off strong showings at the OVC Preview, led by Dylan Ellis’ fourth-place finish in the men’s 8K and Molly Robertson’s runner-up finish in the women’s 6K.

CATS GET COMMIT
A class of 2029 high school football player is already sharing plans to become a Wildcat.  SB Nation reports three-star quarterback Marcus Washington has committed to Kentucky.  UK offered Washington in May and invited him to Lexington for an unofficial visit on September 12th.  He does not yet have a national ranking as a sophomore in high school.

HUGHES TO VISIT LOUISVILLE
A Kentucky football commit is taking a trip to check out Louisville.  Rivals reports four-star safety Tristan Hughes will be in Louisville this weekend as the Cardinals host Wake Forest.  Hughes committed to the Wildcats back in April after also seriously considering Virginia Tech.  The Cleveland-area native will be taking a trip to Michigan next month as well, according to the report.

OVC REACHES TRAVEL AGREEMENT
The Ohio Valley Conference has announced a new corporate partnership with SportsTrip, a sports travel management company. SportsTrip will assist with hotel bookings for OVC events and championships and provide a Fan Travel Portal for fans to book hotels and other travel throughout the year. The partnership was secured by OVC Sports Properties, the Conference’s multimedia rights partner.

PROS

CARDINALS REPORT
The Pittsburgh Pirates took the series over the St. Louis Cardinals with a 2-1 win on Thursday.  Spencer Horwitz hit a sacrifice fly in the bottom of the eighth for what would be the winning run.   Paul Skenes went six and a third for the Pirates, while Alec Burleson hit a home run early for the Cardinals.  With the loss, the Cardinals are guaranteed back-to-back losing seasons for the first time since the shortened 1994 and 1995 seasons. St. Louis is in Milwaukee tonight to face the Brewers with a time-shifted airtime at 10:40 pm on WNBS due to Murray High football. 

TNF RECAP
The Falcons spoiled the Packers' home opener after grabbing a 35-14 win on Thursday Night Football at Lambeau Field.  Michael Penix made his season debut and threw for 256 yards and a touchdown.  Bijan Robinson ran for 194 yards and two touchdowns, while Drake London caught nine passes for 194 yards.  Jordan Love threw for 312 yards, two touchdowns and a pick. Both teams are now 1-2.

AREA HOCKEY ROUNDUP
The Predators fell to the Hurricanes 6-5 in preseason hockey on the road.  The sides will square off in a rematch in Raleigh tomorrow afternoon.  The Blues shut out the Blackhawks 1-0 in preseason hockey in St. Louis.  The sides clash again in Chicago tomorrow night. The Blackhawks have signed forward Oliver Moore to a five-year, 21.25-million-dollar contract.  The 21-year-old appeared in 51 games for Chicago last season.

TITANS REPORT
The new Nissan Stadium is entering the final stretch of construction, with the first areas expected to be turned over to the Titans in January.  Crews are installing seats, finishing the stadium's roof and preparing for a major plumbing test in November.  About 23-hundred workers are on site each day and the stadium is expected to be substantially complete by February.  Demolition of the current stadium could begin around March, while the first event at the new stadium has not yet been announced.

AREA NFL REPORT
The Bears quarterback room looks like a medical facility, but it's appearing more like their third-string signal caller will get Monday night's start.  Starter Caleb Williams is down with a hamstring injury and backup Tyson Bagent is in concussion protocol.  That leaves reserve quarterback Case Keenum, who says he is ready to start, if needed.  He was the only signal caller to attend practice Wednesday.  Rookie practice-squad quarterback Miller Moss took reps with the second team.  The Bears face the Eagles in primetime on Monday at Soldier Field.

text:
October 4th. Jake LangLang is coming to "Little Palestine" in  Bridgeview, Illinois.

A Catholic protest. Not a suggestion. A line in the sand.

Christians in this country are watching neighborhoods change, churches empty, and mosques rise where Christian life used to stand. In Bridgeview, they call it Little Palestine now. Fine. Then say it plainly: a Christian community was remade. The call to prayer replaced the old quiet. Families left. What was once a place with churches became a place organized around a mosque. Vacant Christian buildings get eyed for conversion. And Catholics are told to smile, stay polite, and call it “diversity.”

We will not.

The Church is not a real-estate afterthought. A church is consecrated ground. Turning sacred Christian space into something else is not “progress.” It is a wound. And when it happens while Christians are pressured to stay silent, it is an insult.

Now the question they never want asked:

Imagine Catholics tried this in Gaza or the West Bank. Buy a mosque. Consecrate it. Hang a crucifix. Offer Mass. Would they allow it?

Hell no.

They would riot. They would burn. They would call it occupation, blasphemy, and war. Yet here, in America, we are expected to accept the reverse as inevitable, even virtuous.

That is the double standard. That is why this protest exists.

October 4th is not about hating a people. It is about refusing the lie that only one faith may advance while Catholics must surrender ground, language, memory, and nerve. If Christians have lost their voice in Little Palestine, then it is time to take it back in public, in daylight, and without apology.

Christ is King. The Church does not kneel to fashion, fear, or a one-way “tolerance” that never runs in the other direction.

Be there. Stand. Speak. Do not whisper.

text:
Top public university’s ‘LGBTQ+ lab’ hit with race-bias complaint amid $700K in Trump-era federal funding | Fox News

FIRST ON FOX: A University of Maryland research lab that received nearly $700,000 in additional federal funding from the Trump administration this year is facing a civil rights complaint alleging that it uses race and ethnicity to determine access to some research-related opportunities.

The Equal Protection Project (EPP) filed the complaint with the Department of Health and Human Services' Office for Civil Rights against UMD's Lavender Lab, a National Institutes of Health (NIH)-funded lab that studies suicide, substance use and other health outcomes among LGBTQ+ people and Black, Indigenous and People of Color.

EPP is asking HHS to investigate whether the lab's LGBTQ+ Teens of Color Advisory Board and its research assistant selection practices give priority to non-White applicants.

"Some people may ask what is wrong with prioritizing non-whites in a program which is designed to study non-whites," EPP founder William Jacobson told Fox News Digital. "When you receive federal funding, you cannot discriminate in the administration of your programs."

"You do not need to have an advisory board, you do not need to hire research assistants based on race to fulfill the purposes of this grant," Jacobson continued.

The complaint comes as the Lavender Lab continues receiving millions of dollars through the NIH for research examining alcohol and drug use among "sexual minority adolescents of color."

One of the lab's principal projects, titled "Long-Term and Daily Associations Among Intersectional Minority Stress, Structural Oppression, and Alcohol Use and Misuse Among Sexual Minority Adolescents of Color," began in May 2022 and is scheduled to run through April 2027. The complaint cites approximately $3.6 million in total federal obligations and roughly $2.2 million in outlays at the time of its filing.

NIH records cited in the complaint show the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism provided another $695,192 for the project for fiscal year 2026.

The complaint points first to the lab's LGBTQ+ Teens of Color Advisory Board, which said it was "specifically looking for teens in the US who identify as both LGBTQ+ and Black, Indigenous, and People of Color (BIPOC) to join our board" in an Instagram post.

According to the complaint, board members are paid to help review research, provide feedback and participate in professional-development activities, with some also receiving leadership opportunities.

EPP also targeted the Lavender Lab's research-assistant program, which offers positions to undergraduate and master's-level students.

Although the positions are generally unpaid, the complaint stated that undergraduate research assistants may receive academic course credit, and some students may be able to participate through federal work-study. Research assistants generally commit to at least two semesters and a minimum of eight hours per week.

The lab stated it "especially encourage[s] and invite[s] candidates from traditionally marginalized backgrounds" to apply and that applicants with experience conducting research involving "LGBTQ and BIPOC communities" through "cultural humility, intersectionality, and social justice approaches" will receive the "strongest consideration."

"Discrimination based on race or ethnicity at institutions receiving federal funding is unlawful regardless of which group is targeted or benefits," Jacobson said. "Treating individuals as avatars of their demographic identity rather than as individuals with unique merits and circumstances undermines fairness, merit, social cohesion, and the rule of law."

EPP alleges that the language indicates race or ethnicity may play a role in the selection process. The complaint asks HHS to investigate whether the practices violate Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, which prohibits discrimination based on race, color or national origin in federally funded programs, as well as the Affordable Care Act.

"Because the Lavender Lab is operating under an HHS health care related grant, the non-discrimination provisions of the Affordable Care Act must be adhered to, and HHS has authority to enforce those provisions," Jacobson said.

EPP's complaint also questions federal funding for research focused on intersectionality, which the Lavender Lab says guides its work. The lab studies how sexual-minority status, race, ethnicity and what it calls "structural oppression" affect health outcomes.

"The conduct at the Lavender Lab calls into question whether HHS should be funding intersectionality-focused research at all," Jacobson said. "Intersectionality is a race- and ethnicity-focused group-identity approach. It is no surprise that where the focus is racial identity that programming could cross the line into civil rights violations."

Jacobson said EPP has found federal dollars going to programs that use intersectionality and is calling for tighter rules on that funding.

"We have identified hundreds of millions of dollars of federal funding for programs that incorporate intersectionality," Jacobson said. "Given the civil rights danger from an 'intersectional' approach, we call on the administration to issue a new executive order and agency guidance closing the 'intersectionality loophole' by including intersectionality in the ban on unlawful discriminatory DEI practices in federal grantmaking."

Fox News Digital reached out to the University of Maryland, HHS and the White House for comment.

According to the EEOC, MedStar offered the man an admitting-registrar job in March 2024, then required a post-offer medical evaluation. After learning about his disability, the agency says MedStar refused to medically clear him unless he stopped receiving intravenous treatment, denied requested accommodations and ultimately revoked the offer. 

The lawsuit alleges those actions violated the Americans with Disabilities Act, which bars disability discrimination and generally requires reasonable accommodation unless it would impose an undue hardship. The EEOC filed the case in federal court in Maryland after settlement efforts failed.

- The vol surface reads calm at 14-18, but widening credit spreads say that's a lie.
- Buyback blackout just removed the one structural support layer the market could count on.
- Oil and bond yields are running price discovery until ISM and labor data arrive next week.
- Lean defensive, don't chase the mega-cap bid, and stay light on index exposure until breadth and credit confirm otherwise.

The regime remains Fragile, with no meaningful shift from the prior read. The window of weakness stays open, and energy prices continue to function as the single dominant macro transmission mechanism, driving bonds, equities, and currencies simultaneously. Dealers remain long gamma with and with 10-day realized volatility at 11.69, positioning is stable but offers limited downside protection should the market move toward the 7650 strike. Breadth deterioration is the clearest internal warning signal: more than 65% of index constituents closed lower on the day with an average decline of near 1.5%, and the headline index was carried back toward neutral almost entirely by META, GOOGL, and LLY. The buyback blackout removes the corporate bid at exactly the wrong moment, eliminating a structural support layer as volatility in energy and rates keeps the macro environment unstable. The vol regime reads calm at 14 to 18, but this surface reading is increasingly difficult to square with the underlying breadth damage and widening credit spreads. Swaps fully pricing additional Fed hikes over the next year adds further weight to the rate-driven headwind, and the macro data calendar stays quiet until ISM and labor data arrive next week, leaving oil prices and bond yields as the primary price-discovery mechanism in the interim. The University of Michigan final sentiment read due today is the next near-term catalyst, expected to reflect deterioration tied to elevated pump prices.

text:
When it finally came, the house felt bigger.

Not emptier.

Bigger.

Treatment began on a Tuesday.

That seemed unfair. Life-changing things should happen on dramatic days, not Tuesdays when the trash cans are still at the curb and the neighbor’s dog won’t stop barking.

The infusion center had recliners lined up near windows, warm blankets stacked in cabinets, and nurses who knew how to be cheerful without lying. Claire came with me to the first appointment. Benjamin drove down for the second.

By the third, I went alone.

Not because no one offered. Because I needed to learn that I could.

I brought a tote bag with peppermint candies, lip balm, a novel I did not read, and a notebook where I wrote things I was afraid to say out loud.

I am scared.

I am angry.

I miss the marriage I thought I had.

I do not miss the marriage I actually had.

That sentence stayed with me.

Grief is strange that way. You can mourn the illusion even after you discover the truth. You can miss a man who never existed because you spent half your life setting a place for him at dinner.

Richard tried to come back twice.

The first time, he appeared on the porch with flowers from Kroger and a face arranged into remorse.

“I made terrible choices,” he said.

I stood behind the storm door wearing a knit cap Claire had bought me.

“Yes,” I said.

“I want to support you through treatment.”

“No.”

His eyes widened. “Ellie.”

“You can communicate through Dana.”

“I’m still your husband.”

“Legally, for now.”

He looked wounded, and for once, I did not rush to bandage him.

The second time, he sent a letter.

Four pages, handwritten on expensive stationery, full of memories he had neglected while making them and feelings he had discovered only after consequences arrived. He wrote about our first apartment, the kids as babies, summer trips to Lake Michigan, the way I used to dance barefoot in the kitchen.

At the end, he wrote: I don’t know who I am without you.

I almost replied.

Then I realized that was still not love.

It was dependency wearing perfume.

Madison had her baby in March, a boy named Oliver.

I learned this from Claire, who learned it from someone at the hospital, because Columbus is a city large enough to get lost in and small enough that news finds you anyway. Richard’s name appeared on no smiling announcement, no polished LinkedIn post, no foundation newsletter.

The divorce took eleven months.

Dana was worth every dollar.

The financial review did not send Richard to prison, despite what some people whispered and others hoped. Real life is not always that clean. But it did force repayment, resignation, and the quiet collapse of his carefully built image.

He left the foundation.

He left the firm.

He moved into a condo twelve miles away with gray walls and rented furniture, close enough to remind us he existed but far enough to stop shaping the weather in my house.

I kept the house.

Not because I wanted the symbol. Because I wanted the hydrangeas.

That spring, after surgery and treatment and more scans than I could count, Dr. Kline used the word remission with cautious optimism. She warned me about follow-ups, recurrence risks, lifestyle changes, and the importance of not treating good news like a finish line.

I listened.

Then I went home and sat on the porch.

The hydrangeas had begun to leaf out, small green promises pushing through old wood….

📊 Morning Markets — Friday, September 25

One thing to watch today: Bond yields are at their highest in nearly two decades and the Fed keeps promising more hikes. There's no blockbuster data to save the tape today - just durable goods, Michigan sentiment, and a market at the mercy of the 10-year.

The bond market is running this show, and it's ugly. The 10-year Treasury yield topped 5.15% before easing back near 5.1%, its highest since 2007; the 30-year hit a post-2004 peak around 5.44%; the 2-year touched a 2023 high. Thursday's session buckled under the weight - the Dow fell 162 points to 51,350, dragged by Walmart and IBM, while the S&P and Nasdaq clung near flat. The relentless Fed chorus keeps stoking it: New York's Williams said the Fed will "likely need to hike again this year," and Philadelphia's Paulson said "modest further tightening may be warranted." October hike odds now sit near 66%, up from under 9% a month ago.

Today's data is second-tier but still worth watching: August durable goods orders at 8:30, then the final University of Michigan consumer sentiment at 10:00 - and inside that report is the inflation-expectations gauge the Fed tracks closely. A jump there would pour more fuel on the yield fire; a soft read offers a little relief. The bigger inflation test, Core PCE, doesn't land until Wednesday next week.

One nuance worth holding onto: not all of this is inflation panic. Analysts note the yield surge is partly technical - weak Treasury auction demand and heavy government borrowing - while market-based long-term inflation expectations have stayed relatively contained. That's the thread of hope. Oil eased Thursday, taking some pressure off, and Trump-Xi trade talks stay in focus. So watch the 10-year above all - whether it holds below or breaks back over 5% - plus the Michigan inflation read and whether beaten-down rate-sensitive names can steady into the weekend. The market spent the week getting pounded by the bond market. Today there's no big number to rescue it - just yields, and nerve. Happy Friday - trade it carefully and finish the week strong.

text:
Researchers secretly put GPS trackers inside 205 old printers and monitors to see where America’s electronic waste really went — 69 crossed national borders, 37 reached Hong Kong, and investigators followed the signals to junkyards where electronics were being smashed apart by hand | ScienceBlog

The dead printer had one job left, and that job was snitching.

Hidden inside its casing sat a GPS tracker with its own SIM card, built to wake once every 24 hours, fix its position by satellite, report to a server and nod off again, as a project feature on urbanNext explained the design. After a recycler in Massachusetts accepted the printer, it drifted to a second recycler in Vermont, then to the Chicago area, then across the Pacific to an e-waste junkyard in Hong Kong’s New Territories, as TIME reported.

That printer was one of 205.

Between July 2014 and February 2016, the Basel Action Network, a Seattle watchdog known as BAN, slipped trackers into old printers and computer screens and dropped them at charities and recyclers around the United States. Its findings appeared in a 2016 report bluntly titled Scam Recycling, and the MIT Senseable City Lab, which pioneered the tracking method, turned the daily pings into an interactive map of all 205 routes.

Where the exported devices ended up

Sixty-nine trackers crossed a national border. Of the devices handed to American recyclers, 40 per cent finished up overseas, the report found. Hong Kong received 37, mainland China 11, Taiwan five, Pakistan four and Mexico three. Thailand and Canada took two apiece, and single devices surfaced in the United Arab Emirates, Togo, Kenya, Cambodia and the Dominican Republic.

Some covered close to 19,000 kilometres, per reporting by PBS NewsHour and EarthFix. BAN traced its Hong Kong arrivals to 48 separate sites in the New Territories, an old farming district along the mainland border.

Hong Kong used to be a waypoint. Much of this junk had long been trucked onwards into mainland China, with Guiyu, a cluster of villages in Guangdong province, the most notorious endpoint. BAN’s executive director, Jim Puckett, told PBS that a Chinese border crackdown called Green Fence made it far harder to get whole devices through, so the Hong Kong yards began doing the dismantling themselves.

Inside the New Territories scrapyards

High over the Pacific, Puckett spent his flight squinting at orange dots on a satellite image while the rest of the cabin slept. Next morning he followed those dots down rutted dirt roads until his receiver counted down the distance to a wall made of old shipping containers. Power drills whined on the far side, punctuated by breaking glass.

Inside, workers were stripping LCD televisions by hand. Snapped fluorescent tubes, the slim lamps that once lit those screens from behind, littered the ground, and each one gives off mercury vapour when broken. Nobody wore a mask. At another yard, printers were stacked about four and a half metres high over a lot roughly the size of a football field, and the people smashing them were dusted black with toner, a powder linked to breathing problems.

“People have the right to know where their stuff goes,” Puckett said.

Why shipping beat recycling

“They knew what they were doing was wrong.” So said a manager at Washington’s Department of Ecology in September 2016, as the agency fined Total Reclaim, a leading Seattle electronics recycler, US$444,000. BAN’s trackers had followed the company’s flat screens to Hong Kong, and the company’s own records showed the shipments went back seven years. PBS noted that Total Reclaim had been a founding member of e-Stewards, the green certification scheme BAN itself set up.

Money explains most of it. Commodity prices had slumped, with copper at half its 2011 price and, by the co-owner’s account, steel falling from US$300 to US$60 a ton. Printers are worth next to nothing, and flat screens are slow and expensive to take apart safely because of those mercury lamps. Filling a container with whole units and handing it to a broker simply pays better.

Law offered little resistance. No federal statute banned e-waste exports, and at the time America was the only industrialised nation that had not ratified the Basel Convention, a treaty meant to stop wealthy countries offloading hazardous waste onto poorer ones.

What one investigation can and cannot prove

How much American e-waste really leaves the country?

Estimates barely overlap. A 2013 survey of recyclers by the US International Trade Commission put exports for dismantling at 0.13 per cent of used electronics collected. UN figures cited by PBS ran from 10 to 40 per cent. Parts of the trade have long argued the problem is exaggerated.

Two hundred and five devices cannot settle that. This was one investigation, run by an advocacy group that also operates a certification scheme for the industry, and it focused on printers and monitors, just the sort of low-value, awkward kit that makes a good export candidate. The method was later written up in a peer-reviewed paper in the journal Waste Management, pitching GPS tracking as a way to spot potentially non-compliant recyclers and trace hidden export routes, and discussing where the approach falls short.

What the trackers deliver is evidence precise enough to act on, down to a specific yard on a specific day.

That evidence keeps piling up. In February 2025, BAN hid trackers in 35 monitors and printers left at drop-off points in Adelaide, Melbourne, Brisbane and Sydney, and within a year seven had surfaced in Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia, the ABC reported. Which operators, brokers or middlemen passed them along remained unclear, so the newest trackers have mapped where the devices went while the harder question, who sent them, is still hanging.

text:
IF I WERE ADVISING POPE LEO IN FRANCE…

If I had somehow found myself sitting around a table with Pope Leo and his advisers as they planned this visit to France, I think the first question I would have asked would have been a very simple one: what, when the aircraft takes off again at the end of these few days, do we actually want to have achieved?

It sounds obvious, but I think it's the most important question to ask, because a papal visit can very easily become a succession of speeches, meetings, ceremonies and carefully negotiated encounters, all perfectly worthwhile in themselves, but without any single idea being communicated strongly enough to remain in the national imagination once the Pope has gone home. Leo has only a few days in France and his presence there will be really important to a lot of people, but he cannot reverse generations of secularisation, rebuild parish life, restore vocations or address every political and social problem confronting the country, and so I would want to think really carefully about the thing France most needs to hear from the successor of St Peter at this particular moment in its history and return to it throughout the visit.

For me, the leitmotif would be something along the lines of: France, remember who you are, rediscover who man is, and do not be afraid to rediscover God.

I don't mean that as a nostalgic appeal for France to pretend that the last two hundred years never happened, or as some romantic attempt to recreate an imagined Catholic golden age. France is not going back to the thirteenth century, and evangelisation cannot consist in wishing that it might. What I mean is that France has been engaged for a very long time in one of the great experiments of modern European civilisation: the attempt to construct a society in which Christianity becomes progressively less important to the way people understand themselves, their families, their communities and ultimately the purpose of human existence.

The promise underlying that experiment has been enormously powerful. As religious belief receded, we were going to become freer and more rational; ancient moral constraints would fall away; material prosperity, technological progress and individual autonomy would give men and women possibilities their ancestors could scarcely have imagined. We would retain the humanitarian and moral achievements of Christian civilisation while gradually dispensing with the metaphysical claims upon which so much of that civilisation had been built.

If I were Leo, I think I would have the courage to ask France, very gently and without the slightest sense of triumphalism, how that experiment is actually going.

Are people happier? Are families stronger? Are young people more hopeful about their futures? Has unprecedented material prosperity satisfied the human longing for meaning? Has sexual liberation produced more secure relationships? Has radical individual autonomy made us less lonely? Has removing God from the centre of our culture made the great questions of suffering, love, death, purpose and human dignity disappear, or have we simply deprived ourselves of the language in which previous generations attempted to answer them?

Above all, I think I would ask one question repeatedly, particularly when speaking to young people: what are we telling our children that their lives are ultimately for?

This is where I think the Church has something much more profound to offer modern France than a list of things Catholicism opposes. Christianity offers an account of what a human being actually is, and that account is desperately needed in a culture which increasingly appears confused about the answer.

The Christian claim is that you are not an accidental collection of matter which happens to be conscious for a few decades between birth and oblivion, nor are you simply a consumer whose purpose is to accumulate experiences before death. Your value is not determined by your productivity, intelligence, health, attractiveness, wealth or usefulness to somebody else. You are created deliberately and loved before you achieve anything. Your body has meaning, your freedom has a purpose beyond the satisfaction of appetite, love necessarily involves sacrifice, suffering does not render a life worthless, and the weak and dependent remain infinitely valuable even when they can offer nothing economically useful in return.

Most importantly, Christianity claims that all of this is not simply a comforting philosophy devised to make existence bearable. It rests upon an astonishing historical claim: that God entered His creation in the person of Jesus Christ, suffered, died and rose again, and that consequently neither suffering nor death has the final word.

If that were the central argument, I would then use each stage of the French visit to develop another part of it rather than treating every audience as an entirely separate event.

At the Élysée, I would speak about the limits of politics and remind those exercising political power that human dignity is not something bestowed by the state but something the state is morally obliged to recognise. Governments can create laws and institutions, but they cannot manufacture the meaning of human existence, and history should make us extremely wary whenever political authority begins to imagine that the value of human life is something which can be defined according to utility, dependency or circumstance.

At UNESCO, the same argument could be applied to technology and artificial intelligence. The most important question about AI is surely not simply how intelligent our machines can become, but what kind of human beings we are becoming while we build them. Our technological power has developed at an astonishing speed, but capability and wisdom are not the same thing, and a civilisation which continually asks whether something can be done without first developing a coherent understanding of whether it should be done risks becoming immensely powerful without becoming correspondingly wise.

Then there is Notre-Dame, where the argument becomes almost tangible. France magnificently restored that cathedral after the terrible fire of 2019, and the achievement deserves admiration, but Notre-Dame was not built merely because medieval Frenchmen wanted Paris to possess an exceptionally beautiful building. Those stones were raised by generations of people who believed something to be true. The altar, the windows, the sculptures, the orientation of the building and those extraordinary vaults all belong to a coherent Christian understanding of reality. France has demonstrated that it knows how to preserve the monuments of Christian civilisation; the more interesting question is whether it still understands the faith which made those monuments intelligible.

But if I were Leo, it would be the encounter with young people which I would regard as perhaps the greatest opportunity of the entire journey, because I suspect they need something rather more substantial than another general encouragement to hope.

I would tell them that our culture has given them a deeply inadequate definition of freedom. Freedom cannot simply mean keeping every possibility permanently available, because the greatest things human beings ever do require us to close possibilities down. Marriage, parenthood, friendship, vocation and faith become meaningful precisely because we commit ourselves to something beyond ourselves. A person committed to nothing may theoretically remain completely free, but eventually he may also discover that he belongs nowhere and to nobody.

I would tell them that they do not have to spend their lives endlessly constructing an identity from nothing, as though every human being arrives in the world as a blank sheet upon which an entirely autonomous self must be invented. I would acknowledge their loneliness and anxiety rather than dismissing them as the inevitable complaints of youth, and ask whether a culture offering almost limitless digital connection, sexual freedom, entertainment and consumer choice has actually delivered the happiness it promised.

And then, unapologetically, I would tell them about Christ.

Not a carefully diluted Christ translated into the therapeutic vocabulary of the age until there is almost nothing distinctively Christian left, but the Christ who tells the rich young man that possessions cannot satisfy him; who tells the woman at the well that the thirst she is trying to satisfy is deeper than she realises; who tells frightened disciples not to be afraid; who offers forgiveness to sinners; who weeps at the grave of Lazarus and then tells Martha that death is not the end; and who makes the profoundly countercultural claim that the person who spends his life desperately trying to preserve it will ultimately lose it, while the person willing to give his life away may finally discover what life is for.

I would also make Leo's encounter with the catechumens and newly baptised Catholics central to the visit, because something genuinely interesting is happening among young French people. Thousands are approaching the Church for baptism, many of them having grown up without the cultural Catholicism their grandparents would once have taken for granted. Rather than immediately telling them what their conversion means for the Church, I would want the Pope to ask them what they had discovered.

What did you find here that the surrounding culture was unable to give you? What made you walk into a Catholic church when so many previous generations were walking out? What did you encounter in Christianity which persuaded you not merely to admire it but to change your life because of it?

And then I would listen carefully to the answers, because those young converts may understand something about the evangelisation of post-Christian Europe which those of us who inherited Christianity can easily miss.

Finally Leo will go to Lourdes, and I can hardly imagine a better place to bring the argument together. After the presidential palace and UNESCO, after the speeches, diplomatic receptions and intellectual discussion about the future of Europe, the Pope will arrive at a grotto where an impoverished fourteen-year-old girl once knelt in the mud and said she had encountered the Mother of God.

There is something wonderfully subversive about that progression. The modern world instinctively looks upwards towards power, wealth, expertise, celebrity and influence, whereas Christianity repeatedly directs our attention downwards: towards a stable in Bethlehem, towards fishermen, lepers and the poor, towards a man nailed to a Cross and, at Lourdes, towards Bernadette Soubirous kneeling beside a muddy grotto while respectable society wondered whether she had lost her mind.

That is where I think I would want to leave France, not with an accusation but with an invitation to reconsider the direction in which modern European civilisation has been travelling. France has tried extraordinary material prosperity, consumerism, sexual liberation and radical individual autonomy. It has increasingly tried constructing a public culture in which God is unnecessary to the great questions of human existence. It seems perfectly reasonable, after several generations of this experiment, to ask whether it has delivered the flourishing it promised and whether the loneliness, anxiety, demographic collapse and loss of meaning visible across so much of modern Europe might suggest that something essential has been forgotten.

Christianity does not ultimately ask France merely to preserve its cathedrals, admire its saints or remember that its history was once Catholic. Those things matter, but they are not evangelisation.

The genuinely unsettling Christian proposition is that the faith which produced so much of the civilisation modern France still cherishes might not simply be historically interesting or culturally useful.

It might actually be true.

If I were advising Pope Leo, that is the possibility I would want hanging in the air after he had gone home. I would want a young Frenchman who heard him at the Stade de France, a politician who heard him at the Élysée, an intellectual who heard him at UNESCO and an ordinary family who encountered the visit through television or social media to find themselves returning to the same question.

Perhaps the crisis confronting modern France is not simply that it has forgotten part of its history.

Perhaps, somewhere along the way, it has forgotten something about what a human being is.

And perhaps the answer is not to travel further down the same road, but to turn around and look again at what was left behind.

France, remember who you are, rediscover who man is, and do not be afraid to rediscover God.

text:
At the Élysée Palace in Paris Sept. 25, Pope Leo XIV praised France's work to serve the common good, calling the nation a source of inspiration.

Pointing to the restoration of the Notre Dame Cathedral, he said it demonstrates that “what seemed irreparably destroyed can be reborn through mutual cooperation” and stands as “an eloquent witness to the unity born of commitment to a common cause.”

The Holy Father also cautioned against placing unlimited faith in technological solutions, warning that when science and technology are not guided by wisdom, they can “offer immediate solutions that apparently address people's wishes and their pain, but can seriously divert them from the greater good to which they aspire.” He expressed concern about practices including “genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the trade in human organs or the possibility of arranging one's own death,” insisting that “the protection of every human life is a duty incumbent upon each and every one of us.”

Pope Leo closed with an appeal for peace, urging France to be “a tireless champion of peace and multilateralism” and help build “a peace that is unarmed and disarming.” (OSV News photo/Teresa Suarez, pool via Reuters)

text:
Plant-based meat labels make food seem less masculine, study finds | Eric W. Dolan, PsyPost

A new study indicates that simply labeling a dish as a plant-based meat alternative makes meat-eaters view it as less masculine, leading to more negative evaluations. This resistance to plant-based options tends to be strongest among people who hold hostile sexist beliefs. The findings were published in Social Psychological and Personality Science.

Animal farming places a heavy burden on the environment and raises broad ethical and public health concerns. Plant-based meat alternatives, which are foods made from textured plant protein designed to imitate the taste, appearance, and texture of real meat, offer a way to reduce this impact. But many meat-eaters remain highly resistant to these alternatives. The divide is heavily gendered. For example, a 2024 study covered by PsyPost found that vegetarianism has grown steadily among women over a 15-year period, while rates among men have barely budged.

Researchers suspect this resistance is tied to the cultural symbolism of food. A 2012 study demonstrated that people across multiple cultures subconsciously associate meat with maleness and masculinity. Because meat is symbolically linked to strength and power, cutting it out of a diet can feel like a loss of status. Building on this idea, a 2023 paper conceptualized giving up meat as a direct threat to a man’s sense of manhood, which triggers psychological resistance.

More recently, scientists have noticed that these dietary choices are linked to broader beliefs about social dominance. A 2020 study provided empirical evidence that hostile sexist attitudes are strongly tied to the belief that humans should dominate animals and the natural world. Hostile sexism involves negative evaluations of women and femininity, along with the belief that women are inferior to men.

“There is now quite a lot of evidence that meat is culturally associated with masculinity, and that vegetarians and vegans (particularly vegan men) can be perceived as less masculine,” Kristof Dhont, a reader in psychology at the University of Kent and director of the SHARK Lab, told PsyPost.

“We wanted to find out whether these associations also have implications for perceptions and evaluations of plant-based meat alternatives themselves, even when they closely resemble conventional meat,” Dhont said. “In this sense, the symbolic meaning attached to ‘plant-based’ food could be a barrier to its acceptance.”

The research, led by Alina Salmen alongside Dhont, aimed to see if merely labeling a dish as plant-based alters how people perceive its masculinity and appeal. They also wanted to test whether hostile sexism would amplify these effects, making people who endorse male dominance the most likely to reject feminine-coded alternatives.

To test this, the researchers conducted two experiments. In the first experiment, they recruited 216 university students in the United Kingdom who eat meat. Participants viewed nine images of food, such as burgers, meatballs, and tacos. The images were exactly the same for everyone, but the text labels accompanying them were randomly rotated.

A third of the participants saw a specific dish labeled as “regular meat,” another third saw it labeled as “plant-based meat,” and the final third saw it labeled as “cultured meat.” Cultured meat is real animal tissue grown in a lab from cell cultures, eliminating the need for animal slaughter. Participants rated each dish’s appeal, expected smell, expected taste, and their likelihood of eating it on a 7-point scale. They also rated the perceived masculinity of each dish on a scale ranging from extremely feminine to extremely masculine, and they completed a questionnaire measuring their endorsement of hostile sexism.

Even though the food images were identical, dishes labeled as plant-based were rated as less masculine than dishes labeled as regular meat. The plant-based label also led to worse evaluations in terms of expected taste, smell, and overall appeal. Cultured meat was also evaluated more negatively than regular meat.

When the researchers looked closer, they found that lower masculinity ratings were linked to these negative evaluations, but only for participants who scored higher in hostile sexism. Those with lower levels of sexism did not evaluate the food worse just because they perceived it as less masculine.

In the second experiment, the research team recruited a larger sample of 1,182 adults in the United States, evenly split between men and women, all of whom were meat-eaters. Participants viewed six identical food images, with the labels rotated between “regular meat” and “plant-based meat.” They rated the same qualities as in the first experiment, but the researchers also added a measure of “food distancing.” Participants indicated how much they agreed with statements like, “I would not want to be seen eating this dish in public.”

The second experiment replicated the findings of the first. On a 7-point scale, the average overall evaluation dropped from 5.64 for regular meat to 4.74 for plant-based meat. The perceived masculinity dropped from an average of 4.40 to 3.96. The participants also indicated a stronger desire to distance themselves from the dishes labeled as plant-based.

The researchers identified a psychological chain reaction in the data. The plant-based label led people to view the dish as less masculine, which prompted a desire to distance themselves from the food. This urge to avoid being associated with the dish then predicted a worse overall evaluation.

Hostile sexism played a powerful role in this chain reaction. People with higher levels of hostile sexism were especially likely to distance themselves from dishes they viewed as lacking masculinity, driving their negative evaluations.

“It is perhaps worth highlighting that the effects of the plant-based label were clearly observed not only among men but also among women,” Dhont noted. Both men and women in the study showed this pattern, suggesting that hostile sexism shapes food choices across genders.

“The size of these shifts clearly differs between people,” Dhont explained. “For the overall evaluations the effect was roughly twice the size among those higher in sexism compared with those lower in sexism. The gap between people higher and lower in sexism was even larger when it came to how strongly the label affected perceived masculinity and self-distancing.”

The findings align with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that men who identify as more masculine consume more meat and are highly resistant to adopting plant-based diets. It is worth noting, however, that the 2023 study measured men’s personal masculine identities, whereas the new study focused on the perceived masculinity of the food itself and the observer’s sexist beliefs.

“One key takeaway is that our evaluations of food are not determined only by the food itself,” Dhont said. “The societal stigma surrounding plant-based diets and veganism, including the perceived lack of masculine value, can negatively affect evaluations of plant-based meat alternatives.”

As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. First, the researchers measured perceived masculinity rather than actively manipulating it in a controlled way. This means they cannot say for sure that the loss of masculine symbolism directly caused the negative evaluations. Masculinity and femininity were also measured on a single continuous scale. It is possible that food can hold both masculine and feminine associations at the same time, which future studies might try to measure separately.

There are a few things to keep in mind regarding the participants’ past experiences. Some people might have had prior bad experiences eating actual plant-based meats, which could have influenced their ratings of the images.

“These were judgments of images rather than actual purchasing or eating behavior, so the size of the effect in real-world food choices remains an important question for future research,” Dhont said.

“It would be interesting to see how such findings play out when people actually taste the food or in actual consumption and purchasing behavior,” he added. “For example, we could let people taste plant-based products while experimentally varying how they are labeled, or observe behavioral choices and purchases when people select items from a menu or buffet.”

To successfully promote plant-based diets, marketing strategies might need to account for these psychological barriers. The authors suggest that framing meat alternatives in ways that appeal to modern, flexible ideals of masculinity might help overcome the stigma associated with vegan and vegetarian options.

“Another big question is how we can change the symbolism surrounding meat versus plant-based products, and in turn people’s perceptions and reactions to them,” Dhont said. “What strategies can increase openness to plant-based alternatives without simply reinforcing traditional gender stereotypes?”

"One standard Defendants appear to offer---reflected in letters they sent to Plaintiffs on September 22, 2026, identifying their objectionable reporting—is so vague it hardly does the trick," Kelly said, referring to the Trump administration's allegation that one of the outlets "exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex."

Boutrous also noted during Wednesday's hearing that only one CNN story cited by the administration to highlight why the outlets were being kicked out was written by a reporter with access to the White House and that the stories cited "are just garden variety reporting."

Kelly, in his ruling, noted this and that the CNN story cited as a national security concern — a report about the planned rebuilding of a bunker under the East Wing — was published months before reporter Klein's press pass was renewed this summer.

"None of Defendants' arguments convince the Court that Plaintiffs are not likely to succeed on their due process claim," Kelly wrote.

Moreover, Kelly wrote that the plaintiffs had shown "that they are likely to suffer irreparable harm absent a temporary restraining order," and that it would be in the public's interest to reinstate reporters' press badges.

"Plaintiffs- and the public—have an abiding interest in maintaining the status quo ante given the importance of the free press, which ' stands as one of the great interpreters between the government and the people,'" the ruling said.

At the start of Wednesday's hearing, Kelly noted that he had presided over a similar case in 2018, when Trump booted then-CNN correspondent Jim Acosta after a heated exchange between him and the president, and had to abide by past precedent in the court.

“There is a due process claim and a due process issue that seems to me the first stop in figuring out how to resolve the motion,” Kelly said at the hearing.

Kelly's ruling Thursday said that the circumstances here "are not so 'extraordinary' as to permit deviation" from the principles of due process "that a deprivation of liberty 'be preceded by notice and opportunity for hearing.'"

TV networks stand with CNN

Thursday's ruling means the television pool, of which CNN is one of five members, could resume live and taped coverage of presidential events—though the organizers have yet to share any updated guidance.

Under a longstanding arrangement, the five networks take turns filming the president and providing live footage to one another and the wider press corps. Local TV stations, newspaper websites and media outlets worldwide rely on that coverage.

In a show of solidarity, the five major networks said they would not cover the president's speeches and appearances after Trump barred CNN from fulfilling its assigned duties in the White House pool on Monday.

"The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting," ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC said in a rare joint statement.   KEK

text:
HM Dele Alake and the Quiet Making of a Nigerian Minerals Renaissance

Our elders say one hand cannot lift a load onto the head, owọ́ kan kì í gbé ẹrù dé orí (one hand cannot lift a load onto the head), and nobody who has watched Nigeria long enough needs the point explained. Nation-building is a heavy load that needs many useful and active hands under it, steady ones that do not let go when the weight shifts. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, has had many such hands around him over the decades. Few have been as constant, or as unshowy about it, as Dr Henry Oladele Alake, the Honourable Minister of Solid Minerals Development.

Dr Alake was born and raised in Lagos, first at Surulere Baptist Primary School, then at Igbobi College, and later at the University of Lagos. He joined the Concord Group of newspapers in late 1985, and journalism became his first home. By 1989, he was editor of Sunday Concord, a post he held until 1995. That was the era of the June 12 struggle, and he was not a spectator. He worked in the thick of the Abiola campaign, and after the annulment, the Abacha regime hounded him for his candour, which pushed him into exile. There he worked alongside NADECO figures and, importantly, alongside President Tinubu, in the fight to restore democracy. Those years forged a bond that no later appointment would have to create. It was already made.

When democracy returned, Lagos became the proving ground. In June 1999, Governor Tinubu named him Special Adviser on Information and Strategy, and that October he became the state's Commissioner for Information and Strategy, serving until 2007. Eight years is a long time to hold one of the most exposed jobs in any government. He held it through the bruising early days of the Fourth Republic, when Lagos was practically at war with the centre. Those who dealt with him then remember a man they could rely on to explain a policy plainly and defend it without flinching. In 2014, he returned to the national stage as media director of the Buhari campaign, and in 2023 he directed media and communications for the Tinubu/Shettima Presidential Campaign Council.

Loyalty is easy to claim, so let me offer evidence of a kind that does not depend on his office. Long before anyone was talking about Aso Rock, Alake was among those who lent his voice to projecting President Tinubu on all known fora, virtual and non-virtual platforms, including a weekly programme anchored by Prince Ade Omole many years ago that carried the Tinubu message to audiences beyond Nigeria's shores. When the 2023 campaign came, and Prince Omole headed the Diaspora Directorate, Alake joined a virtual session to address the London audience, at a moment when Diaspora influence mattered and needed persuading. Nobody was paying him for these appearances. He simply showed up, as he always has. That is what a pillar does: it carries weight without being noticed until someone tries to remove it.

Then came the surprise. In 2023, the President put a career journalist in charge of solid minerals. Sceptics rolled their eyes, and some said so openly. Even Governor Abdullahi Sule of Nasarawa, whose state now sits at the centre of the lithium story, has admitted he doubted the appointment of a media professional to such a technical portfolio. The doubters have since had to eat their words. Solid minerals revenue rose from about ₦6 billion in 2023 to more than ₦38 billion in 2024, and about ₦71 billion by 2025, with more than $2.6 billion in processing projects attracted. Sule now says Alake has become a better mining engineer than he is.

The numbers came from decisions that were not always popular. Like Jesus clearing the corrupt merchants and money changers out of the temple, Alake began by cleaning the dirty house. He revoked 1,633 licences for non-payment of annual fees in late 2023 and 924 dormant ones in early 2024, freeing ground for serious operators. He rewrote the community development agreement guidelines so that host communities must consent, and he set up the Mining Marshals to confront illegal mining. His central principle is simple enough to fit on a poster: nobody gets a mining lease without a plan for adding value at home. Nigeria has spent decades digging up its wealth and shipping it away for others to finish, and he has insisted that has to end. The result is now visible. 

West Africa's largest lithium processing plant has been commissioned in Nasarawa State. The Nigerian Geological Survey Agency has confirmed a polymetallic belt in Kaduna State, holding platinum group metals, gold, nickel, copper, lithium, and rare earths. If the Renewed Hope agenda is about diversifying an economy that has leaned on oil for too long, then this ministry is one of its most concrete answers.

This week the story moved to New York, where Alake spent the 81st United Nations General Assembly doing what he does best, which is turning conversation into commitments. As chairman of the Africa Minerals Strategy Group, he pressed the case for a Continental Integration and Economic Assurance Declaration, meant to give Africa's mineral value chains a unified architecture. He also proposed a Mine Emergency and Community Development Fund and an African safety facility to bring artisanal miners into the formal fold. That last proposal deserves more attention than it received. It grew from the deaths of miners in unsafe pits, which tells you he treats this as a human question and not only an investment one.

Then, on Wednesday, at Nigeria's Mission House in New York, the Honourable Minister and Christopher Landau, the United States Deputy Secretary of State, signed and exchanged a framework agreement to bring American investment into Nigeria's mining sector. The government estimates the mineral resources deal at $700 billion. The document covers geological data and exploration, mineral development and processing, infrastructure and technical capacity, and it is meant to give private American and Nigerian firms a government-backed platform on which to do business. 

Alake's own words at the ceremony were characteristically plain. He said some agreements manage the present and some shape the future, and that this one belonged to the second kind. He was equally honest about what comes next, telling the room that a signature is only a promise and that results are the proof. Landau, for his part, called Nigeria Africa's fastest-growing economy and a regional power, and said the two countries had done things together in the past eighteen months that they had never done before. 

President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, has set a target for the country of a one-trillion-dollar economy by 2030. It is a bold number. The Minister for Finance has acknowledged that it will take sustained growth of ten to twelve per cent a year, against a present GDP of roughly $375 billion, and sceptics among economists have said so loudly. I will not pretend the road is short. But no nation has ever built a trillion-dollar economy on crude oil and good intentions alone, and this is where Alake's contribution becomes clear. He has spent three years driving the piles deep into the bedrock: the licensing clean-up, the value-addition rule, the lithium refineries, the community agreements, and now a partnership with the world's largest economy. Piling is unglamorous work. Nobody photographs it, and once the concrete is poured, nobody sees it again. But every tall building stands on it, and the taller the tower, the deeper the piles must go. When Nigeria's trillion-dollar tower rises, a good part of what holds it up will be what DR HENRY OLADELE ALAKE buried in the ground.

There is a private side to the man that colleagues of every stripe mention. He is warm and easy to reach. He will take a call, receive a stranger and laugh readily, and he has never mistaken office for altitude. Yet friendliness is not softness, and those who have tried to lean on him have found a wall. He is firm about licences, about the rules of engagement, and about what Nigeria will and will not accept from investors. In my experience, that combination is rarer than it should be in public life. Most officials are either approachable and useless or effective and unbearable.

His handling of the opposition shows the same temperament. Alake has the newsman's instinct for the argument, and the Yoruba proverb ẹni mọ ọ́ kọ́, ẹni kò ọ́ mọ̀ fits him well (those who know him do not confront him, and those who confront him do not know him). Those who have watched him work know better than to pick a fight, because he goes through the facts in a level voice until the questioner either agrees or has nothing left to say. Only the uninformed step up to him, and they do not stay long. He does not suffer fools gladly. That is astuteness of the old school, the kind that wins arguments and leaves you with scars of battle, and the opposition parties, who have thrown plenty at this administration, have not found an easy target in him.

HM Alake has gone from a Surulere classroom to a Lagos newsroom, through exile and government, to the top table of African minerals diplomacy, and he has done it while staying recognisably the same man. He was a hand under the load for Asiwaju Tinubu when it cost something to be one, and he is still there now that it carries a title. The weight of the President's trillion-dollar ambition is heavy, and it will take many hands to lift it. This is one that has never let go.

Hon. Tosin Olayinka, LL.B (Hons), B.L., LL.M (London)

text:
14 Tishrei - Dedication of the Temple - 826 BCE

On this day in 826 BCE, King Solomon completed the dedication of the First Temple. The Book of Kings records that Solomon and all Israel with him, a vast assembly gathered from the far north down to the brook of Egypt, celebrated seven days and seven days, fourteen days in all. The Book of Chronicles makes the reckoning explicit. There were two separate weeks. First came the seven days of dedicating the altar and the House, and then, immediately after, the seven days of the festival of Sukkos. Working backward from the day the people were finally sent home, the twenty-third of Tishrei, through the festival and the closing day that follows it, places the dedication on the eighth through the fourteenth of Tishrei. It ended on the day before Sukkos began.

The Talmud treats this as the source for the principle that one celebration may not be folded into another. Had it been permitted, Solomon would simply have carried the dedication forward into the festival rather than holding the two weeks distinctly apart. The same passage records something astonishing about that first week. Yom Kippur fell inside it, and the Jewish people did not fast that year at all. The dedication of the Temple overrode it. Afterward they were seized with dread that they had brought punishment on themselves for eating on the holiest day of the year, until a voice from heaven reassured them that every one of them was destined for life in the World to Come.

The dedication had nearly failed before it began. When Solomon came to bring the Ark into the Holy of Holies, the gates of the Temple locked shut against him. He offered twenty-four songs of praise and was not answered. Only when he set aside his own merit and invoked his father's instead, asking God to remember the kindnesses of David His servant, did the gates open. The Talmud says that at that moment the faces of David's enemies darkened like the bottom of a pot, because all Israel understood that David had been forgiven.

Captive elephants are often deprived of the freedom, social bonds, and natural environments they need to thrive, and are kept chained and in isolation without adequate food or water, leading them to lash out and pose a risk to the public when used in crowded settings.

Mechanical elephants are increasingly used in temples, for safari rides, at weddings, political rallies, and in advertisements, film, and photo shoots.

text:
ARE THE FLORIDA GATORS THE STRONGEST TEAM IN COLLEGE FOOTBALL?

The Wall Street Journal has published 900 words suggesting yes, and I need to walk through the arithmetic, because somebody should.

The headline number is 14,443 pounds. That is how much the Gators improved their combined maxes across four lifts. The story helpfully notes this is enough to pick up an African elephant.

Now divide it.

An FBS roster is capped at 105 players. So 14,443 divided by 105 is about 138 pounds per player.

Across four lifts.

That is roughly 34 pounds added to each man's max on the squat, the bench, the clean and the dead lift over an entire offseason.

Thirty four pounds. One plate and a change of socks.

That is not a transformation. That is what happens when a nineteen year old lifts regularly for four months and eats. It is the default outcome of showing up.

But 34 pounds does not make a headline, so you stack 105 players times four lifts, arrive at five figures, and reach for an elephant.

The elephant is not a unit of measurement. The elephant is a press release.

And speaking of, one of the photographs in the piece is credited to UAA Communications, which is the University Athletic Association. Florida's own athletic department.

The school supplied the pictures for the story about how good the school is.

Then there is the squat. A running back put up 600 pounds, which the article calls astronomical and says the staff would not let him add more weight to the machine.

The machine.

Sir, a squat rack is not a machine. And 600 is a strong number for a running back and a Tuesday in most SEC weight rooms. Astronomical is doing an enormous amount of work in that sentence.

Now the resume. Three wins, 99 points of combined margin, which sounds terrifying until you look at the opponents.

FAU, 66 to 21.

Campbell, 52 to 3.

Campbell is either a university in North Carolina or a soup manufacturer in New Jersey, and based on that score I am not prepared to rule either one out. Somebody check whether the Gators ran out onto the field and hit a can.

And Auburn, 44 to 39. On the road. By five.

So 94 of those 99 points came against a Group of Five team and an opponent with a condensed vegetable division. The one time they played an SEC opponent, a mediocre one, they won by a field goal and change.

And now they are a home favorite against the number four team in the country, which is somehow being reported as a surprise rather than as a home team getting points in Gainesville, which happens every year, in every sport, in every stadium with a fan base.

Apparently Florida is back.

Texas was back three weeks ago. I own a hat about it.

Speaking as a Miami graduate, let me offer the correct September posture. My school beat Florida A&M 77 to 7 this month. I did not learn a single thing about my team that day, and neither did anyone else.

Beat somebody. Then call the Journal.

@GatorsFB, serious question, are you 34 pounds strong? Because that is the number. I have seen dads at Planet Fitness make that jump between Thanksgiving and Easter.

@OleMissFB, you are welcome to weigh in, because your month looks nothing like theirs.

Louisville, ranked, 41 to 38. LSU, ranked, 32 to 24. And a girl named Charlotte, 41 to 9, because everyone needs a Saturday off.

Two ranked opponents beaten. And you sent Lane Kiffin back to Baton Rouge with a full understanding of how Oxford felt about December.

That is not a rough month. That is the best month anybody has had.

So are you frightened that Florida found the weight room?

Kickoff is Saturday. One of you is about to find out whether any of this was ever about the weight room.

The elephant can wait.
