text:
🪑🌾 Sjoe! We found the Reserve Bank — now where did we put the title deeds? ~ 🌱🏛️ Less monument polishing, more institutional gardening ~ 🇿🇦🔌🌱 The institutional wiring job has reached the land department.
South Africa already possesses the one institutional design that has demonstrably protected value under pressure. The Reserve Bank Governor operates under constitutional independence: fixed term, removal only for cause, published criteria, written reasons, judicial oversight. 

That design has kept the currency standing while the broader state recorded incomplete asset registers, continued private rentals of up to R6 billion a year, and a property portfolio of roughly R155 billion that still struggles with vacancies and verification gaps. 

The same design can now be applied to land. 

A one-term Land Governor, insulated exactly as the Reserve Bank is insulated, would keep Section 25 reform alive while giving markets rules they can price. 

Trevor Manuel’s thirteen-year fiscal record supplies the concrete calibration point. Destiny is not asking for nostalgia. It is asking whether competence will finally be allowed to outrank loyalty for one finite term so the light planted by Mandela and currently shining through Kganyago can grow into productive land governance.

That is the claim. Everything that follows is evidence arranged to test it.

1. The Seed That Was Planted and Then Under-Watered

Nelson Mandela served one presidential term, 1994 to 1999, and left. He did not cling. He did not rearrange the furniture of power so that the same face could remain indefinitely. He treated finite tenure itself as a form of strength: leadership measured by the quality of the precedent left behind rather than by the number of years occupied. 

In the early years of democracy this choice carried unusual force. 

The constitutional settlement of 1996 had already embedded limits and balances; Mandela’s personal decision to honour a single term reinforced the principle that power is held in trust, not in perpetuity. 

Later political culture largely set that model aside. 

Cabinets rotated, appointments proliferated, and the quiet discipline of exit lost its prestige. The conversation now returns to it because every claim of renewal must still be tested against the willingness to set a high bar and then step aside. 

Linking that single term to a possible one-term Land Governor role is not sentiment. It is institutional memory. The seed was the demonstration that exit can be an act of power.

Political scientists have long noted that term limits do more than constrain ambition; they alter incentives. When leaders know the clock is running, the premium shifts from personal continuity to institutional legacy. 

Mandela’s departure created space for successors to be judged on delivery rather than inheritance. That space narrowed in subsequent decades as the appointment filter grew denser. The under-appreciation of the original precedent is therefore not accidental. It is the predictable result of a system that rewards occupancy over exit.

Sjoe!
A man who could have stayed chose to leave, and the country spent the next three decades proving how rare that choice remains.

Stirring Questions: 
Does treating Mandela’s single term as mere personal modesty beg the question by assuming that the institutional precedent he set has no continuing force? 
What measurable difference would a genuine one-term limit on a Land Governor make to the risk premium investors currently attach to South African land? 
If finite power was the original seed, why has later practice so consistently preferred indefinite occupancy of the appointment filter? 

These questions matter because a country that forgets the difference between a seed and a monument will keep planting statues while the soil remains unworked.

2. The Light That Is Already On

Lesetja Kganyago has held the Reserve Bank Governorship under the protection of Section 224. In January 2025 he was unanimously elected Stellenbosch University’s 16th Chancellor and formally installed on 20 June 2025. 

The conversation treats this not as ceremonial decoration but as living proof that rules-based independence can still function under pressure. 

Broader economic costs linked to state capture have been estimated as high as R1.5 trillion; the Zondo Commission’s more precise accounting of tainted expenditure is substantially lower, yet the scale of institutional damage is not in dispute. 

Through that period the currency retained a degree of stability that fiscal and administrative systems elsewhere did not. 

Kganyago is not offered as a political saviour. He is offered as operational evidence that when the appointment filter is constrained by fixed term, cause-only removal and public criteria, measurable results become possible. 

The light is no longer only historical memory. It is currently switched on inside one institution.

The ceremonial extension of that independence into a university setting carries its own quiet signal. Stellenbosch, once an Afrikaner stronghold, now places a black central banker in its highest ceremonial office. 

The appointment does not rewrite history; it demonstrates that institutional forms can travel across domains when the underlying rules remain intact. Monetary policy and academic governance are different crafts, yet both benefit from insulation against short-term political weather. 

The fact that the same individual can move from one to the other without loss of credibility suggests that the design itself, rather than any single personality, is doing the protective work.

Sjoe!
The currency kept its footing while the furniture went missing. Independence, it turns out, is not a mood. It is a structure.

Stirring Questions: 
If independence has protected the currency, why has the identical design never been applied to the domain where uncertainty most directly deters investment and formal jobs? 
Does assuming that ceremonial roles cannot influence institutional culture beg the question by treating symbolism as the opposite of substance rather than one of its possible instruments? 
What would falsify the claim that Kganyago’s record is transferable? 

These questions matter because a country that can see the light in one building and still refuse to wire the next is choosing darkness for reasons that have nothing to do with electricity.

3. The Mechanism That Already Exists

An independent Land Governor would copy the Reserve Bank template exactly: fixed non-renewable term, removal only for cause, published objective criteria, written reasons for every major decision, automatic judicial review. 

Section 25 would remain intact. Equitable access would remain the constitutional duty. The only change would be that operational decisions would move one step further from the electoral cycle and the loyalty filter. 

The state currently owns a property portfolio valued at approximately R155 billion—roughly 88 000 buildings and 5 million hectares—yet still spends up to R6 billion a year on private rentals while many of its own assets stand vacant, poorly maintained or incompletely recorded. 

Auditor-General findings on DIRCO’s movable assets have repeatedly highlighted verification failures. The 2024 Expropriation Act permits nil compensation in defined circumstances; that provision has raised the downside risk that lenders, insurers and equity partners must price. 

The conversation’s claim is simple: the administrative culture that cannot fully account for its own chairs and heaters is not the culture that should be scaled into a comprehensive national land registry without institutional insulation.

International experience with independent property or land agencies in other middle-income democracies shows that credibility, once established, compounds. 

Markets reward institutions that treat their own rules as binding. 

South Africa already possesses the constitutional language and the operational precedent. What it has lacked is the decision to apply the same logic to the asset class that most directly shapes long-term investment and formal employment. 

Incomplete registers are not a temporary inconvenience; they are a daily signal that title remains harder to price than it should be. 

An independent office would not eliminate political debate. It would relocate the operational decisions one step further from the short-term incentives that currently dominate.

Sjoe!
A state that cannot find its own heaters is asking the market to trust it with the title deeds of the nation. The chairs, it turns out, are not a metaphor.

Stirring Questions: 
What measurable metrics—complete registers, reduced private rentals, productive hectares transferred with retained employment, net investment inflows—would demonstrate that an independent Land Governor is working? 
Can ordinary legislation create independence robust enough to survive political cycles, or is constitutional protection required? 
If the current climate cannot manage the assets it already owns, what happens when the scale of the register multiplies? 

These questions matter because they keep the argument falsifiable. 

An independent office is not a slogan. It is a testable design. The country can measure whether it delivers predictability and jobs or whether it becomes another elegant framework that dies quietly in the policy cemetery.

4. The Bridge That Still Stands

Trevor Manuel served as Finance Minister from 1996 to 2009. During the core Mbeki years average real GDP growth reached approximately 4.1–4.2 percent. The government recorded budget surpluses in 2006/07 and 2007/08. Debt-to-GDP fell to around 23–26 percent. 

Net job creation in strong years approached or exceeded 500 000 posts. 

That period remains the last clear demonstration that remedial policy could coexist with macroeconomic capacity. Later years saw slower growth, rising debt and the dual movement of an unreformed loyalty filter plus intensified racial ownership gates. 

The conversation does not treat Manuel’s record as nostalgia. It treats it as the concrete calibration point against which any future intensity of race-based measures can be tested. 

Placing competence of that profile over the land-race nexus for one finite, rules-insulated term would signal that productive use, title security and measurable outcomes now take priority. 

The bridge between Mandela’s seed and Kganyago’s living light already exists in the historical data. The only question is whether anyone will walk across it.

Fiscal credibility is not an abstract virtue. 

It is the condition that allows long-term capital to price risk and commit. During the surplus years the state was able to expand social spending while still reducing the debt burden. That combination is rare. It required both political will and technical discipline. 

The subsequent erosion of those conditions did not occur in a vacuum; it coincided with the retention of an appointment practice that Zondo later identified as subordinating constitutional standards of professionalism to party loyalty. 

Recalling the earlier calibration is therefore not a call to freeze history. It is a call to recognise the last period in which the numbers and the intentions moved in the same direction.

Sjoe!
The country once produced budget surpluses and half a million jobs a year while still advancing redress. Treating that period as permanently unavailable says more about institutional incentives than about historical necessity.

Stirring Questions: 
If the Manuel years demonstrated that remedial tools could operate alongside strong growth and job creation, what evidence would falsify the claim that further radicalisation of ownership gates is required? 
Does the coincidence of slower growth and intensified racial rules raise the question of causal direction? 
What institutional interests are served by treating the earlier calibration as permanently unavailable? 

These questions matter because a country that cannot recognise its own successful periods is condemned to treat every shortfall as a mandate for more of the same intensity.

5. The Loop That Keeps Closing on Itself

Under-delivery has repeatedly been met by tighter ownership thresholds and numerical targets while the loyalty-based appointment practice identified by the Zondo Commission has remained largely unreformed. 

Excellent frameworks are written, budgets are allocated, and large sums return unspent. Incomplete registers persist. Acting appointments multiply. Ministerial churn continues. 

The diagnostic loop is closed: shortfall is interpreted as proof that racial intensity was insufficient, so intensity rises again, while the variable most consistently left untouched is the appointment filter itself. 

Explicit sunset clauses on remaining race-based instruments, a return to the earlier intensity that once produced growth and surplus, and competence leadership insulated like the Reserve Bank form the only sequence the conversation identifies as capable of interrupting that loop. 

Destiny’s possible call to Manuel is therefore not about one man returning. It is about whether South Africa will choose to break the cycle so that the seed and the living light can finally grow into productive land governance.

Governance theory describes this as a classic principal-agent problem. The public, as principal, wants competence and delivery. The political system, as agent, optimises for loyalty and short-term control. 

When the appointment filter remains unreformed, every new framework risks joining the cemetery of elegant documents that never left the page. 

The economic cost is not only the money left unspent. It is the signal sent to investors that even well-designed policy can be hollowed out by implementation culture. Capital prices that signal every day.

Sjoe!
South Africa writes some of the best policy documents on the continent and then watches them die quietly while the register remains incomplete. The cemetery is becoming overcrowded.

Stirring Questions: 
Does treating under-delivery as automatic proof of insufficient racial intensity beg the question by assuming the cause rather than testing the unreformed loyalty filter? 
What measurable outcomes would justify extending or ending a sunset clause? 
Why has the system consistently left the appointment practice unreformed while expanding the intensity of the rules that surround it? 

These questions matter because they determine whether remedial policy remains a temporary bridge or hardens into permanent racial administration of the state. They also determine whether the next generation inherits an invoice or a working title deed.

Synthesis: The Evidence That Holds

History supplies the seed of finite power. The Reserve Bank supplies the living proof that independence works. State asset data supply the evidence that the present administrative culture cannot safely scale. Fiscal records from 1996–2009 supply the last measurable period of capacity. Zondo and subsequent implementation shortfalls supply the diagnosis of the closed loop. 

Together these independent lines form a cumulative evidence network: each strand is falsifiable, each reinforces the others, and none depends on ideology for its force. 

The claim that a one-term, rules-insulated Land Governor role for a figure of Manuel’s demonstrated competence is the practical next step is therefore not a preference. It is the conclusion that currently best fits the converging evidence. 

It can be tested. 

Complete the registers, reduce the private rentals, transfer productive land with retained employment, record net investment inflows, and the design succeeds. Fail those metrics and the design fails. That is the standard the conversation insists upon.

The strength of the evidence lies precisely in its independence. 

Constitutional design, audit findings, fiscal history and implementation outcomes were not coordinated to produce a single narrative. They simply point in the same direction. When multiple cameras record the same event from different angles, the overlapping image becomes harder to dismiss. 

South Africa’s institutional predicament is visible from several angles at once. The practical response that fits all of them is the one that already works where it has been tried.

Objections, Briefly Met

Some will say the proposal abandons redress. It does not. Section 25 remains. Equitable access remains the duty. Only the operational method changes from political discretion to rules that markets and courts can test. 

Others will say one man cannot matter. The argument has never been about one man. It is about whether competence of proven profile will be allowed to operate inside an institutional form that already works. 

Still others will say external pressure is the real issue. The conversation treats external pressure as convertible into negotiated time once visible institutional insulation and measurable outcomes appear. The alternative is the familiar loop: more intensity, more incomplete registers, more missing furniture, and another generation paying for frameworks that never left the cemetery.

The Choice That Remains Open

The seed was planted in 1994–1999. The light is already on inside the Reserve Bank and, in ceremonial form, at Stellenbosch. The bridge of measurable capacity still stands in the fiscal record of 1996–2009. 

The mechanism that can extend the light into land already exists in the constitutional template of Section 224. 

The only remaining variable is whether South Africa will break the closed loop that converts every shortfall into a mandate for more of the same intensity while leaving the appointment filter untouched. 

A one-term Land Governor role, insulated exactly as the Reserve Bank is insulated, occupied by competence of Manuel’s demonstrated profile, is the practical next step that keeps reform alive and gives markets rules they can price. 

The alternative is already known. The chairs remain missing. The frameworks keep dying. The invoice to the next generation keeps growing.

Sjoe.
The Renaissance light is on. The only question left is whether anyone will walk toward it.

Paws & Pints of Des Moines, Iowa  is planning to renovate and expand the old Bar K near Riversport and the Oklahoma River.

After opening the sprawling indoor/outdoor facility in early 2023, Bar K suddenly closed all three of its locations in July 2025.  In addition to Oklahoma City, they also operated in Kansas City and Saint Louis.

Plans show a new 7,725-square-foot addition to the north to include dog daycare and grooming.

There are also plans to replace the outdoor artificial turf and do considerable renovation to the entire complex.

Paws & Pints is similar to Bar K in that it seeks to blend a social bar and restaurant scene with dogs and dog lovers.

They offer daily or monthly memberships as well as trivia nights and dog-focused events.

The news comes as the Riversport area to the immediate south prepares to host whitewater events for the 2028 Summer Olympics.

text:
In the early morning light of the Oklahoma frontier, Mary Fletcher, a mere twelve years old, began her arduous daily routine. The heavy wooden buckets, brimming with water from the communal well, were a constant reminder of her solitary existence. Each trip, her small frame straining under the weight, was a testament to her burgeoning strength and unwavering resolve. 

She polished boots for the rough-and-tumble cowhands, her hands, though small, moving with a practiced efficiency that belied her age. The scent of leather and dust became as familiar to her as the taste of determination. In the afternoons, she ventured to the river, gathering bundles of firewood, each twig and branch a small victory against the biting cold of the approaching winter. 

These were not just chores; they were acts of survival, meticulously performed by a girl who refused to be defined by her circumstances. Her quiet diligence, her unwavering spirit, began to catch the eye of the townsfolk, who, in their own subtle ways, offered support, recognizing in Mary a kindred spirit of the frontier.

text:
Long before there was a French Quarter, there was a footpath connecting the Mississippi River to Bayou St. John, worn in by centuries of trade with people who used the bayou as a shortcut to the river instead of paddling the long way around. That path became Bayou Road, and it's often called the oldest road in New Orleans.

It's the reason the city sits where it does. Bienville chose this stretch of the Mississippi specifically because that shortcut existed, a faster route inland than the river's long winding bends offered on their own. Everything that followed, the French Quarter, the grid of streets radiating out from it, traces back to a trail that predates any of it by generations.

Walk Bayou Road today and it looks like any other quiet residential street, oak canopy, old houses, nothing marking it as the reason the whole city exists. That's part of what makes New Orleans history so layered, the most consequential paths are often hiding in plain sight, disguised as ordinary streets. Did you know the French Quarter's location was basically decided by a shortcut? 
-Nola History

text:
🇮🇷|730 kilometers, 39 tunnels, 201 bridges: Iran has just opened a "back door" to bypass the US Navy blockade.

In September 2026, Iran officially announced the completion of track-laying for the entire Chabahar-Zahedan railway line. Spanning 630 kilometers (or 735 kilometers including branch lines), the railway traverses Sistan and Baluchestan the most desolate province in southeastern Iran and comprises 39 tunnels (totaling 17 kilometers), 201 bridges and culverts, and 33 stations. It has a designed annual capacity of 2.2 million passengers and 7.7 million tons of cargo.

This is no ordinary railway. It represents Iran's first strategic countermove forged in steel and concrete to assert its land-based power following the US Navy's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

I. Chabahar: Iran's Only "Blockade-Proof" Gateway to the Sea

Over 90% of Iran's maritime trade relies on the Strait of Hormuz. The US has targeted 85% of Iranian oil tankers, sunk five of them in the area, and deployed Marines to the strait. Hormuz acts as a noose tightening around Iran's throat.

However, Chabahar is Iran's only port on the Indian Ocean; located hundreds of kilometers east of the Strait of Hormuz, it faces the Arabian Sea directly. It lies outside the scope of the US Navy's blockade. While the US Navy can establish a choke point at Hormuz, it cannot simultaneously blockade the entire Arabian Sea.

The problem was that Chabahar was previously an "isolated port," it lacked a connection to Iran's national railway network. Once cargo was unloaded at Chabahar, it had to be transported by truck, resulting in low efficiency, high costs, and limited capacity.

This 730-kilometer railway transforms Chabahar from an isolated port into a hub connected to Iran's nationwide rail network.  Cargo is unloaded at Chabahar and loaded onto trains; passing through Zahedan, it connects to Iran's national railway network. From there, goods can be transported to Tehran, Mashhad, and Tabriz, and subsequently reach Central Asia, Russia, and Europe via the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC).

II. Forty Years of Sanctions: A Railway Forged Under Pressure

Every kilometer of this railway was carved out under the shadow of sanctions.

The engineering challenge was immense. Sistan and Baluchestan is one of Iran's poorest, most remote, and topographically complex provinces. The project involved 39 tunnels, 201 bridges, nearly 2,000 drainage structures, 70 million cubic meters of earthworks, and the pouring of 2.5 million cubic meters of concrete. The use of 90,000 tons of domestically produced steel rails saved $52 million in foreign currency.

However, sanctions made everything more difficult. Foreign contractors withdrew, Western equipment could not be imported, and technology transfers were cut off. Iran had to rely solely on its own engineers and domestic materials. The Iranian armed forces were directly involved in construction, with an IRGC commander hailing it as a "national masterpiece."

The U.S. sanctions waiver for Chabahar Port is set to expire on April 26, 2026. This means any foreign company doing business with Chabahar faces the risk of being cut off from the U.S. dollar financial system.

Yet, Iran built it anyway.

III. All Eyes Are on This Railway

🇮🇳 India: The Only Route Bypassing Pakistan

India has invested $120 million in equipment for Chabahar Port and proposed an additional $400 million to $500 million over the coming years to expand the port and support railway construction.

India's strategic logic is clear: Pakistan stands between India and Central Asia. Pakistan does not permit the transit of Indian goods, and the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) excludes India. The Chabahar-Zahedan railway represents India's only overland route to Central Asia and Afghanistan.  However, the expiration of the U.S. waiver placed India in a dilemma. While India maintained its $120 million commitment, progress slowed significantly. Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi publicly urged India "not to abandon Chabahar," describing it as India's "Golden Gate."

🇰🇿 Kazakhstan: A Gateway to Global Markets

In June 2026, during a meeting with the Deputy Prime Minister of Kazakhstan, Iran’s Minister of Roads and Urban Development, Sadegh, stated clearly: "Once the Chabahar-Zahedan railway connects to the national rail network, Kazakhstan's capacity to access global markets will expand significantly." Iran also offered land at Chabahar Port for Kazakh enterprises to establish logistics centers.

For a landlocked nation like Kazakhstan, Chabahar represents the nearest Indian Ocean port not controlled by Russia or Pakistan.

🇦🇫 Afghanistan: A Lifeline Bypassing Pakistan

By 2026, trade volume between Afghanistan and Iran had reached $3.6 billion. Between March 2025 and March 2026, over 640,000 tons of cargo were transported via the Khaf-Herat railway, a sharp increase from less than 15,000 tons during the same period previously.

The completion of the Chabahar-Zahedan railway provides Afghanistan with a trade route that completely bypasses Pakistan. Afghan imports and exports can travel via the Iranian rail network to Chabahar, from where they can be shipped to India, the Gulf states, and Southeast Asia.

IV. The Bigger Picture: From Maritime Blockade to Overland Breakthrough

The Chabahar-Zahedan railway is not an isolated project; it is part of a systematic strategy through which Iran has been compelled to shift its focus from maritime power to land-based power.  Iran is simultaneously advancing four overland corridors:

◽ East-West Railway Corridor: Spanning 10,400 km from China through Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan into Iran, it cuts transit time from 30 days by sea to 15 days by rail.
◽International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC): Connecting Iran with Russia and India; the Chabahar-Zahedan railway is the critical missing link.
◽Shalamcheh-Basra Railway: A mere 32-kilometer stretch that opens up a route linking Iran, Iraq, and Turkey to the Mediterranean.
◽ Iran-Pakistan Corridor: Connecting Pakistan and Central Asia via the Mirjaveh and Rimdan border crossings.

These corridors share a single goal: enabling Iran to continue trading even under a U.S. Navy blockade.

 The U.S. blockaded a strait; Iran built a railway.

In February 2021, a Nevada Highway Patrol trooper pulled Stephen Lara over on I-80 for supposedly following a truck too closely. Lara, a retired Marine driving cross-country to see his daughters, was carrying $𝟖𝟕,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐢𝐧 𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬. A drug-sniffing dog reacted to the cash. That was enough.

Troopers seized every dollar, even after Lara produced bank records and pay stubs proving where the money came from. He was never charged with a crime. The DEA then blew past Nevada's own statutory deadlines to either charge him, file a forfeiture case, or hand the money back. It took 𝐬𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐬 and a lawsuit from the Institute for Justice before he saw a dime of it again.

““𝘛𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘪𝘴 𝘢𝘣𝘴𝘰𝘭𝘶𝘵𝘦𝘭𝘺 𝘢𝘵𝘳𝘰𝘤𝘪𝘰𝘶𝘴 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘵𝘺, 𝘭𝘰𝘤𝘢𝘭, 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘵𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘧𝘦𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘭 𝘨𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘯𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘭𝘭𝘶𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘦𝘢𝘤𝘩 𝘰𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘰𝘯 𝘵𝘢𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘴𝘴𝘦𝘵𝘴 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺'𝘳𝘦 𝘴𝘶𝘱𝘱𝘰𝘴𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦 𝘴𝘦𝘳𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨,”” Lara said.

He didn't stop at getting his own money back. He sued to challenge the scheme itself, and in January 2025, Washoe County Judge Connie Steinheimer ruled that Nevada's Department of Public Safety had no legal authority to route seizures through a 𝐟𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐩𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐞 state lawmakers never approved. ““𝘞𝘩𝘪𝘭𝘦 𝘧𝘦𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘭 𝘭𝘢𝘸 𝘤𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘭𝘺 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘷𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘴 𝘕𝘦𝘷𝘢𝘥𝘢 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘰𝘱𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘵𝘰 𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘱𝘢𝘵𝘦 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘧𝘦𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘭 𝘦𝘲𝘶𝘪𝘵𝘢𝘣𝘭𝘦 𝘴𝘩𝘢𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘨𝘳𝘢𝘮, 𝘕𝘦𝘷𝘢𝘥𝘢'𝘴 𝘓𝘦𝘨𝘪𝘴𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘩𝘢𝘴 𝘺𝘦𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘢𝘤𝘤𝘦𝘱𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘰𝘧𝘧𝘦𝘳,”” Steinheimer wrote — effectively banning the practice statewide.

The state is appealing to the Nevada Supreme Court. Lara is still pursuing damages for due process violations and the seven months the government held his savings hostage. ““𝘐 𝘧𝘶𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘥 𝘰𝘯 𝘴𝘦𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩 𝘶𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘭 𝘸𝘦 𝘴𝘶𝘤𝘤𝘦𝘦𝘥 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘸𝘦'𝘳𝘦 𝘷𝘪𝘤𝘵𝘰𝘳𝘪𝘰𝘶𝘴,”” he said.

text:
A SEVEN-YEAR AI CONTRACT AND A SEVEN-DAY HORMUZ OFFER LIFTED FUTURES OVERNIGHT. ONLY ONE IS SIGNED:

US stock futures sit near their overnight highs with 90 minutes to the opening bell, and tech is out in front. Each since Thursday's close: S&P 500 futures at 7,794.25, +27.25 pts / +0.35%; Nasdaq 100 futures at 30,967.25, +201 pts / +0.65%; Dow futures at 51,888.00, +171 pts / +0.33%; Russell 2000 futures at 2,866.30, +9.50 pts / +0.33%.

The verdict: two overnight headlines did the lifting, and they are not the same kind of news. One is a signed seven-year contract that sent a cloud company up 17% before the bell and has tech leading. The other is an Iranian offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in seven days, on terms Washington has said it will not go back to, and oil fell about 2% on the diplomacy anyway. The first will still be true at 9:30am. The second can be undone by the next headline.

The signed one landed at 4:01pm ET Thursday. Akamai Technologies (AKAM) at $110.41, -$8.03 / -6.78% on Thursday, and $129.51 premarket, +$19.10 / +17.30% from that close, said privately held AI developer Anthropic committed $11.6B over seven years to run computing work on Akamai's cloud, the servers it rents out worldwide.
- About three-quarters of Akamai's whole market value at Thursday's close, $15.9B
- Akamai expects to spend about $5.5B on equipment to serve it, $1.7B of that this year
- Anthropic can add up to $9B more, and gets a warrant - the right to buy up to about 5% of Akamai's stock at $111.33 a share

Chipmakers are rising alongside: iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX), a fund of the largest US-listed chip companies, at $566.07, +$0.35 / +0.06% on Thursday, and $574.89 premarket, +$8.82 / +1.56% from that close. Akamai itself is on none of the six Len5 watchlists: at Thursday's close it sat 33% under its May high at about 43 times its past year's profit - neither the steady climb the Momentum Len5 wants nor the discount the value-minded Len5es wait for.

The conditional one came out of the UN General Assembly in New York. Iran's Foreign Minister, Abbas Araghchi, told reporters Iran had sent a seven-day plan to US mediators this week. Per Iranian state media: "If certain conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz will be open at the end of seven days, and talks will be restarted." Brent crude, the global benchmark, is at $104.93 a barrel, -$1.67 / -1.57% since Thursday's settlement - the official end-of-day price. West Texas Intermediate, the US benchmark, is at $92.46, -$2.15 / -2.27%.

The strongest facts against that half of the morning:
- The terms. Araghchi said the conditions are "nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad MOU," the June ceasefire deal that collapsed in early July. The Trump administration has said it will not return to those terms, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio says there have been "no breakthroughs."
- The ships. Transits through the strait fell to nine, by Reuters' early ship-tracking count published Friday, on a route that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil.
- The missiles. This morning the Houthis in Yemen fired dozens of missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities said they intercepted six ballistic missiles, and emergency alerts sounded in Mecca, Jeddah and Yanbu - the Red Sea port at the end of the kingdom's cross-country oil pipeline.

Oil fell through all three. Traders are weighting a diplomat's sentence above a missile barrage aimed at the Gulf's biggest oil producer. That may prove right, but it is the half of this rally most exposed to a single headline.

The fear gauge sides with the buyers: the VIX, which rises when investors pay up for protection against a stock slide, is at 15.06, -0.61 / -3.89%. The holdout is the bond market. The 10-year Treasury yield is at 5.177%, +0.015 point since Thursday's 5.162% close, after touching 5.225% late Thursday. The 2-year yield, the one most tied to what traders expect from the Federal Reserve, is flat at 4.895%; futures traders still see about two-in-three odds of another rate increase at the Fed's October 27-28 meeting. The 10-year reaches households through mortgages: Mortgage News Daily's average 30-year fixed mortgage rate hit 7.45% Thursday, its highest since April 2024.

Europe, five hours into its session, is trading the same cheaper oil. Each so far in Friday's session, trading now: FTSE 100 at 10,709.63, +29.64 pts / +0.28%; DAX at 25,453.04, +186.51 pts / +0.74%; CAC 40 at 8,099.89, +18.46 pts / +0.23%. Europe's oil producers are lower, the other side of the same barrel.

Overnight moves often fade by the 9:30am open, and the first US report lands an hour before it. Eastern time:
- 8:30am: the Census Bureau's advance report on August orders for durable goods - goods built to last three years or more. Forecast: about -0.3%, after July's +1.1% to $339.3B. Excluding transportation, where aircraft orders swing the total: +0.6% expected vs July's +0.4%.
- 9:20am: Kansas City Fed President Jeffrey Schmid speaks.
- 10:00am: the University of Michigan's final September consumer survey. Early read: sentiment 47.8, down from 51.7 in August; households expecting 4.6% inflation over the next year, the highest since June.

What would change the read is Washington's answer. A US reply that starts Iran's seven-day clock would give oil's drop the footing tech's gain already has; a refusal, or another strike in the Gulf, would show how much of that drop was the offer. No date is set for a reply. The number that decides it until then: $94.61, WTI's Thursday settlement. Oil back above it says traders have stopped paying for the offer.

Anthropic's $11.6B is promised for seven years, in writing. Iran's seven days have not started, and they do not start until Washington says yes.

Not investment advice.

Never bet on Microsoft.

Last year, we built Properstar Messages, a real-time chat that connects real estate buyers, renters and agents worldwide. It's now the foundation of our app.

But we did one mistake, and not a small one. We used Azure Communication System, aka ACS. 

Properstar has been partnering with Microsoft since the early days and even in our previous ventures. So when they offered an SDK to have all the features from Teams, we said LFGO!!!

Took us about 9 months to build the app, not only the chat, but the whole email proxy logic and the specifics of the real estate market.

Yesterday, we received a notice that we have about 2 years to migrate the app, as ACS is deprecated 😭

That means we'll have a handful of devs that will be busy with a tech migration instead of shipping new features and improvements to our users...

I really hope AI will help us run the migration in a fast way.

If I can give you my advice: if you consider Microsoft for your company (as you wouldn't consider it as an indie), run away 😆

text:
Stop Chasing Viral: 7-Exit Entrepreneur Dominick Miserandino on Storytelling, AI & Scaling Your Brand

What does it take to cut through the noise when the rules of media, marketing, and AI change every week? In this episode of Carson's Corner: Entrepreneurship & Investing, Carson Jones sits down with Dominick Miserandino, a serial entrepreneur and media advisor with seven partial and full exits who has advised more than 200 businesses, from startups to names like NASA, Hearst Magazines, the Wall Street Journal, and Dell.

Dominick explains why the rules of storytelling haven't changed since people gathered around the campfire, only the platforms have. He and Carson dig into why chasing virality can pull a business off-brand, how social algorithms reward controversy over substance, and why trust, not attention, is what leads to the transaction. They also get into over-automation and the flood of AI emails, and Dominick shares a real estate operator whose sales dropped after he replaced people with AI. Along the way he offers practical advice on picking one platform that works before expanding, and on "bucketing" your time with new tech so you don't lose your baseline.

The conversation wraps with exit strategy, including how to tell when it's time to let go of a business, and why in-person events with "no hard pitches" build better relationships than any sales script.

text:
TL;DR: reasoning/communication/curiosity/creativity. Based on inidividual passions/agency.

More details:
1. depends on where you think AIs will be in ten years. some say, "Hey, find a cure - make no mistakes", so it is pointless to "train" kids. But we do not know that, so let me share my 2 cents

2. "With intelligence on tap, agency is the main thing. (Karpathy)". Solving problems and creating things is hard work. Evolution is against you, shouting DO NOT MAKE EFFORTS. Supposedly 80 percent of people are 'averse to thinking' (some studies say)? But there is one hope: work based on LOVE. When kids are not tired from fulfilling meaningless chores, they work hard, when they choose to, because the thing is appealing to them. Personally appealing at the current moment.

3. But how can the educator find out what the kiddo would like to engage with. Interest-based homeschooling has some data on that - you offer different classes, projects, activities, observe what happens and support or switch. There could be "growth guides" monthly/weekly talking to kids, mapping kids' aspirations and obstacles. Based on mutual trust, not on judgment or "we both know that I need you to learn history". Humans. Supporting the kids/being their allies - offering classes, forming informal teams, vibecoding skill-building gadgets, orchestrating 1:1 tutoring .. just like a homeschool mom would.

Very expensive utopia, I know. One day it will be possible.

4. Meta skills around agency. One important thing: I think the most important aspect is "personality". You cannot really decide "kids should be founders/social workers/artists" because THIS IS SO IMPORTANT TO TRAIN THEM IN. Their personal passions/agency is everything. OK, so is there still some common denominator educators can offer? Currently I think about four angles

REASONING/problem-solving/cultivation of thinking. Logic, deduction, induction, philosophy. Escape rooms, Poly Bridge, Among Us, mystery stories, math, .. whatever gets them to "solve something". Mental gyms.

COMMUNICATION/storytelling/people/teamwork/being together. You can achieve only so little alone. Explaining your ideas helps you organize them. Writing, sharing, negotiating, leadership, decision-making processes, course correction, emotional intelligence, dealing with stress, relationships, your needs, other people's needs, projects, maintaining vision. When you are trained in this, "talking to machines" is just another natural tool in trying to achieve something. Again: you must not kill the desire to work with others by assigning stupid school projects.

CURIOSITY/cultivating awe about the world/getting knowledge. Little kids are very interested in trying to make sense of the environment they were born into. Older kids are assigned "compulsory reading" and, when interested in something (polar bears or Mars), assigned "essays" and "chores" around it. But you can offer great bite-sized info, videos (not childish), or interactive materials, even bite-sized books, but written from the point of "I love this subject", not "textbook". I consider showing kids the world very important, because when you do not even know that 'art therapy' or 'ecosystem regeneration' or 'role-playing' or 'uncontacted tribes' exist, you cannot fall in love with it and decide to improve the field...

CREATIVITY: by this I mean exposing kids to creative flow, being stuck, overcoming blocks and sharing. Game design is great for this, but really anything: the Montessori maxim: when the kiddo is focused/in flow, never interrupt or direct. "Following the inner teacher" is more important than judging if this LEGO build, or this picture, or DnD story "is useful" from the point of view of adults.

.. I am legally required to document my son's learning progress. I do those "portfolios" divided into those four areas (reasoning/people/curiosity-world/creativity-building). I also include things not traditionally considered learning: movie nights, traveling, abandoned projects, YouTube, great discussions.. and twice a year we go through the "portfolio" to reflect on what felt important, useful, what he wants to go back to.. also to see the progress (two years ago and now??). I believe this instills: "we learn all the time", "you are capable", "following passions helps you grow", etc.

"But Mirka, this is nice and all, but what is the actual actionable step for school??" I currently do not have an idea around AI tutors, because they still feel so lonely, as opposed to being under the influence of a really skilful and flexible instructor, who can read into kids' current agency. Maybe

* Recess is already great. There is no other platform promoting those values in such diversity

* keep talking to the parents about the high value of reasoning/communication/curiosity/creativity activities based on inner motivation/agency

* keep having great instructors: An example: "I usually try to alternate between a group project and an individual project to keep everyone engaged. Sometimes they are a one-class project and sometimes they span several weeks. I sort of gauge how long the project will go based on excitement. Sometimes I think something will be a one-and-done class and then it'll go for a while, other times I think it's longer term but it's not vibing with the students as well. If I'm not sure how they're feeling, I ask them if they want to continue the same project next week or start something new. 

I usually pick the next project based on how the kids are feeling after the last one, so I don't plan too far in advance. For example, one of the kids mentioned loving murder mysteries off-hand, and I was like, that's a great idea for a group project. I try to keep things interesting and change things up so it never feels repetitive." (Lanie from Storytelling)

Sorry if this feels so old-school and not tech- enough :)

text:
hi there,

@0xCyberThrone has a campaign that really separates reputation from contribution, and the way they measure both is interesting.

Reputation is tied to the wallet you connect. If your NFT portfolio and on-chain activity look solid, you're good. Just tweeting about it won't boost your reputation score, which is a nice change.

Then there's Contribution. This comes from the content you create on X regarding CyberThrone and how you interact with the project's posts. They're not just counting tweets; they want to see the quality of what you share, the authenticity of your interactions, and your involvement in the NFT community.

One clear limit is that only five tweets a week count toward your Contribution score. If you post more than that, they'll only track your best-performing ones.

So instead of flooding the timeline with random tags or whitelist requests, it's smarter to focus on a specific topic about CyberThrone and go deep. Maybe dive into their collection of 8,888 NFTs with over 250 traits or talk about what holders can access, like digital content and IP usage rights.

CyberThrone aims to blend art, music, finance, and tech. The best content isn't just about being "bullish." It's about helping newcomers grasp what the project offers, what holders gain, and how they can leverage that experience.

Fewer posts with real insights and value? That's what will make a difference.

20,000 small businesses. One message to the FTC: don’t let rules aimed at “surveillance pricing” sweep in the everyday discounts ecommerce businesses use to compete.

Last month, we sounded the alarm about the FTC’s proposed personalized pricing policy and asked ecommerce businesses to tell us how it could affect them.

They did. We heard from family farms, consumer brands, ecommerce platforms, and small businesses across the country about the role that loyalty rewards, welcome offers, abandoned-cart discounts, win-back campaigns, subscriptions, and other promotions play in serving customers and competing with much larger companies.

EIA took those voices to Washington. In our comments to the FTC yesterday, we urged the Commission to draw a clear line between genuinely deceptive pricing practices and ordinary promotional activity that gives consumers a lower price.

Our message is simple: protect consumers from deceptive pricing without creating unintended consequences for the small businesses that depend on ecommerce to grow.

We break down what we told the FTC—and what comes next—in our latest post.

This Week's Ag Review
Friday, September 25, 2026

This Week's Top 5 Ag Stories

The Pollination Pivot
The U.S. corn crop has entered its make or break pollination window, revealing a sharp east west split in soil moisture that is dividing production potential across the Belt.

Herd Rebuilding Stalls
Despite record high calf prices, a combination of high interest rates and lingering western drought continues to stall beef cow retention across the Plains.

Renewable Diesel Pullbacks
Slower than expected domestic refinery expansions are shifting near term soybean crush expectations, adjusting baseline demand assumptions for the complex.

Mississippi River Levels Watch
Low water advisories are creeping back into river logistics discussions, forcing grain exporters to monitor crucial inland shipping lanes as mid summer drying sets in.

EPA Targets Herbicide Runoff
New draft rules regarding spray drift mitigation are sending chemical dealers and producers scrambling to interpret upcoming compliance and application strategies.

Agriculture This Week: The Big Picture
Agriculture markets moved through another week of competing narratives as producers, livestock operators, and industry participants balanced tighter supply expectations, changing weather patterns, and shifting demand conditions.

The July USDA supply and demand updates continued influencing the agricultural landscape, reinforcing the idea that while some commodities are facing improved production prospects, others are dealing with tighter availability and ongoing supply challenges.

For grain producers, attention remains focused on crop development as corn and soybean fields move deeper into critical growing stages. Weather remains the dominant factor, particularly across areas of the western Corn Belt where moisture concerns continue to influence crop expectations. 

For livestock producers, the story remains centered around tight cattle supplies, drought impacts, and the ongoing challenge of rebuilding herd numbers following years of liquidation.

The Reality From the Windshield: Strong demand is supporting markets, but local weather and supply realities are ultimately determining the direction of individual operations.

Grain & Crop Update

Corn: Crop Potential Meets Weather Reality
The corn market entered the second half of July with production expectations still strong, but weather concerns preventing the market from completely ignoring potential crop stress. The USDA continues projecting a large U.S. corn crop, supported by favorable early season conditions. However, the market is entering the period where timely rainfall and temperature patterns become increasingly important.

Fields across the central Belt are hit and miss, with the next ten days serving as the primary yield determination checkpoint as pollination progresses. The structural east west divide is becoming more obvious by the day; while parts of Illinois and Indiana boast excellent canopy color, western Corn Belt dryness remains a nagging concern. 

On the demand side, ethanol margins remain solidly in the black, providing reliable domestic support, while export inspections hold steady against heavy South American competition.

Soybeans: Demand vs. Global Supply
Soybeans continue to face a balancing act between strong domestic demand and large global production. The domestic crush complex remains a powerful engine, driven by long term renewable fuel demand and steady livestock feed usage.

However, South American competition continues to cast a long shadow on the export front. As the crop moves closer toward key pod development stages in August, rain making systems will need to deliver to secure the high end yield projections currently baked into the balance sheets.

Wheat: A Global Market With Domestic Challenges
The winter wheat harvest is rapidly wrapping up across the Plains, shifting focus to spring wheat development in the north. While domestic dryland yields have been highly variable, the overarching narrative remains global. High export volumes out of the Black Sea region and competitive European pricing continue to keep a lid on sustained domestic rallies, despite localized quality premiums.

Corn Belt Ag Update

Extreme Variations Divide Top Production States
As mid summer settles across the heart of the country, the Corn Belt has split into two vastly different operational realities. Crop potential is heavily dependent on geography, with the western and northern edges facing a critical deficit of moisture compared to the central and eastern states.

The primary concern across the western Corn Belt is a depleted subsoil safety net. While regions like Minnesota (84% good to excellent) and Wisconsin (83%) are pushing ahead with robust crop ratings, western Iowa and adjacent Plains borders are dealing with intensifying dryness that has triggered localized crop stress just as fields enter peak water demand periods. Irrigators in these western reaches are running pivots continuously to offset the topsoil moisture deficit, driving up energy and input lines on the summer ledger.

For livestock operations nestled within the broader Belt, the immediate challenge centers on forage logistics. Pastures on the western fringes are drying down rapidly, keeping dryland wild hay yields well below historical baselines and forcing producers to rely heavily on premium alfalfa supplies or make early livestock tracking decisions.

Livestock Industry Update

Cattle: Supply Remains the Story
The cattle industry continues operating under historically tight inventory conditions. The effects of previous multi year herd liquidation remain visible throughout the industry. Fewer calves translate directly to higher costs, and the bidding war for feeder cattle remains fierce at video sales and local barns.

Heifer retention also remains delayed; high interest rates and localized forage deficits mean heifers are still heading to feedlots rather than staying in the breeding pasture. While cash cattle traded slightly softer late this week, the underlying fundamental supply story remains incredibly supportive for the long haul.

Beef Industry Update
Packers, retailers, and consumers continue navigating a challenging environment. Overall beef production remains below previous years, keeping retail beef prices elevated at the grocery store. While consumer demand has shown remarkable resilience in the face of inflation, packer margins are being squeezed tightly between high live cattle acquisition costs and wholesale beef pricing thresholds.

Pork & Poultry
The pork sector is finding seasonal support in summer grilling demand. Export opportunities to Mexico and East Asia remain a bright spot, though hog producers continue to manage thin margins driven by volatile feed pricing. In poultry, flock sizes have stabilized and feed cost relief has helped margins. Focus remains heavily on biosecurity as seasonal wild bird migrations loom later this year.

Corn Belt Weather Watch

Regional Synopsis & Storm Potential
The Corn Belt is characterized by a sharp meteorological division as we pass mid July. A high pressure ridge parked over the Southwest is pushing dry, warm air into the western fringes of the Plains and Western Corn Belt, depleting topsoil moisture. Conversely, the Eastern Corn Belt remains under a more active, humid northwest flow, keeping fields adequately watered but increasing humidity and disease pressure.

Scattered, fast moving thunderstorm complexes are expected to track along the edge of the high pressure ridge. While these systems offer high intensity, localized rainfall, they also bring the threat of straight line wind damage and hail to pollinating corn. Deep, soaking rain systems are noticeably absent from the 8 to 14 day outlook for the western dry zones.

State by State Conditions

Nebraska: Soil moisture is short to very short. The crop stage is focused on corn silking and beans blooming. The 7 day outlook brings dry, hot south southeasterly winds with only spotty storm potential.

Iowa: Soil moisture is adequate east, but short west. Rapid pollination is underway, and the 7 day outlook brings moderating temperatures, though the western third of the state critically needs rain.

Illinois: Soil moisture is adequate to surplus with a high percentage of corn silking. The upcoming outlook features humid, timely rain events and low heat stress.
Indiana: Soil moisture remains at a surplus, causing some crop root systems to stay shallow. The outlook maintains a continued wet bias, with operators monitoring for ponding.

Minnesota: Soil moisture is adequate as the crop catches up after a late start. The 7 day outlook indicates moderate temperatures and favorable growing conditions.

Critical Agricultural Impacts
High heat in western regions during afternoon hours threatens to dry out silks before successful pollination can occur. Meanwhile, high humidity and wet leaves in Illinois and Indiana are creating prime conditions for fungal diseases like Gray Leaf Spot and Tar Spot, with spore traps already showing early activity. On the balance sheet side, high pumping costs are accumulating quickly in dry western zones as pivots run nearly continuously.

From Washington
The policy desk in Washington has been active this week, with several developments directly impacting the farm gate. Legislative leaders indicate that a full, multi year Farm Bill is unlikely to pass before the fall deadlines, making another temporary extension the most probable path forward.

Discussions are underway regarding supplemental funding for livestock producers impacted by western drought and forage losses, though allocation timelines remain uncertain. Additionally, federal agencies are closely monitoring renewed trade frictions with major North American partners, emphasizing the need for grain and meat exporters to diversify global destinations.

Commodity Corner: Market Intelligence
Corn: Market direction was mixed this week, heavily influenced by weather and pollination success. The market is actively balancing large national acreage expectations against real western dryness.

Soybeans: Prices finished mixed as export demand squares off against global supply. Domestic crush margins remain strong, but lagging export sales keep upside limited.

Wheat: Trade was highly volatile, driven by global supplies and international export flow. Large Russian and Black Sea volumes continue to act as a firm price ceiling.

Live Cattle: Prices remain firm on exceptionally tight supplies, with packers forced to pay up for quality finished cattle.

Feeder Cattle: Bidding remains strong due to lower feed costs and a historically small calf crop, sparking deep competition for limited grass ready calves.

Hogs: Market tone is improving on seasonal domestic pork demand, with strong belly prices supporting packer margins.

Agriculture Business & Industry News

Inputs & Commercial Processing
Producers are closely watching the input markets as prepay season begins to loom on the horizon. While fertilizer prices have stabilized relative to the wild swings of previous years, high interest rates are making the cost of carrying inventory incredibly expensive for both local retailers and farm operations. Diesel prices have eased slightly, providing some relief as harvest prep begins.

In processing, ethanol grind rates remain strong, supported by solid domestic blending margins and steady export demand. For soybeans, several new processing facilities in the Midwest are fully online, intensifying localized basis competition for physical bushels. Meat packers, however, continue to face underutilized processing capacity due to the limited cattle supply, leading to reduced shifts at several major beef plants.

Historical Agriculture Moment
Ninety years ago, the Great Plains was locked in the historic 1936 Heat Wave. Nebraska hit an all time record of 118°F (48°C) that July. Without modern hybrid seed genetics or deep well irrigation, the crop was lost in days. It serves as a timeless reminder of why today's risk management tools and conservation practices matter so deeply to the survival of the family farm.

Farm & Ranch Calendar
July 24: USDA Cattle on Feed Report. Traders expect tight placements to continue reflecting the smaller calf crop.
July 31: Final recommended date for mid summer pasture weed control before problem seeds set.
August 12: August USDA WASDE Report, featuring the first survey based crop yield estimates of the season.
Late August: State Fair season kicks off across the Midwest take time to support local 4 H and FFA youth.

Producer Perspective

Agriculture has a way of reminding us that national statistics rarely reflect what you see looking out your own kitchen window. A projected record large national crop doesn't put moisture in a parched dryland field in Nebraska. A historically strong cattle market doesn't pay the bills if you don't have the grass or water to carry the cows. Every single operation is running its own race, dealing with its own micro climate, input costs, and marketing challenges.

The most successful producers we know aren't trying to out guess the national averages. They are focusing on what they can control: protecting their soil moisture, managing their unit cost of production, and utilizing disciplined marketing strategies to lock in margins when the market offers them.

Looking Ahead
The next several weeks will remain absolutely critical for the 2026 agricultural economy. Late July and August weather patterns will write the final chapter on yield potential, while livestock producers must continue making hard management decisions regarding herd retention in a high cost environment.

Stay safe, look out for your neighbors, and keep working the plan.

💱 Washington is reportedly exploring ways to expand dollar-backed stablecoins overseas, strengthening the dollar’s reach while potentially creating additional demand for U.S. Treasuries. 
 
Look at what has been happening around it. 

The OCC has been progressively opening the door for banks to operate directly with digital assets and permitted DLT networks, including holding the native assets required to use them. At the same time, regulated stablecoin frameworks are increasingly linking digital money to traditional reserve assets, including government debt. Japan’s JPYC offers a useful example, with its issuer expecting a substantial share of reserves to be held in Japanese government bonds. 

On the infrastructure side, IBM is now connecting tokenised banking infrastructure with Swift through ISO 20022. 

These may look like separate developments, but they are solving different layers of the same transition. Banks gaining access to DLTs, sovereign debt underpinning digital money, and traditional financial rails connecting to blockchain settlement. 
 
The next problem is interoperability. Moving regulated value between banks, jurisdictions and different networks without fragmenting liquidity. 

Meanwhile, Stronghold has been moving in a remarkably similar direction. StrongholdNET is increasingly centred on regulated bank to DLT settlement and ISO 20022, while its infrastructure is becoming more multichain, spanning ecosystems including Stellar and Ripple’s XRP Ledger. At the same time, its expansion into Japan and Korea places Stronghold in markets where stablecoins, tokenised assets and institutional settlement are rapidly moving from policy discussions into regulated financial infrastructure. 

No evidence connects Stronghold to this initiative. 
But perhaps the more interesting question is not who will issue the next stablecoin. It’s who has been building the rails it will need.

What are the new heaven and the new earth?
Answer
In Revelation 21:1, John sees something spectacular: “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” This new earth and new heaven are sometimes referred to as the “eternal state.” As seen in Revelation chapters 21—22, the new earth will be the eternal dwelling place of believers in Jesus Christ. Scripture gives us a few details of the new heaven and new earth.

The current heaven and earth have long been subject to God’s curse because of mankind’s sin. All creation “has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth” (Romans 8:22) as it awaits the fulfillment of God’s plan and “the children of God to be revealed” (verse 19). Heaven and earth will pass away (Mark 13:31), and they will be replaced by the new heaven and the new earth. At that time, the Lord, seated on His throne, says, “I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:5). In the new creation, sin will be totally eradicated, and “there shall be no more curse” (Revelation 22:3, NKJV).

The new heaven and new earth are also mentioned in Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; and 2 Peter 3:13. Peter says that the new heaven and new earth will be “where righteousness dwells.” Isaiah says that “the former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.” Things will be completely new, and the old order of things, with the accompanying sorrow and tragedy, will be gone.

The new earth will be free from sin, evil, sickness, suffering, and death. It will be earth as God originally intended it to be, prior to the curse of sin. It will be Eden restored.

A major feature of the new earth will be the New Jerusalem. John calls it “the Holy City . . . coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). This glorious city, with its streets of gold and pearly gates, is situated on a new, glorious earth. The tree of life will be there (Revelation 22:2). This city represents the final state of redeemed mankind, forever in fellowship with God: “God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. . . . His servants will serve him. They will see his face” (Revelation 21:3; 22:3–4).

In the new heaven and new earth, Scripture says, there are seven things notable for their absence—seven things that are “no more”:
• no more sea (Revelation 21:1)
• no more death (Revelation 21:4)
• no more mourning (Revelation 21:4)
• no more weeping (Revelation 21:4)
• no more pain (Revelation 21:4)
• no more curse (Revelation 22:3)
• no more night (Revelation 22:5)

The creation of the new heaven and new earth brings the promise that God “will wipe every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). This event comes after the tribulation, after the Lord’s second coming, after the millennial kingdom, after the final rebellion, after the final judgment of Satan, and after the great white throne judgment. The brief description of the new heaven and new earth is the last glimpse into eternity that the Bible gives.

Iran's foreign minister has made Tehran's offer public: Hormuz reopens seven days after Washington accepts its conditions.

Abbas Araghchi says mediators submitted the plan to the White House this week; it would take effect the day after US acceptance, with talks on ending the war restarting.

The terms track the 14-point memorandum Trump signed in June: a US return to it, an end to the naval blockade, release of frozen funds and an end to Israel's war in southern Lebanon.

In exchange, Iran would reopen the strait on routes agreed with Oman and re-enter nuclear negotiations.

Tehran presents this as a single step, where Reuters reported on Thursday that the two sides were discussing a phased exchange. Mohsen Rezaei, the Supreme National Security Council secretary, says the conditions must be met before the strait reopens or talks resume.

US negotiators dismissed an earlier Iranian offer on the strait, telling Tehran it does not control the waterway, the Times of Israel reported.

A mediator told CBS the talks are positive but early; Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there had been no breakthroughs.
