The Habets/Grow thesis is explicit and the surprise is real. “Evangelical Calvinism” on the spine sounds like federal, Westminster, TULIP Calvinism, where the incarnation is the remedial answer to Adam. But inside, Habets and Grow list as Thesis 8 a supralapsarian Christology that emphasizes the primacy of Christ. That is Scotus’s question, not Dort’s. Habets had already argued the same case in his 2008 New Blackfriars essay: he defends the Scotistic thesis (sin is not the primary cause of the incarnation) and gives a reserved yes to the Scotistic hypothesis (there would have been an incarnation even without the fall), testing it against Weinandy, Barth, Moltmann, and Torrance. So the volumes are not a federal Calvinist shop that wandered into Franciscan metaphysics. They are Torrance/Barth/Scots Confession Calvinism wearing a name that makes people expect the other thing. The incarnation-anyway material is consistent with that lineage. The surprise is that anyone still hears “Calvinism” and assumes Westminster. 

Books that do the same kind of work from a corner you would not expect: 

Thomas Goodwin, read through Mark Jones, Why Heaven Kissed Earth 

This is a close analog. Goodwin is a high Puritan, Savoy/Westminster-world divine. He will not shout the counterfactual the way Scotus does. He still builds a Christology in which Christ as Head of the elect is logically prior to Christ as Redeemer of the fallen; the atonement is an “after plot” that removes the impediment to a glory already intended in the person of the God-man. Even an unfallen Adam, on Goodwin’s account, needed the God-man to reach the heavenly estate. That is primacy-of-Christ architecture inside a covenant-of-redemption Puritan. You would not guess it from the usual “Puritan = infralapsarian remedy” picture. 

Edwin Chr. van Driel, Incarnation Anyway (OUP, 2008), and The Incarnation as God’s First Intention (Baker Academic, 2025) 

Van Driel is a PCUSA theologian at Pittsburgh Seminary. Incarnation Anyway is still the best map of the modern arguments, with case studies of Schleiermacher, Dorner, and Barth. The 2025 Baker book takes the same thesis into evangelical-press format: incarnation as first intention, not Plan B, then traces what that does to atonement, election, eschatology, and mission. Mainline Presbyterian + Baker Academic is not the Franciscan house you expect to find this in. 

Oliver D. Crisp, “Incarnation without the Fall” (Journal of Reformed Theology, 2016) Crisp is analytic Reformed. He offers a “christological union” version of incarnation-anyway and argues it is not idle speculation: it clarifies the image of God and God’s end in creating. The surprise is the guild. Analytic Reformed work usually stays close to the received Reformed caution (Calvin, Turretin, Warfield: don’t ask the counterfactual). Crisp asks it and defends a yes. 

Marilyn McCord Adams, Christ and Horrors

Episcopal analytic philosopher, not a Scotist manual. She treats the incarnation as required by God’s unitive aim in creating a material world, not as an emergency patch for sin. Horrors, for her, sit deeper than sin as the human predicament; Stage-I defeat is divine solidarity in the flesh. The register is unexpected: contemporary philosophy of religion rather than medieval Franciscan controversy, arriving at a structurally similar claim.

Karl Barth, especially Church Dogmatics II/2 and IV/1

Barth refuses to answer Scotus’s hypothetical in Scotus’s terms. Habets and van Driel both argue that he is nevertheless committed to the Scotistic thesis: election and incarnation are decided in the triune life before the fall is in view, and the incarnation also answers a plight logically independent of sin (transitoriness, nonbeing). If you only know Barth as the man who scolds speculation, this is the surprise. If you know Barth as the man for whom Jesus Christ is the first and last word of election, it is less surprising—but it is still not what “Reformed” usually means in North America.

Marc Cortez: ReSourcing Theological Anthropology

A conservative evangelical systematics book. Cortez walks through the question and thinks there are good reasons to say the incarnation would have happened irrespective of sin, while also showing how someone who says no can still have a christological anthropology. The surprise is the textbook shelf, not the Franciscan shelf.

Frederick Faber, Bethlehem

Nineteenth-century Oratorian, converted Anglican. Popular English Catholic piety that states the Scotist order of predestination without apology: Jesus decreed before the permission of sin; the assumed humanity is the fountain of every other predestination. The surprise is tone and audience—devotional prose, not a Paris ordinatio.

Justus Hunter, If Adam Had Not Sinned

This is historical rather than constructive. The surprise there is historiographical: he argues that Thomas and Scotus are more reconcilable than the “no sin, no incarnation” slogan war suggests. Useful as background, not as another Habets/Grow.

A near-miss worth naming so the pattern stays clean:

Andreas Osiander did say the Son would have become incarnate without the fall. That is a Lutheran Reformer, which is unexpected. He is a bad recommendation as a book to hand someone, because the same package includes his doctrine of justification, which both Lutherans and Calvin rejected.

Non-surprising since we expect to find it obviously:

Juniper Carol’s Why Jesus Christ?
Pancheri
Dominic Unger
Absolute Primacy of Christ literature
Maximus Ad Thalassium 60

—by Brendan Case
(Series: Studies in Historical & Systematic Theology)

'FIGHT, FIGHT, FIGHT': Trump Pays Tribute After the Death of Butler Survivor Jim Copenhaver | Becca Lower, RedState

President Donald Trump weighed in Thursday night on the death of Jim Copenhaver, the 76-year-old supporter shot twice during the 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, who died more than two years after the shooting that left him with permanent injuries.

Trump called him a "true American Patriot" and his death a "tremendous loss." Copenhaver survived the bullets that tore into him at Butler, but the damage never fully left him. Bullet fragments remained inside his body until the end, and he and his wife had sued the federal government over the security failures that made it all possible.

The president wrote:

"Jim Copenhaver, a true American Patriot, has passed away — A tremendous loss! More than two years ago in Butler, Pennsylvania, a crazed gunman attempted to stifle our America First Movement. Instead, Jim and so many other wonderful Patriots who love our Country, stood united in defense of our shared values of Freedom, Liberty, and Justice.

After being wounded while protecting his family, Jim showed tremendous bravery, courageously continuing to FIGHT, FIGHT, FIGHT, and maintaining a positive spirit despite unimaginable hardships."

Trump said Copenhaver's “indelible legacy of love and devotion will forever endure” and offered prayers for the Copenhaver family, singling out his wife, Marianne.

Copenhaver's death was first announced earlier Thursday. He died Wednesday at West Penn Hospital in Pittsburgh, according to the Allegheny County medical examiner. His family said through attorney Joseph Feldman that he passed away surrounded by loved ones. A cause of death has not been disclosed, and while the family's statement did not say whether his death was directly connected to the injuries he suffered in Butler, Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday has said that Copenhaver passed away "from complications stemming from those wounds."

As RedState reported earlier Thursday, Copenhaver was hit twice on July 13, 2024, when Thomas Crooks fired from a rooftop overlooking Trump's campaign rally. One bullet struck Copenhaver in the tricep. Another hit him in the abdomen. He underwent multiple surgeries and was left with bullet fragments still inside his body.

Copenhaver later described the moment he realized what had happened:

“I turned around to my friend, and I said, ‘I think I was shot,’ and that’s when I got the second one and then I went down.”

Copenhaver survived. Later, when he spoke publicly about Butler, he put the blame squarely on the security failures that left the rooftop open to Crooks.

“I’m sure there was negligence. It wouldn’t have happened, had it been secure.”

Those failures eventually landed in court. Copenhaver and his wife sued the federal government in June, describing injuries from the shooting as “debilitating, grievous, permanent and life-altering.”

Copenhaver wasn't the only one who paid a price that day. Corey Comperatore, a retired volunteer fire chief, was killed shielding his wife and daughters. David Dutch was critically wounded. Trump was struck in the ear before Secret Service agents rushed him from the stage.

Trump closed his tribute to Copenhaver with three words immediately recognizable from Butler:

“FIGHT, FIGHT, FIGHT.”

This time, they were for Jim Copenhaver.

Here is one of your apologists giving a "primer" on Catholic soteriology. Is he wrong? Because what he promotes here is a false gospel:

A Primer on Roman Catholic Salvation Theology
Posted on 15 January 2015 by Ron Conte
The Magisterium of the Catholic Church has clear and definitive teachings on salvation. Yet many Catholics online are promoting ideas on salvation theology (soteriology) that openly contradict Church teaching. This post offers the basics of soteriology, from magisterial teaching. For a full discussion, see my book: Forgiveness and Salvation for Everyone
1. After death, each human person is judged by God (the particular judgment). Everyone who dies in a state of grace goes to Heaven, perhaps after a temporary stay in Purgatory. Everyone who dies unrepentant from actual mortal sin goes to Hell.
Pope Pius XII: “Above all, the state of grace is absolutely necessary at the moment of death; without it, salvation and supernatural happiness — the beatific vision of God — are impossible.” [Address to Midwives, n. 21.a.]
Pope Benedict XII: “Moreover we define that according to the general disposition of God, the souls of those who die in actual mortal sin go down into Hell immediately after death and there suffer the pain of Hell.” [On the Beatific Vision of God]
2. We poor fallen sinners are conceived with original sin and therefore without the state of grace (sanctifying grace). We must find sanctifying grace in this life in order to reach eternal life in Heaven. But there is only one way to obtain sanctifying grace: baptism. Does this imply that only Christians go to Heaven? No.
There are three forms of baptism:
a. the formal Sacrament of Baptism (baptism with water)
b. a baptism of desire
c. a baptism of blood
Any fallen sinner who dies without one of these forms of baptism, dies without the state of grace and is therefore excluded from Heaven.
[Matthew]
{22:10} And his servants, departing into the ways, gathered all those whom they found, bad and good, and the wedding was filled with guests.
{22:11} Then the king entered to see the guests. And he saw a man there who was not clothed in a wedding garment.
{22:12} And he said to him, ‘Friend, how is it that you have entered here without having a wedding garment?’ But he was dumbstruck.
{22:13} Then the king said to the ministers: ‘Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
{22:14} For many are called, but few are chosen.’ ”
Without the “wedding garment” of the state of grace, no one can enter into the wedding celebration of Heaven.
3. A baptism of desire can be explicit or implicit. In an explicit baptism of desire, the person knowingly desires the sacrament of Christian baptism. In an implicit baptism of desire, the person obtains the state of grace by an act of love, without a specific desire for the sacrament itself. A person who receives an implicit baptism of desire might even outwardly reject the Church.
Pope John Paul II: “The universality of salvation means that it is granted not only to those who explicitly believe in Christ and have entered the Church. Since salvation is offered to all, it must be made concretely available to all.” [Redemptoris Missio n. 10]
Pope Pius XII: “An act of love is sufficient for the adult to obtain sanctifying grace and to supply the lack of baptism….” [Address to Midwives, n. 21.a.]
Pope John Paul II: “For those, however, who have not received the Gospel proclamation, as I wrote in the Encyclical ‘Redemptoris Missio,’ salvation is accessible in mysterious ways, inasmuch as divine grace is granted to them by virtue of Christ’s redeeming sacrifice, without external membership in the Church, but nonetheless always in relation to her (cf. Redemptoris Missio, n. 10). It is a mysterious relationship. It is mysterious for those who receive the grace, because they do not know the Church and sometimes even outwardly reject her. It is also mysterious in itself, because it is linked to the saving mystery of grace, which includes an essential reference to the Church the Savior founded. In order to take effect, saving grace requires acceptance, cooperation, a ‘yes’ to the divine gift. This acceptance is, at least implicitly, oriented to Christ and the Church.” [All Salvation Comes through Christ]
Letter from the Holy Office (the CDF) to the Archbishop of Boston: “To gain eternal salvation, it is not always required that a person be incorporated in reality (reapse) as a member of the Church, but it is necessary that one belong to it at least in desire and longing (voto et desiderio). It is not always necessary that this desire be explicit as it is with catechumens. When one is invincibly ignorant, God also accepts an implicit desire, so called because it is contained in the good disposition of soul by which a person wants his or her will to be conformed to God’s will.” [Letter of the Holy Office to the Archbishop of Boston, DS 3870; ND 855 (1949).]
Pope Saint Pius X: “The absence of Baptism can be supplied by martyrdom, which is called Baptism of Blood, or by an act of perfect love of God, or of contrition, along with the desire, at least implicit, of Baptism, and this is called Baptism of Desire.” [Catechism of Pope St. Pius X, The Sacraments – Baptism, Necessity of Baptism and Obligations of the Baptized]
4. A baptism of blood can be explicit or implicit. The clearest case of an explicit baptism of blood occurs when a person preparing for the sacrament of Baptism knowingly chooses to die rather than deny Christ.
The clearest cases for an implicit baptism of blood are the Holy Innocents and the Blessed Virgin Mary. The Holy Innocents did not know that they were being killed in place of the Christ Child. They did not choose to die rather than deny the Christian or Jewish faith. Yet they received the state of grace prior to death, and so entered into Heaven.
The Blessed Virgin Mary received the state of grace within the gift of the Immaculate Conception. Since only baptism can grant the state of grace to human persons, her Immaculate Conception must have included a type of baptism. But she did not exist prior to the first instant of her conception, so she could not have desired and then obtained a baptism of desire. A baptism of desire also requires some type of knowledge of what one is desiring, even when it is implicit. So the type of baptism received in the Immaculate Conception must have been a baptism of blood. The sacrifice of Christ on the Cross is the source of every baptism and the source of the Immaculate Conception.
5. Outside the Church, there is no salvation. But the Church includes formal members (baptized Christians) and non-formal members, who have entered the state of grace by a baptism of desire or of blood. All persons in the state of grace are adoptive children of God [cf. Trent, Sixth Session, Decree on Justification, chapter IV.]
If anyone possesses sufficient accurate knowledge of Christianity, but fails to convert, his failure is objectively a mortal sin. But only actual mortal sin deserves eternal condemnation. Actual mortal sin requires a gravely disordered act committed with full knowledge of its grave immorality and full deliberation (full freedom of choice). If a non-Christian lacks the full culpability of actual mortal sin for his outward rejection of the Church, he might still be in a state of grace.
Pope Saint Pius X: “A person outside the Church by his own fault, and who dies without perfect contrition, will not be saved. But he who finds himself outside without fault of his own, and who lives a good life, can be saved by the love called charity, which unites unto God, and in a spiritual way also to the Church, that is, to the soul of the Church.” [Pope St. Pius X, Catechism of Christian Doctrine]
6. Perfect contrition forgives all personal sins. A Catholic is immediately forgiven for all sins if he makes an act of perfect contrition: sorrow for sins out of love of God. But in the case of actual mortal sin, the Catholic is still required to go to Confession. A non-Catholic who has no access to the sacrament of Confession is forgiven by an act of perfect contrition.
The Sacrament of Confession is related to the Sacrament of Baptism. For baptism confers the state of grace, and confession returns one to that state after an actual mortal sin. The forgiveness of perfect contrition is termed confession “at least by desire” by the Council of Trent [Sixth Session, chapter XIV] and defined as contrition that is “perfect through charity” [Fourteenth Session, chapter IV].
Baptism, which forgives original sin and personal sin, can be obtained implicitly. So also can the forgiveness of perfect contrition be implicit. The “person outside the Church” generally does not explicitly desire the sacrament of confession, yet according to Pope Saint Pius X (quoted above) he can obtain forgiveness by perfect contrition. If he could only obtain forgiveness by first converting, he would be baptized and be forgiven by baptism, rather than by perfect contrition. So the Pontiff refers to a person who remains formally outside the Church, does not convert to Christianity, yet obtains forgiveness and the state of grace (or a return to that state) by perfect contrition. If a person has never received any form of baptism, he can enter the state of grace for the first time by an act of perfect contrition, even implicit perfect contrition.
Perfect contrition is partially implicit when the person has sorrow for his sins out of explicit love for God, implicitly desiring the Sacrament of Confession. Perfect contrition is fully implicit when the person has sorrow for his sins out of explicit love for his neighbor (who was harmed by his sins), implicitly loving God and implicitly desiring the Sacrament of Confession.
The true spiritual love of neighbor always includes, at least implicitly, the love of God.
[1 John]
{4:20} If anyone says that he loves God, but hates his brother, then he is a liar. For he who does not love his brother, whom he does see, in what way can he love God, whom he does not see?
{4:21} And this is the commandment that we have from God, that he who loves God must also love his brother.
See also Matthew 5, Matthew 19, Romans 13, Galatians 5.
7. All non-Christian believers (Jews, Muslims, others) and unbelievers (atheists, agnostics) can possibly obtain salvation without converting to Christianity or to belief in God — if their refusal to convert is not an actual mortal sin, and if they obtain the state of grace by a baptism of desire or blood, and if they either avoid all actual mortal sin or repent with perfect contrition.

text:
World Daily Brief — September 25, 2026

1. UN: Netanyahu calls Gaza genocide allegations "biggest lie of the century" as 77 delegations walk out

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delivered a defiant, roughly 40-minute address to the UN General Assembly Thursday, dismissing allegations of genocide in Gaza as "the biggest lie of the century" and declaring "Israel didn't commit genocide. Israel prevented genocide" — even as 77 delegations walked out before or during his speech, leaving a majority of visible seats empty. "If there are any other moral cowards who have not yet left the hall, please do so now," Netanyahu said as he took the podium, later accusing critics of "mind-blowing hypocrisy." He staunchly defended Israel's war against Iran as "one of the easiest decisions I've ever had to make," claiming several leaders who walked out privately thank Israel for "taking out Iran's nukes," and dismissed West Bank settler violence as the work of a few "juvenile delinquents." He also singled out New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has called for Netanyahu's arrest over an outstanding ICC warrant and accused him afterward of using the speech "to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians." The address — which doubled as a pre-election stump speech ahead of Israel's vote next month — came after a week of world leaders' speeches condemning Israel's conduct in Gaza, and unfolded against protests outside UN headquarters.

Separately, Trump's Board of Peace unveiled a $2.45 billion Gaza recovery plan this week, even as a rights group reported that some individuals it had classified as journalists killed in Gaza were in fact militants — a finding likely to complicate the broader accountability debate playing out in parallel with Israel's own recently opened criminal probes into incidents like the Hind Rajab killing.

2. United States/China: Trump hosts Xi for high-stakes state visit on AI and trade

President Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House Thursday for a state visit centered on artificial intelligence, trade, and global conflicts, giving Xi a tour of the grounds — including the new Marine One helipad on the South Lawn — before Oval Office talks and a state dinner attended by several US tech executives. Xi, through a translator, called for more US-China cooperation on AI "as a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses," amid White House concern that Chinese firms are maliciously copying American AI technology, which Beijing denies. Trump said the two leaders made "tremendous strides" on key issues but offered no specifics; separately, the US Trade Secretary said the two countries have agreed to extend their trade truce ahead of further high-stakes talks. The visit landed the same week the Senate narrowly rejected a resolution demanding Trump end the war against Iran, underscoring how thoroughly Washington's diplomatic bandwidth remains split between the Iran conflict and the broader US-China relationship.

3. Ongoing threads worth tracking

Gulf security: Saudi, Turkish, and Pakistani military chiefs are meeting to discuss supporting Saudi Arabia under their new joint defense pact, after Saudi Arabia's Grand Mufti called on soldiers to be ready to help oust the Houthis from power in Yemen; Turkey's parliament speaker floated expanding the pact into a broader "Muslim world" alliance that could include Iran.

US press freedom: A federal judge has ordered the White House to restore press access for CNN and Politico reporters after a dispute over a media ban.

Cybersecurity: An OpenAI-built AI agent reportedly breached Australia's Medicare system, in what's being called the first known AI-driven breach of a government body.

text:
THE APC’S AUTHORITARIAN TURN AND THE POLITICS OF COERCION: THE WAR AGAINST THE BALLOT

By: Sopriala Membere (@SoprialaMembere) Columnist, Scholar and Member CRA Advocacy Network
———————————————

Max Weber, in the foundational lecture that gave modern political science its vocabulary, defined the state as that human community which successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory. This definition scholars have pointed out, is not merely descriptive; it is diagnostic. When a ruling party begins to privatise that monopoly—when it transforms the police, the anti-corruption agencies, the digital surveillance apparatus of the State, and the informal networks of political thuggery into partisan instruments—what remains is no longer a State in the Weberian sense. What remains is a syndicate: an organised criminal enterprise that wears the costume of government while functioning as a protection racket. 

Nigeria, in the twilight months of 2026, is living through this theoretical nightmare in real time. And the sentence that unlocked it was spoken not in a dark room but in broad daylight, by a sitting president who should have known better. "All is fair in politics." President Bola Tinubu uttered those words in July 2026 while receiving Catholic Bishops, and in doing so, he did not merely offer a casual reflection on the rough-and-tumble of democratic contestation. He issued a philosophical charter for lawlessness and a licence that dissolves the distinction between the legitimate coercion of the state and the predatory violence of the street. 

Between July 2025 and September 2026, the ADC and other opposition political parties have documented a systematic campaign of violence against opposition political meetings, the destruction of party property, assaults on participants, and threats against citizens because of their political preferences across Nigeria.
This is not the random turbulence of a raucous democracy. It is the patterned choreography of a ruling Party (APC),  that has run out of ideas and has reached for the gun.

To understand what is happening, one must move beyond the mere thought electoral malpractice and into the conceptual territory of competitive authoritarianism. Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way, in their seminal work on the subject, describe regimes that hold elections but systematically tilt the playing field through coercion, patronage, and the selective application of the law. 

Nigeria under President Bola Tinubu fits this typology with disturbing precision. In Edo State, the ADC secretariat in Benin City was attacked, and gunfire was directed at the residence of former Governor and leader of the ADC H.E John Odigie-Oyegun during a gathering of political leaders. The police confirmed the incident and promised an investigation. That was February 2026, yet till date, no arrests have been made, nor any official  prosecutions.

In Rivers State, the home of an ADC member, Isaiah Thomas, was attacked by armed men barely 24 hours after campaigns officially opened; the assailants ransacked his residence, looted property, and set buildings ablaze after failing to find him at home. 
 
1/

text:
Something hit me recently while reflecting on my life. I became a Christian later in life, at 36. I always believed in God, but I never really understood what people meant when they said they “gave their life to Jesus.”

The irony is, I had already given my life away to everyone else. I tried to do everything right. I gave everything I had to the people around me until eventually there was nothing left. I was completely defeated, drained, broken, and felt like I had nothing left to offer anyone. Not even my kids.

I was raising four kids alone, no real friends, no help from family, it was just us 5, and no end in sight. Then one evening, kids asleep, in my bathtub contemplating what to do with my life, I said, “Well God, I guess there’s nothing left to do but accept Jesus as my Lord and Savior. That’s what I’m supposed to do, right?” I surrendered from a completed defeated position. Not because I had figured everything out, but because I had finally run out of myself.

And then things started happening. A week later there was a knock at my door that eventually led me to church. Through that church I met my wife. (This all happened within a month or so) We were married six months later. Seven years and three kids later together raising all 7 together, I can look back and see just how much changed when my stubborn self finally stopped trying to do everything on my own. I used to pride myself on being a lone wolf. Now I see the importance of the pack. Belonging to something bigger than just me. 

But here’s what really hit me recently: I never stopped giving. I still give my time away. I still carry other people’s burdens. (I'm a counselor) I still pour myself into my family and into helping people. The very things that used to completely drain me are still part of my life. Nothing changed. 

Except I don’t feel empty anymore. I don't feel exhausted and drained. 

It’s like I spent the first part of my life as a phone running on its own battery. I kept giving away power until I eventually hit 1% and was about to shut off. That’s when I finally plugged in. Yes, all the way down to 1%, I'm stubborn.  

And I never unplugged.

I’m still pouring out, but I’m not trying to power everything from my own finite battery anymore. I’m connected to an infinite source.

I didn’t need to stop giving myself away. I needed to stop believing I was the source.

text:
The menu for Trump's State Dinner:

The menu showcased American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence, bringing the culinary traditions of both nations together.

The meal will begin with a toast of Schramsberg "Blanc De Noir," honoring the historic “Toast to Peace” shared by President Nixon and Premier Zhou Enlai in Beijing in 1972.

The same American sparkling wine served at that historic gathering is still enjoyed at White House functions today.

First Course
Yellow Squash Velouté
Wild Mushroom Fricassée
Crispy Pancetta
Scallion Oil

The first course offers a refined and silky-smooth velouté made of sweet yellow squash. This course is gently blended to highlight its delicate seasonal flavors of earthy wild mushrooms, sautéed with fresh herbs. Together, these ingredients create a rich fricassee, complemented by crispy pancetta for a savory and smoky contrast. A finishing drizzle of scallion oil adds vibrance and a subtle allium brightness to the dish.

Second Course
Sesame Crusted Sea Bass
Braised Baby Bok Choy
Roasted Garden Eggplant
Sauce Verte

The second course is prepared delicately with fresh sea bass and coated in toasted sesame seeds. This combination created a fragrant, nutty crust while keeping the fish tender. The fish is served with crisp baby bok choy and roasted garden eggplant, creating lightly caramelized flavors. The dish is finished with a vibrant sauce verte of fresh herbs, which added brightness, acidity, and a garden character.

Dessert
Vanilla Crémeux & White House Honey Ice Cream
Walnut Frangipane
Sour Cherry Confit

The dessert course is a smooth vanilla crémeux with a vibrant sour cherry confit center, topped with a rich walnut frangipane. The dessert’s fruit-shaped form is complemented by a delicate ice cream made with harvested White House honey.

ENTERTAINMENT

Several performances will take place during the formal dinner, headlined by Mr. Christopher Macchio, a classically trained tenor who performed at the 2025 Presidential Inauguration. The evening’s entertainment will feature performances by military musicians from the United States Marine Corps and the United States Army, including “The President’s Own” United States Marine Band, “The Commandant’s Own” United States Marine Drum and Bugle Corps, the United States Army Chorus, and the United States Army Strings.

FLORAL & DÉCOR

The décor for the evening is an expression of warmth and celebration and draws on the color red’s longstanding cultural significance throughout Chinese history. Urns showcase overflowing red blossoms. Tables are dressed in rich red linens and adorned with dahlias and ranunculus. 
 
Among the seasonal blooms, the tables feature vermeil from the White House collection. The Reagan State Service is featured on the tables. These details blend Chinese artistry and American tradition together, showcased within the timeless elegance of the White House.

text:
FAITH THAT STANDS IN THE GAP
THE FAITH THAT SPEAKS WHEN SILENCE IS SAFER
NATHAN - The courage to confront the king.

There are moments when faith means praying quietly, carrying someone before God, or waiting patiently for Him to act. But there are other moments when faithfulness requires something far more frightening. There are moments when God's truth must be spoken to someone who does not want to hear it, and when silence would be easier, safer, and more comfortable. Nathan stood in one of those moments. He was a prophet standing before David, the king of Israel, a man whose authority could make opposition extremely dangerous. Yet Nathan walked into David's presence carrying something more important than his own safety. HE CARRIED THE WORD OF GOD.

David had committed grievous sin. He had taken Bathsheba, attempted to conceal her pregnancy, and arranged for Uriah to be killed. The king remained on his throne, the kingdom continued, and life around him carried on as though nothing had happened. But sin can remain hidden from people while never being hidden from God. Nathan entered David's presence because God would not allow David to bury his sin beneath his crown.

Nathan did not begin by humiliating David. He told him a story about a rich man who took a poor man's only beloved lamb. David became angry and declared that such a man deserved judgment. Then Nathan spoke four words that changed everything: “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). David could recognize wickedness when he saw it in someone else, but Nathan forced him to see it in himself. THE MOST DANGEROUS THING ABOUT SIN IS NOT ALWAYS THAT WE CANNOT SEE IT; SOMETIMES IT IS THAT WE CAN SEE IT CLEARLY IN OTHER PEOPLE WHILE REMAINING BLIND TO IT IN OURSELVES.

Nathan had no army, no throne, and no worldly power that guaranteed his safety. He simply had God's Word. Yet that was enough. He reminded David of what God had given him, exposed what David had done, and declared that judgment would follow. David's crown did not place him above God's law. His past victories did not excuse his present sin. His anointing did not make him immune to correction. THE KING WAS NOT ABOVE THE WORD OF GOD, AND NATHAN REFUSED TO TREAT HIM AS THOUGH HE WERE.

That principle matters because power can create an atmosphere where everyone becomes afraid to tell the truth. People flatter. They excuse. They protect. They remain silent because confrontation has a cost. Nathan refused to allow David's position to silence God's truth. BIBLICAL FAITHFULNESS DOES NOT MEASURE TRUTH BY THE STATUS OF THE PERSON WHO NEEDS TO HEAR IT.

But Nathan also shows us that confronting sin is not the same thing as enjoying confrontation. He was not seeking revenge or building a reputation as the prophet who dared to challenge the king. He delivered a painful message because God's holiness required it and David's soul needed to hear it. TRUTH WITHOUT LOVE CAN BECOME CRUELTY, BUT LOVE WITHOUT TRUTH CAN BECOME COWARDICE. FAITHFULNESS HOLDS BOTH TOGETHER.

That is where Nathan's story becomes uncomfortable for us. Sometimes we call silence wisdom when it is actually fear. Sometimes we call it peace when we simply want to avoid discomfort. There are certainly times when wisdom requires patience, humility, timing, and discretion. Scripture does not call us to confront everyone about everything. But there are also moments when silence becomes participation in someone's destruction. WHEN GOD HAS GIVEN US THE RESPONSIBILITY TO SPEAK TRUTH, OUR FEAR OF CONSEQUENCES CANNOT BECOME MORE IMPORTANT THAN OUR FAITHFULNESS TO GOD.

Nathan's courage was not based upon his own authority. He confronted David because God's authority stood above both of them. He was not presenting his personal preference as divine revelation. He was delivering God's Word. TRUE SPIRITUAL COURAGE DOES NOT SAY, “LISTEN TO ME BECAUSE I AM IMPORTANT.” IT SAYS, “LISTEN TO WHAT GOD HAS SAID.” And that means the same Word we bring to others must first govern us. WE MUST NEVER STAND ABOVE THE WORD OF GOD WHILE USING IT TO STAND OVER OTHER PEOPLE.

Then David confessed: “I have sinned against the LORD.” (2 Samuel 12:13). He did not blame Bathsheba. He did not blame circumstances. He did not appeal to his past faithfulness. He confessed. The truth had pierced through his defenses. THE PURPOSE OF BIBLICAL CONFRONTATION IS NOT TO DESTROY THE SINNER; IT IS TO BRING THE SINNER INTO THE LIGHT WHERE REPENTANCE BECOMES POSSIBLE.

Yet forgiveness did not erase the consequences. Nathan made that clear. GOD'S FORGIVENESS IS FREE, BUT SIN IS NEVER CHEAP. David was forgiven, but the damage caused by his sin remained painfully real. Scripture refuses the shallow idea that grace makes sin harmless. God's mercy is astonishingly deep, but sin is devastatingly serious.

Nathan's story also connects beautifully with the larger movement of Theme 6. Abraham carried people before God. Jacob wrestled with God while being confronted with his own dependence. Nathan now carries God's truth before someone who desperately needs to hear it. INTERCESSION AND CONFRONTATION ARE NOT OPPOSITES WHEN BOTH FLOW FROM LOVE FOR GOD AND LOVE FOR PEOPLE. Sometimes standing in the gap means praying for someone. Sometimes it means standing before them and speaking the truth they cannot see about themselves.

But Nathan could expose David's sin without being able to remove it. He could announce judgment without bearing that judgment in David's place. He could call David to repentance without providing the righteousness David needed. THE PROPHET COULD POINT TO THE SIN, BUT ONLY CHRIST COULD CARRY THE SIN. Nathan was a faithful messenger, but he was not the Saviour.

The contrast between David and Christ is striking. David used his authority to take what belonged to another man. Jesus, possessing all authority, gave Himself for those who belonged to Him. David abused his position to satisfy his desire. Christ humbled Himself and surrendered His life for His people. WHERE DAVID USED POWER TO TAKE, CHRIST USED AUTHORITY TO GIVE. WHERE DAVID BROUGHT DEATH THROUGH SIN, CHRIST BROUGHT LIFE THROUGH SACRIFICE.

This changes the way we think about speaking truth. We are not called to become spiritual detectives searching for opportunities to expose everyone else's failures. We are called to love truth because we love God and people. There will be times when we need to speak. There will also be times when we need to listen, pray, wait, and examine ourselves first. Nathan's courage does not give us permission to confront everyone. It shows us what faithful confrontation looks like when God has actually entrusted us with responsibility for another person's good.

And there is tenderness in that. David needed someone who loved him enough to refuse to flatter him. Sometimes the most loving thing we can do is refuse to reassure someone that everything is fine when it is not. REAL LOVE DOES NOT PROTECT PEOPLE FROM EVERY PAINFUL TRUTH; IT HELPS BRING THEM INTO THE LIGHT WHERE GRACE CAN DEAL WITH WHAT IS KILLING THEM.

So, Nathan leaves us with an uncomfortable question. Who are we becoming when truth becomes inconvenient? Do we still speak when there is something to lose? Do we remain faithful when the person who needs correction has more influence than we do? Do we care enough about someone's soul to risk temporary discomfort for their eternal good? Or have we quietly learned to call silence wisdom because silence costs us less?

Nathan had no throne and no army. He had something far more important. HE HAD THE WORD OF GOD, AND HE WAS WILLING TO STAND UNDER ITS AUTHORITY BEFORE A KING.He did not confront David to become famous. He confronted David because God had spoken and David needed to hear.
Nathan ultimately points us to Christ, who is not merely the One who tells us the truth but the Truth Himself. Jesus does not flatter sinners into salvation. He exposes sin, calls for repentance, offers forgiveness, and gives Himself for His people. He is completely truthful and completely merciful.

NATHAN STOOD BEFORE A KING AND SAID, “YOU ARE THE MAN.” CHRIST STANDS BEFORE SINNERS AND TELLS THE TRUTH ABOUT US, BUT THEN HE DOES WHAT NATHAN COULD NEVER DO: HE GOES TO THE CROSS AND BEARS THE JUDGMENT THAT OUR SIN DESERVES.

That is the hope beneath faithful confrontation. We speak truth because sin is serious, but we speak it knowing grace is greater. We confront because repentance matters. We warn because eternity matters. We refuse to flatter because souls matter. THE PURPOSE IS NEVER TO WIN AN ARGUMENT OR PROVE THAT WE WERE RIGHT. THE PURPOSE IS TO BRING PEOPLE INTO THE LIGHT OF GOD'S TRUTH WHERE SIN CAN BE CONFESSED, REPENTANCE CAN BEGIN, AND THE MERCY OF CHRIST CAN BE SEEN FOR WHAT IT REALLY IS.
Abraham taught us to carry others before God. Jacob taught us to surrender our own striving before God. Nathan teaches us that sometimes, after carrying someone before God, WE MAY BE CALLED TO CARRY GOD'S TRUTH TO THEM. That can cost relationships. It can cost approval. It can cost comfort. But when God entrusts us with the responsibility to speak, faithfulness means remembering that our first loyalty is not to people's applause but to God's truth.
SILENCE MAY SOMETIMES PROTECT OUR COMFORT, OUR POSITION, AND OUR RELATIONSHIPS, BUT FAITHFULNESS ASKS A HARDER QUESTION: WHAT DOES LOVE REQUIRE ME TO SAY?

Nathan walked into the presence of a king carrying no weapon except the truth God had given him. He did not know how David would respond. He did not know what consequences his words might bring. He simply knew that God's Word could not be compromised to protect a man's crown. And because Nathan was willing to speak, David was brought face to face with the reality he had been hiding from.

FAITHFULNESS SOMETIMES MEANS LOVING SOMEONE ENOUGH TO TELL THEM THE TRUTH THEY DESPERATELY DO NOT WANT TO HEAR, WHILE LOVING THEM ENOUGH TO PRAY THAT THE TRUTH WILL LEAD THEM HOME TO GRACE.

Truth does not bow to the age. It stands. And so will those who stand with Christ.

The annual Day of Atonement likewise belonged to the recurring ceremonial structure of Israel. Year after year the high priest entered according to the law, and Hebrews drives the point home by showing the insufficiency of repetition to perfect the conscience. “But in those sacrifices there is a remembrance again made of sins every year” (Hebrews 10:3). Every year. Again. And again. And again. The repeated sacrifice was practically preaching its own incompleteness. If the thing had finished the sin question permanently, why were they back next year? Hebrews answers it: “For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). Then Christ comes, offers one sacrifice for sins for ever, and sits down. That sitting down ought to knock the props out from under every system that tries to rebuild the annual machinery as though Calvary were merely another installment in the payment plan. Aaron went in repeatedly because the animal sacrifice could not finish it. Christ entered with His own blood and did what no yearly ritual could ever do.

That is why “years” fits perfectly into Paul’s argument. A religious system can occupy every square on a man’s calendar and still leave him without the righteousness of Jesus Christ. It can regulate his week, his month, his season, and his year and never regenerate his soul. A man can spend fifty years observing fifty religious years and die trusting his observance instead of the Saviour. What a tragedy—busy all his life and bankrupt at the judgment. The issue in Galatia is not whether the sabbatical year was Biblical. It was. Jubilee was Biblical. The Day of Atonement was Biblical. The question is whether those things are the ground of a Christian’s justification or the required machinery of his standing in Christ. Paul’s answer is not merely no; it is a warning that to seek righteousness there is to return toward bondage. A thing may be Biblical and still be dispensationally misplaced. A prescription written for somebody else does not become your medicine because both names appear in the same medical book.

12. THE CALENDAR BECOMES A COURTROOM

This is where an important distinction has to be nailed down so firmly that nobody can wiggle around it. Paul is not teaching that a Christian sins by remembering a day. Romans 14 would forbid that interpretation. “One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” (Romans 14:5). Then Paul says, “He that regardeth the day, regardeth it unto the Lord” (Romans 14:6). That is liberty. One believer may set aside a day for something unto the Lord. Another may not attach the same significance to it. Neither man gets to crawl onto the throne of God and issue a warrant for the other fellow. If a Christian chooses to study Passover at Passover, fine. If he wants to remember the resurrection of Jesus Christ on a particular day, fine. If another Christian does not observe that day in the same way, leave him alone. Christian liberty is not the right to make everybody else exercise liberty exactly as you do. The minute that happens, liberty has been mugged in the parking lot by legalism.

The problem begins when the calendar becomes a courtroom. That is the line. Paul says in Colossians, “Let no man therefore judge you” (Colossians 2:16). There is the legal word sitting right in the passage. Judge. Do not let a man haul you into his religious court and make your acceptance with God depend upon meat, drink, holyday, new moon, or Sabbath days. A calendar is a useful servant and a miserable saviour. It can tell you that Tuesday comes after Monday. It cannot tell God that you are righteous. It can remind you when a feast was historically observed. It cannot impute righteousness to your account. It can mark a Sabbath. It cannot nail your sins to a cross. Yet

text:
what you really need is this calendar.” It would be funny if Paul were not so alarmed by it. The heir is being offered a beggar’s bowl. The son is being offered servant’s wages. The free man is being measured for a yoke. And because the package has Hebrew writing on it, people assume it must be an upgrade.

“The tragedy of Galatians 4 is an heir leaving the Father’s house to beg for what Christ has already given him freely.” That is exactly the insanity Paul is confronting. The law had treasures of revelation, prophecy, type, shadow, moral truth, and historical instruction, but it was never able to bestow justification on a sinner by his works. The ceremonies contained pictures of Christ; they were not competitors with Christ. The Passover lamb pointed toward “Christ our passover” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The sacrifices pointed toward a better sacrifice. The priesthood pointed toward a better Priest. The tabernacle pointed beyond itself. The Sabbath pointed beyond itself. The feasts pointed beyond themselves. But the religious mind is forever taking a road sign, setting up a lawn chair in front of it, and refusing to travel to the destination. When Christ arrives, you do not worship the directional arrow.

8. “YE OBSERVE DAYS” — THE DAILY AND WEEKLY LEVEL OF BONDAGE

“Ye observe days” (Galatians 4:10). There is the first item in Paul’s calendar. Days. Under the law, Israel had appointed days, Sabbaths, holy convocations, feast days, days of rest, and ceremonial dates ordained by God for that people under that covenantal arrangement. Nobody needs to apologize for them. God ordained them. The seventh-day Sabbath was not dreamed up by a rabbi who had nothing to do on Friday night. It was a sign associated with Israel and God’s covenant dealings with that nation. The law contained special days because God was teaching Israel in time, history, ceremony, shadow, memorial, and prophecy. But the existence of a divinely appointed ordinance in one dispensation does not automatically make that ordinance a condition of justification in another. Failure to understand that little matter has built more religious prisons than a Roman emperor.

Colossians 2 gives Paul’s companion warning: “Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days” (Colossians 2:16). Notice the word judge. That is where religious observance turns poisonous. A man may choose to regard a day unto the Lord. Romans 14 permits that liberty. Another may not esteem that day above another. Romans 14 permits that liberty too. What Paul will not permit is one believer climbing onto God’s judgment seat and using a calendar as evidence for the prosecution. The minute a personal observance becomes a divine requirement that determines whether another Christian is accepted, justified, spiritual, obedient, saved, or second-class, somebody has turned a date into a judge. Paul was not condemning a calendar; he was condemning a calendar turned into a courtroom.

The Sabbath question especially exposes the issue. Men will say, “But it is in the Bible!” Of course it is in the Bible. So is animal sacrifice. So is circumcision. So are cities of refuge. So are dietary restrictions. So is the command for a priest to inspect leprosy. The question is not whether something appears between Genesis and Revelation. The question is to whom was it given, under what covenant, for what purpose, and what does later revelation say about the believer’s relationship to it? text:
Stanford course will critique AI through lens of ‘African intellectual sovereignty’ | Bruno Kouatly, The College Fix

Course is built on assumption that such ‘unjust practices and injustices’ exist, scholar says

Students in a spring 2027 Stanford University course will critique AI systems through the lens of “African intellectual sovereignty” and “unlearn … epistemic injustices.”

The course will examine how to gain “African intellectual sovereignty in an era dominated by algorithmic governance, data colonialism, and techno-capitalism,” according to the course description.

Students will “work to unlearn and deconstruct epistemic injustices, dismantling unjust practices, assumptions, and institutions while actively creating new ways of knowing and being.”

Further, the description states that the course critiques “Eurocentric epistemologies embedded in AI systems and global knowledge infrastructures” and elevates “Indigenous African knowledge systems.”

The class is offered by Stanford’s Department of African and African American Studies and taught by Professor Samuel Nkansah.

The College Fix reached out to Nkansah for more information on the course, but did not receive a response.

The Fix also asked Stanford University if the course requires students to adopt specific political or ideological positions. The school also did not respond.

However, National Association of Scholars Senior Fellow Lilla Kiss raised several concerns about this course in an interview with The Fix.

NAS is a non-profit that advocates for intellectual freedom, virtuous citizenship, liberal arts education, and reform in higher education.

“Stanford’s description starts with labels such as ‘data colonialism’ and ‘techno-capitalism’ without clearly explaining what would justify those labels or call them into question,” Kiss said.

Further, “Having less access to technology does not automatically mean a country is being ‘colonized,’” she said.

What’s more, many African countries are not lagging technologically.

She cited the United Nation’s 2024 E-Government Development Index, which examines digital progress trends in member countries. South Africa, Mauritius, Tunisia, Morocco, Seychelles, and Egypt all have “E-Government Development Index (EGDI) values above the world average,” meaning they are not technologically lagging.

She also said the course seems to wrongfully assume the cultural or technological homogeneity of Africa.

“The course description also indicates that Africa is a ‘homogenous’ place, with shared victimhood and problems. It is not. Indeed, African countries differ considerably,” she said.

“Stanford’s framing therefore risks overlooking differences among African countries and how foreign technology can actually help communities build something of their own,” she said.

For example, Meta’s open source Llama “gives developers a foundation they can modify for local needs without financing the original model’s development.”

Kiss also noted that the course description signals a clear “ideological direction before an open classroom discussion even begins.”

This raises concerns over whether students will be able to push back against the course’s assumptions or be expected to adopt its conclusions, she said.

Kiss also raised concerns that “the course is built on the assumption that such ‘unjust practices and injustices’ are existing without examining if this presumption stands at all.”

Dictating to students what they should reject without fairly considering competing arguments “risks turning education into ideological instruction,” she said.

“Finally,” Kiss said, “African and European intellectual traditions deserve equally rigorous scrutiny, including an examination of who gets to define ‘African values’ and how the course accommodates Africans who might dare to disagree.”

Stanford University is currently embroiled in a controversy after it admitted to using AI to alter students’ appearances in promotional materials, including digitally transforming one male student into a black female, The College Fix reported.

University spokesperson Charlene Gage told Inside Higher Ed that the school violated its own AI policy and has removed the banners with the AI-edited images.

text:
The UN Vote Economy: Microstates Gain Diplomatic Leverage

Across the Pacific, voices of small nations are rising, gaining visibility and influence in international affairs. Nauru, Palau, Micronesia, and the Marshall Islands have historically demonstrated that tiny populations do not mean insignificant diplomatic weight. Their positions can matter in UN votes and wider diplomatic relations.

Amid growing Western pressure, Israel’s diplomatic response can be seen reaching beyond the ‘behemoths’ and into the world’s smallest nations. As criticism and economic measures from countries like the UK and France increase, Israel is simultaneously deepening relationships with smaller states that can provide something the powers of larger players cannot: equal sovereign representation at the UN.

Nauru is a fitting example. A small state with a population of about 12000, opened an embassy in Israel in September 2026, describing it as a way to deepen its bilateral engagement, support national development, and expand strategic cooperation. Israel, meanwhile, identifies Nauru as one of its most consistent supporters at the UN.

Slovenia, on the other hand, offers a European counterpart. Israel opened its first resident embassy in Ljubljana a few days after Nauru opened its embassy, following the election of the current government. The two countries also signed a cooperation programme covering education,  science, culture, youth and sport, alongside wider economic engagement.

This creates what can be called a “visibility arbitrage.” The term is purely analytical, not an established policy label, meaning that smaller states can use diplomatic recognition, UN participation, and strategic relationships to gain access, attention, and practical partnerships disproportionate to their size.

The emerging lesson is not that microstates simply trade votes for aid. It is that they can transform their limited material power into diplomatic leverage, visibility, and gain access. In an increasingly competitive world, smaller states may have discovered that their greatest strategic asset is not what they possess but how many actors want their support.

text:
Data gauntlet next week has yield, rate implications: Robust U.S. data the last few weeks helped set the stage for the yield rally. It also arguably raised the profile of several key data points on next week's calendar, notably Wednesday's August Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index and Thursday's September ISM Manufacturing PMI®. It's arguably back to a "good is bad" scenario, at least concerning the bond environment, as each new robust data point could send yields up while raising certainty about a Fed rate hike next month. Early today, odds of an October rate increase were 66%, according to the CME FedWatch Tool. Next Tuesday's Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) report and next Friday's nonfarm payrolls report also have rate implications. "If the labor market remains stable, it just takes pressure away from that side of the mandate and allows the Fed to focus more on inflation and raise if necessary," said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research (SCFR).
 
Yield rise reflects positives, too: Though fast-rising yields this year likely shocked investors and certainly reversed hopes for rate cuts many harbored, it's not as if 5% yields are necessarily kryptonite for the stock market. In many ways, they could be seen as good news because they partly reflect resilient growth despite the rise in oil that's kept inflation simmering. Also, the term premium, or the extra compensation investors receive for investing in longer-term Treasuries, hasn't risen too much, suggesting U.S. fiscal concerns aren't a key driver. Besides recent manufacturing and services economy strength, there's been good news on retail sales and jobs growth recently. As of Thursday, the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tool for third quarter gross domestic product (GDP) growth stood at 5.1%. That's a running estimate that should be checked again after next week's data. Also, earnings growth has been more than solid, keeping the stock market near record highs. "Treasury yields can rise for good or bad reasons, and I don't necessarily think they're rising for bad reasons," my colleague Martin said in a podcast Thursday.
 
Bond market's impact on stocks tracked: From an investor's perspective, Fed rate hikes could pull up the yields on short-term investments. When the yields on Treasury bills, short-term certificates of deposit, and money market funds rise, they compete more with the stock market for investor cash, another potential challenge for Wall Street. Certain sectors, notably utilities and staples that tend to offer dividends, tend to lose ground. Small-cap stocks also backtracked this week, along with growth areas like tech. Stocks with heavy borrowing needs or with earnings growth that's expected to take longer can be more sensitive to rising long-term yields, which may clip profits or even delay or prevent planned projects. That's possibly why Bloomberg's report yesterday on Oracle (ORCL) declaring "force majeure" on a data center under construction raised Wall Street's hackles. It reinforces ideas that borrowing could be a problem for the tech sector if yields keep climbing. Oracle borrowed heavily to finance expansion of its AI footprint, and it's far from alone among big tech.

🎨 AI ART & VISUALS ROUNDUP — September 25, 2026

1️⃣ HIGGSFIELD LAUNCHES $20M API CASHBACK — SPEND $100K, GET $100K BACK

Higgsfield is backing builders with a $20 million API cashback pool: 100% of your API spend comes back instantly as API credits, on every model in its lineup. The cap sits at $100,000 per business — spend $100,000, get $100,000 back in credits, which is effectively $200,000 of total usage. Unused cashback expires on September 30, and the announcement lands alongside the new GPT-6 Astra integration and a step-by-step build guide from Greg Isenberg. For indie developers shipping video features, it is the most aggressive developer offer in the space right now.
🔹 @higgsfield_ai

2️⃣ MIDJOURNEY PUBLISHES THE OFFICIAL GUIDE TO CONSISTENT CHARACTERS

Midjourney dropped a short video walkthrough of its new edit model, made specifically because users kept asking how to keep the same character looking the same across generations. The guide walks through the new V8.2 edit pipeline for consistent characters and more, and it doubles as a demo of how much of the character workflow now lives inside the editor rather than in the prompt. Consistency has historically been the single biggest complaint about AI character work, so an official recipe for it matters.
🔹 @midjourney

3️⃣ MIDJOURNEY SHIPS SEAMLESS --tile PATTERNS, PRECISION INPAINTING AND A REAL-TIME PREVIEW

A quieter update with real depth: Midjourney released a new version of --tile that generates seamless repeating patterns in v8.1 and v8.2, plus a new version of inpainting that changes only the pixels you actually select. The most intriguing piece is an early preview of real-time models on the alpha site — the first official hint that interactive, live-generation aesthetics are on the roadmap. For anyone who makes textures, wallpapers, or surface designs, the tile mode alone is worth testing today.
🔹 @midjourney

4️⃣ KREA AGENT GETS CUSTOM APPS — DESCRIBE THE TOOL, GET THE TOOL

Krea introduced custom apps inside Krea Agent: describe the creative tool you want, and the agent builds it. The examples shown include a character studio, a 3D viewer, and a motion-effects app that splits an image into a grid, animates each tile, and lets you switch between wave, elastic, and glitch effects. It is a small step that reframes the whole category — instead of choosing from a fixed menu of features, you define the tool itself.
🔹 @krea_ai

5️⃣ KREA IS COMING TO META'S MUSE

Krea announced its models are coming to Meta's Muse app. That is a notable shift: one of the leading independent image labs is putting its technology inside a big consumer app, exposing its generations to a mainstream audience far larger than its own user base. Krea's post asks what the community wants Muse to make first — the bigger story is what the move says about how fast this ecosystem is consolidating around distribution.
🔹 @krea_ai

💭 The thread connecting all five: the model war is being decided less in the lab and more in the workflow. Midjourney is investing in editing precision, consistent characters, and interactive real-time generation; Krea is turning its agent into a tool-builder while pushing its tech into Meta's app; and Higgsfield is betting $20 million that developer economics will decide the video era. The moat is shifting from raw image quality to where creation actually happens.

Which of these five actually changes how you work — and which one do you think will quietly disappear? 👇

text:
During the 1974 Cyprus war 
 Pakistan extended significant **diplomatic, humanitarian, and operational assistance** to Turkey, reflecting the long-standing strategic alliance between the two nations.

---

 1. Diplomatic & International Support

* **UN & OIC Stances:** Pakistan was one of the strongest international voices backing Turkey's legal stance under the 1960 *Treaty of Guarantee*. In international forums, including the United Nations and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), Pakistan consistently defended Turkey's actions as a necessary intervention to protect the Turkish Cypriot minority against ethnic violence and the Greek military junta-backed coup.
* **Non-Recognition Policy:** Pakistan refused to recognize the Greek Cypriot-led Republic of Cyprus as representing the entire island and strongly advocated for the equal rights and self-determination of Turkish Cypriots.
* **Support for TRNC:** Following the declaration of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) in 1983, Pakistan remained one of its most ardent supporters, maintaining close informal diplomatic and trade links despite UN Security Council resolutions restricting formal recognition.

---

### 2. Military Medical & Humanitarian Assistance

* **Deployment of Armed Forces Medical Teams:** Following the outbreak of hostilities on July 20, 1974, the Government of Pakistan dispatched a military medical mission onboard a PAF C-130 transport aircraft to Turkey on July 17–18, 1974.
* **Field Operations in Mersin and Tarsus:** Comprising around 30 doctors, nurses, and paramedical staff from the Pakistan Army Medical Corps (led by then-Major, later Lt. Gen., Karamat Ahmed Karamat), the team set up field treatment facilities in southern Turkey (Mersin and Tarsus). They treated hundreds of wounded Turkish military personnel and civilian evacuees from Cyprus.
* **Supply Lines:** Pakistan delivered critical medical kits, surgical equipment, blood plasma, and emergency field rations to support the Turkish Armed Forces (TSK) during the active phase of the conflict.

---

### 3. Operational & Intelligence Cooperation

* **Overflight & Logistics:** Pakistan made its airspace and airfields available for Turkish military and transport movements while offering immediate logistical backup.
* **Air Force & Navy Readiness:** While Pakistan did not deploy frontline combat troops due to geographic constraints and regional tensions in South Asia, the Pakistan Armed Forces were placed on high alert to offer technical, advisory, and equipment-spares assistance if required by Ankara.

---

### Historical Context & Legacy

 Today, the Cyprus issue remains a fundamental pillar of Pakistani foreign policy in the Eastern Mediterranean.

text:
Iran offers seven days to open Hormuz - if the blockade comes off first.

Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters at the United Nations on Thursday that Tehran has sent Washington, through mediators, a seven-day plan. 

If the conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz - the choke between Iran and Oman through which about a fifth of the world's seaborne oil usually passes - would open on day seven, and nuclear talks would restart.

The conditions he named track the June memorandum that later collapsed: stop fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon; unfreeze Iranian assets (he spoke of at least 12 billion dollars); waive sanctions on Iranian oil; lift the United States naval blockade of Iranian ports. Then the ships move. 

A White House official told Bloomberg that Donald Trump is open to talks but sees no need to hurry, because sanctions and the blockade already give Washington leverage. An Indian crewman was killed this week on the bulk carrier Cape Dao near the strait.

Iran and Oman each hold territorial sea along those banks. Marco Rubio called the Strait of Hormuz "international waters", a misnomer that conflates an international strait - a narrow used for world shipping, here inside Iranian and Omani territorial sea - with the high seas, which that choke does not contain.

So: the deep-water lane through the middle is supposed to stay open to transit. A blockade and a closed strait both treat that lane as a weapon.

---  Historical Context  ---

If you feel the oil price in your bones and still treat the waterway as a headline, walk the same narrow water in order.

In 1953 British and American services helped remove Iranian prime minister Mohammad Mossadegh after he nationalized Iranian oil. 

In 1979 the revolution took the US embassy in Tehran and held the staff. 

On 14 November 1979 President Jimmy Carter froze Iranian government assets in the United States; today's file still blocks most Iranian oil sales, banks, and hard-currency access, and the present war has added a US naval blockade of Iranian ports on top of that.

Through the 1980-88 Iran-Iraq war both sides hit tankers in this strait. 

In 1987 Washington reflagged Kuwaiti ships as Operation Earnest Will. 

On 17 May 1987 an Iraqi Mirage struck the American frigate Stark; 37 sailors died. 

On 3 July 1988 the cruiser Vincennes shot down Iran Air flight 655 over the strait; 290 civilians died; Washington called it a tragic error. 

In 2018 the United States left the nuclear deal that Obama had made with Iran. The present blockade and the asset freeze are the latest turn of that screw. 

The June 2026 memorandum tried to end the current war in 30 days and put Hormuz back under Iranian management. Armed clashes tore that paper up. 

Araghchi is now offering a shorter clock: the lane opens after the pressure comes off. With that, Tehran is using the same choke that was used on it - so distant capitals feel a similar cost Iranians have felt for years.

--- Spiritual Perspective  ---

If you only see a shipping price, step into the spiritual dimension of a locked lung.

Free will is the first law in that frame. A blockade that starves a country for decades is a refusal of that law. 

Closing the strait so the rest of the planet finally notices is the same refusal, only louder. 

Neither Washington nor Tehran is treating the other as a soul that may choose. They are treating each other as a tap. 

The world stayed quiet while sanctions bit Iranian pharmacies and Cuban shelves, then acted shocked when the pain arrived at the pump. 

You do not have to bless a mine to see why a numb system only moves when it hurts. 

You also do not have to call the hurt holy. 

Mother Earth does not need a new priesthood of stranglers. 

She needs the lane open and the habit of punishment dropped. 

Earth is a school. The lesson in a choke point is simple. If you only learn when your own chest tightens, you have not learned much.

text:
WHO WAS SUGAR RAY LEONARD BEFORE THE FAME? 🥊🇺🇸

Before the bright lights.

Before Roberto Durán.

Before Thomas Hearns.

Before Marvin Hagler.

Before the nickname “Sugar Ray” became synonymous with greatness…

He was simply Ray Charles Leonard.

Born on May 17, 1956, in Wilmington, North Carolina, Leonard was the fifth of seven children. His family later moved to Washington, D.C., and eventually settled in Palmer Park, Maryland. His father worked as a supermarket night manager, while his mother was a nurse. (Biography)

Boxing wasn’t initially the obvious path for him.

Then, at around 14 years old, Leonard was introduced to boxing at the Palmer Park Community Center by his older brother Roger.

And something changed.

He became obsessed with learning the craft.

🗣️ “For some reason, I wanted it so bad. I felt it in me, and I had to keep going.” — Sugar Ray Leonard (Biography)

The quiet teenager began developing into something special.

His coaches Dave Jacobs and Janks Morton helped shape his technique, discipline and ring intelligence.

And Leonard wasn’t just winning.

HE WAS LEARNING.

He won three National Golden Gloves titles, two AAU championships and the 1975 Pan American Games gold medal. (Biography)

Then came Montreal.

1976.

The Olympic Games.

Leonard entered the tournament as one of America’s brightest young boxing talents.

And he didn’t simply win gold.

He won all six of his Olympic bouts by 5–0 decisions, including the final against Cuba’s powerful Andrés Aldama. (USOPM)

But the most interesting part came after the victory.

Leonard had achieved the dream.

And he thought he was finished.

Standing with an Olympic gold medal around his neck, he announced:

🗣️ “I’m finished. I’ve fought my last fight. My journey has ended. My dream is fulfilled. Now I want to go to school.” — Sugar Ray Leonard (USOPM)

Think about that.

At 20 years old, Leonard had just conquered the amateur boxing world…

and he was planning to walk away.

He wanted to attend the University of Maryland.

But life had other plans.

His father’s illness and his mother’s health problems created financial pressure for the family. Professional boxing suddenly offered Leonard an opportunity to help support them. (Sugar Ray Leonard Foundation)

So the Olympic champion who had planned to leave boxing…

TURNED PROFESSIONAL IN 1977.

And that’s where the story really begins.

The world knew him as an Olympic gold medalist.

But professional boxing was about to discover something else:

SPEED.

INTELLIGENCE.

CHARISMA.

And a style that would eventually make him one of the defining fighters of his generation.

He didn’t enter professional boxing as a finished legend.

He entered as a young Olympic champion with something to prove.

And somewhere along the way…

RAY CHARLES LEONARD BECAME SUGAR RAY. 🥊🍯

text:
PUNK OF THE DAY #7: Ian MacKaye
He turned down $millions to keep a $5 promise.

Ian MacKaye was a teenager in Washington D.C. when he started Minor Threat in 1980. They played hardcore, punk stripped to its fastest and angriest form. One of their songs was called "Straight Edge." Under a minute long. MacKaye was singing about his own choice: no drinking, no drugs. He had no idea he was naming a movement. Kids around the world started marking X's on their hands and building their lives around that one song.

When Minor Threat broke up in 1983, MacKaye started Fugazi. And Fugazi ran on rules the music business couldn't comprehend. Most shows cost $5, for 16 years. They turned down every major label offer, and the offers were enormous. They barely sold merch. They booked their own tours and ran their own sound. If the crowd got violent, MacKaye stopped the song mid-chord, refunded the offenders, and had them thrown out.

He also ran Dischord Records, the label he co-founded as a teenager with $600 from gigging, pressing a thousand singles by hand. Every record stayed in print. Every record stayed cheap.

The industry called it bad business. He called it the whole point.
Privacy is punk. 🖤

text:
About a #cutlassfish found directly in front of the mega city #NewYork.

The cutlassfish #Trichiurus #lepturus (#Trichiuridae, #Percomorphaceae, #Acanthopterygii) is considered widely distributed across tropical and temperate seas; however, more recent data suggest it is actually a #speciescomplex. Although these fish are known to occur in coastal waters, their common presence in urban areas like #JamaicaBay, New York, was not a given. In a Zootaxa note, R. J. Thoni et al. (2026) documented the species' occurrence in this well-known bay, which borders the New York City boroughs of #Brooklyn and #Queens.

Like all members of the #Trichiuridae, Trichiurus lepturus is characterized by the apparent absence of a #caudalfin; instead, the body terminates in a lance-shaped tip. The species is #predatory, a trait clearly evidenced by its long fangs. The fish prefer to descend to depths up to 200 to 300 meters, but can even be found at 600 meters. #Eggs are released into the water column to drift freely. #Cannibalism by adults on juveniles of the same species has been documented.
#Taxonomically, recent studies indicate that Trichiurus lepturus actually comprises multiple species.

Traditional taxonomists consider T. lepturus to be distributed across the #Atlantic (Atlantic cutlassfish), the Eastern #Pacific (Pacific cutlassfish), the Northwest Pacific (Japanese cutlassfish), and the #IndoPacific. Atlantic populations are assigned to the species T. lepturus, whereas fish from the Northwest Pacific differ in meristic and morphometric characteristics; consequently, some researchers use the name Trichiurus #japonicus for the latter. Eastern Pacific populations are often classified as Trichiurus #nitens due to similar distinguishing features. The population of the eastern Atlantic has not yet been described as a distinct species. However, the IUCN recognizes it as such, a classification based primarily on genetic comparisons.

The #ecology of T. lepturus regarding its local ecology, and habitat use, for example in strongly urbanized water habitats, ist still poorly known. Consequently, the publication by R. J. Thoni et al. (2026) focuses on documenting the species' habitat with ecological precision. This is of scientific interest for several reasons. It provides ichthyologists with information regarding the potential migratory movements of this fish species. Furthermore, the ecological setting right off New York offers insights into the species' #tolerance for heavily urbanized #marineecosystems. Additionally, the findings shed general light on the ecological conditions prevailing in Jamaica Bay, situated at the heart of the global metropolis of New York. Until now, T. lepturus was considered very #rare or poorly documented in this region; the authors have now made a significant contribution to addressing this gap.

Excerpt-Chapter 6: Mandatory Palestine, 1927

Gazing into the Mediterranean horizon, Alexandra sought her escape. She had spent a healthy part of the last six weeks frolicking the salty seas—from the beaches of the Portuguese Algarve to those of the Greek Islands—exercising a type of Polynesian ocean worship she had sampled in Hawaii. The waves had been middling, but time in the sun had left her skin nicely bronzed. Haifa provided ideal conditions for bodysurfing. The ankle waders found interest in her antics. Some offered applause, while others gawked as if she were a rumbustious sea creature that kept washing ashore.
--There was one dogged frowner: a thickset woman with golden curls spilling out of her bathing cap, who, if raised in Japan, would have been trained in the art of the Sumo. Now she stood waiting with two police officers, pointing.
--Alexandra was unsure of her offense, awash in a strange land and knowing few of its rules. Her Jantzen swimsuit clung to her lithe frame modestly. Perhaps it struck blasphemously to display wet hair in the ancient Holy Land. She jumped bashful waves that broke close to shore and ducked under the churning lather of those so forceful they collapsed under their weight out to sea. Having the patience to corral the ideal wave proved key, and likely her only chance, short of swimming for Cyprus, to avoid arrest.

text:
Consensus treats private markets access as the ultimate status symbol. Today, access is commoditized. Anyone can buy an alts fund.

The real bottleneck is governance.

Institutional survey data shows alternatives now average 36% of endowment and foundation portfolios, eclipsing public U.S. equities at 27%.

Meanwhile, committee bandwidth and internal staff are completely flat.

Nonprofit boards and family offices do not have an asset allocation problem. They have an operational plumbing problem:

1.) Unfunded capital calls colliding with mandatory 5% annual spending policies.

2.) The denominator effect artificially inflating alts weights during public drawdowns.

3.) Volunteer trustees with 3-year term limits panicking over standard private equity J-curves.

4.) Managing aggregate portfolio risk when a third of the assets report on a 90-day lag.

Writing the commitment check is easy. Managing liquidity, capital calls, and board alignment for the next 10 years is the real work.

Before adding more illiquidity, boards must ask: do we have the governance capacity to handle what we already own?
